3. Empirical Strategy 3.1 Two-Way Fixed Effects Estimators We implement a staggered difference-in-differences estimator with two-way fixed effects, taking advantage of recent advances in econometric methods that account for heterogeneity in treatment effects across cohorts and locations. We focus specifically on changes in the conditional mean of the number of startups, using a Poisson model. The typical two-way fixed effect model estimates, for each census tract 𝑖 at time 𝑡, an equation of the following form: 𝑌𝑖𝑡= 𝛽× 𝐷𝑖𝑡+ 𝛾𝑖+ 𝜆𝑡+ 𝜖𝑖𝑡 where 𝑌𝑖𝑡 represents the number of startups, 𝛾𝑖 is a tract fixed effect, 𝜆𝑡 a year fixed effect, 𝐷𝑖𝑡 is a binary treatment representing the entry of a third place into a tract, and 𝜖𝑖𝑡 is a random error.

The coefficient of interest is 𝛽, representing the average proportional increase in the number of firms between treated and non-treated neighborhoods. We extend this model by building on Wooldridge (2021) and other work that seeks to account for treatment heterogeneity and avoid “prohibited” comparisons that may create biased estimates (de Chaisemartin and d’Haultfoeuille 2020; Callaway and Sant’Anna 2021). Similar to Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), the Wooldridge approach accounts for this issue by incorporating cohort and time-specific coefficients. Specifically, in each year 𝑡, for each census tract 𝑖 that was first treated on year 𝜏, we implement the regression, 𝑌𝑖𝑡= 𝛽𝑡𝜏× 𝑔𝑖𝜏× 𝜆𝑡+ 𝛾𝑖+ 𝜆𝑡+ 𝜖𝑖𝑡 where 𝑔𝑖𝜏 is an indicator representing the individual year in which tract 𝑖 was treated (and 0 if it is never treated), and 𝛽𝑡𝜏 the individual coefficients for each treatment cohort and year. We report the average marginal effects (as Poisson elasticities) for our main estimate. Standard errors are clustered at the county level.

One disadvantage of implementing this extended two-way fixed effects model is that it requires including a fully interacted set of indicators by treatment cohort, which removes all 14 variation in the pre-period, and hence does not allow estimating pre-trends in the level of entrepreneurship before the introduction of Starbucks into a neighborhood. Therefore, we complement the Wooldridge estimator with event study estimates using the approach by Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021). This approach uses linear regression and a doubly-robust control approach to account for selection into treatment. When we run this model, we prefer using the number of new firms as the dependent variable, instead of a transformation such as the logarithm or the inverse hyperbolic sine, given recent concerns over the lack of validity of these transformations around zero (Cohn et al, 2022).

For the rejected Starbucks analysis, we focus on a comparison between treated and nevertreated tracts, since the tracts that reject a Starbucks are by definition never treated. For the other analyses, we compare treated tracts to not-yet-treated tracts. Focusing on not-yet-treated neighborhoods in these cases allows us to partially account for selection issues. Given the possibility that neighborhoods that are good candidates for a coffee shop are different from others in ways that are unobservable to us, we see the locations used as controls in the not-yettreated specification as also appealing to Starbucks, but simply receiving the café later.

4. Results 4.1 Event Study Estimates Our first set of results, in Figure 2, presents event studies estimating, for each neighborhood, the difference in the number of new firms before and after the opening of the first Starbucks (coefficients are reported in the Appendix).

Panel A uses the tracts with a rejected Starbucks as controls. There are no pre-trends in the number of startups before Starbucks. After the entry of Starbucks, the coefficient shows minimal effect at year 0, and then increases and becomes positive and significant after year 2.

Panel B considers the number of startups after the opening of Magic Johnson Starbucks coffee shops. The effect is substantially larger than that of a typical Starbucks. The number of startups increases slightly in year 0, and plateaus at a higher level after two years from opening.

The increase is significantly larger than the other analyses. This difference is consistent with Magic Johnson’s thesis that these neighborhoods were severely lacking local establishments.

Panel C expands our analysis to all census tracts without coffee shops. The estimates have more precise standard errors than those in Panel A. The point estimate is slightly higher, 15 though within the same confidence interval. The plot shows flat pre-trends before the introduction of a Starbucks, and an increase over time after. By year 7, the neighborhood is producing 3.9 additional startups, relative to a sample mean of 21 startups per year.

Across these analyses, the results document a positive increase in entrepreneurship for neighborhoods where a Starbucks opens, and no previous trend. In each of the panels, the effect takes several years to emerge. The gradual increase of the effect provides comfort against the potential confounding role of other businesses opening contemporaneously with Starbucks as part of broader real estate development efforts. For example, when a shopping mall opens, a Starbucks may open at the same time as other local stores. However, if this type of bias existed, then we should have seen differences in registrations for such businesses at year 0 or even year - 1, before the establishment opened.

4.2 Average Increase in Neighborhood Entrepreneurship We next consider the average effect of receiving a new Starbucks on neighborhood entrepreneurship. Moving beyond event studies allows us to use count data regressions through Poisson specifications rather than linear models. Estimating both Poisson and linear models also allows us to evaluate the extent to which some outlier census tracts may be driving our results.

Table 3 column 1 reports a Poisson regression with rejected Starbucks. For this column, we use the traditional Poisson two-way fixed effects estimator to allow us to incorporate two treatments simultaneously: our main treatment—the opening of a Starbucks—and a placebo treatment which is equal to 1 when the rejected Starbucks was expected to open and 0 otherwise.

The coefficient for actual Starbucks entry is positive and significant with 0.09, while the one for the rejected Starbucks is noisy with a negative value. While the entry of an actual Starbucks predicts more entrepreneurship, the mere expectation of entry does not.

Column 2 reports the extended Poisson two-way fixed effects. Here, and in all subsequent columns, we focus on the average change in startups during the first seven years. The coefficient is 0.112 and significant at the 1% level, which suggests an 11.8% increase in the number of new firms registered each year. Column 3 is the linear estimate. The coefficient estimates an additional 5.74 firms per tract, implying an increase of a 18% increase in new firms, relative to the mean.

16 Columns 4 and 5 exhibit estimates of the increase in startups following of the opening of a Magic Johnson Starbucks. As in the event study, the effect is much larger for the Magic Johnson cafés. We estimate an increase of 30% to 36% on average in the first seven years, or 4.3 to 5.9 firms, relative to the mean number of startups per tract, in this sample.

Columns 6 and 7 study all tracts without coffee shops. The effects are more precise. The estimate for our linear specification represents an increase of 13.6%, more than twice as large as the Poisson model (5.5%), suggesting that, while effects are positive on average, there are some outlier tracts.

Together, these results document an economically important increase in new business formation in neighborhoods where a Starbucks coffee shop opens. The next sections focus on understanding whether the underlying mechanism at play is networks or signaling.

4.3 Neighborhoods with Prior Coffee Shops and with Non-Starbucks Coffee Shops In Tables 4 and 5, we begin to investigate whether a Starbucks café creates a new space for socializing, which in turn promotes local entrepreneurship.

Table 4 reports the change in entrepreneurship when Starbucks enters a neighborhood that already has cafés and when cafés other than Starbucks enter a neighborhood. We report both average effects and year-by-year effects. Column 1 presents coefficients for the effect of opening a Starbucks among neighborhoods with no prior cafés—i.e., the same treatment as in the prior section. Column 2 considers neighborhoods with prior cafés. The differences are stark. Starbucks does not increase neighborhood entrepreneurship among neighborhoods that already had coffee shops. The difference between the two columns is consistent with the benefit of Starbucks being dependent on the local incidence of institutions and locals’ ability to form and sustain social networks. By and large, the mode of entry for Starbucks is similar for the neighborhoods in either column, as are their demographic characteristics (see Table 2). However, the effect of Starbucks is different depending on whether local residents already have other locations that serve as substitute establishments to socialize. If the Starbucks effect were due to signaling, we would not expect the presence of other coffee shops to matter.

Column 3 exhibits estimates for the change in new startups following the opening of a coffee shop that is not a Starbucks, among neighborhoods with no prior cafés. Recall that during this period Starbucks was distinctively focused on creating a third-place experience for 17 neighborhoods, while most other competing brands were not. Therefore, while the entry of a coffee shop may still create the opportunity for social interaction, its effect should be smaller, and potentially zero. Indeed, we observe only a small and fleeting effect for coffee shops that are not Starbucks.

It is useful to clarify the relationship between column 2 and column 3, since, because of differences in their samples, they are not the inverse of each other. Column 2 focuses on neighborhoods with more than one coffee shop. The average number of coffee shops in a tract that Starbucks enters in this sample is 2.5, and 25% of tracts have 3 or more. Column 3 focuses on tracts with no coffee shops, with treated tracts receiving their first one. The effect in both columns is small or zero, which means that Starbucks has little effect when there are several other potential third places (2.5 coffee shops on average), and that adding a single coffee shop that may or may not serve as a third place to a neighborhood with no coffee shops is not enough.

In Table 5, we compare the effect of Starbucks cafés to that of other companies that operate on different models. The first column considers Dunkin’ Donuts, the largest U.S. coffee chains brand in the nation that, in contrast to Starbucks, does not expressly seek to create a third-place experience. Dunkin’ sells coffee at sit-down coffee shops, but many of its stores do not offer seating, and those that do lack the lighting, amenities, and comfort level to encourage long stays.

Figure 4 makes evident how different Dunkin’ and Starbucks are. Using data from SafeGraph, a company offering geolocated data and visit information for U.S. points of interest, we estimate the average number of hours that visitors remained in each location for Dunkin’ and Starbucks, excluding devices that remained in the shop longer than 4 hours, as those are likely owned by employees. As the figure shows, people spend far more time at Starbucks than Dunkin’ coffee shops. These differences motivate our empirical comparison. While Dunkin’ also selects promising neighborhoods, they do not offer a third place. If a network mechanism is driving the result, then the effect of the opening of a Dunkin’ Donuts should be close to zero.

The first column of Table 5 shows that this is the case. In column 2, we examine the effect of a different coffee chain, Caribou Coffee. Caribou offers a third place concept similar to Starbucks’, mostly in Minnesota and Wisconsin. Figure 5 shows that the distribution of visit length across these two chains is similar. Table 5 shows that the estimated effect of the opening of a Caribou Coffee location is positive and significant, with a point estimate close to that of Starbucks’ (2.3 for Caribou vs 2.7 for Starbucks). Altogether, 18 these results suggest that our estimated increase in neighborhood entrepreneurship following the entry of coffee shops is driven by the extent to which this coffee shop creates space that allow people to form and sustain their social networks.

4.4 Additional Evidence for Social Networks Mechanisms Using Geolocated Data In this section, we investigate heterogeneity across some features of Starbucks cafés to ask whether those Starbucks cafés that are set up to create more social interaction produce larger effects. To do so, we use the 2019 monthly patterns data from SafeGraph. These data track the number of visitors from census block groups to specific point-of-interests, such as cafés, as long as they at least see four visitors in a month. We develop two measures: the number of visitors in 2019 (adjusted for differences in how well SafeGraph covers each state), and the size of the lot (in square meters) in which each Starbucks is located, which is estimated using satellite images.

These two measures are imperfect proxies for the volume of social interactions produced by a given café, but each offers distinct advantages. The number of visitors a café receives over the course of a year directly reflects the potential to form social networks. However, this measure runs the risk of bias because, while our data are for 2019, the effects we measure is after Starbucks openings that occurred years earlier. It is possible that the high levels of socialization we observe in each café may be the result of previous success in the neighborhood brought along by earlier entrepreneurship.

The size of the lot, in contrast, is less likely to be biased, because the specific lot size does not typically change over time in most Starbucks locations. However, the size of a Starbucks is a less direct measure of the opportunity to form social networks than actual visits. In addition, because lots can be shared with other establishments (e.g., with hotels), the analysis must focus only on the subsample of lots that can be measured independently in SafeGraph.13 In spite of these differences, the measures are highly correlated, as shown in Appendix Figure A6.

Panel A of Figure 3 studies visitor foot traffic. We split the locations by the estimated visits received during 2019 into quartiles and run a Poisson regression. We use a traditional two-way fixed effects estimator because it allows us to consider all treatments simultaneously and use the 13 In the SafeGraph dataset, the variable is polygon_class. Consistent with a network story, a higher level of traffic matters for our effects. Starbucks cafés with below-median traffic in 2019 have about a third of the effect as those with above-median traffic.

We next study establishment size. We divide Starbucks locations into four natural groups. Those that are very small (less than 50 m2) and almost always exist in a physical structure with other shops (e.g., in malls, airports, or Target stores), small locations (between 50 and 200 m2), medium locations (between 200 and 500 m2), large locations (over 500 m2). The results in Panel B show an increasing relationship between the square footage of a Starbucks and new firm formation. The null effect on small locations in malls also suggests that the co-opening of a Starbucks together with other establishments (e.g., other stores in a mall) is not a main determinant of our effect.

In short, it is precisely those establishments that offer the features conducive to an effective third place, such as opportunities for a high level of local interaction and the open space to do so, paired with a large number of visitors, for which we see large increases in neighborhood entrepreneurship following their opening.

4.5 Differences in Startup Industry We provide further evidence on the mechanism by studying the industry of the startups formed. As Magic Johnson noted, Starbucks could serve as “the anchor to attract other businesses” to a neighborhood. In this case, the presence of Starbucks would serve as a catalyst for the local and retail economy. If so, then the benefits we document would be economically important, but less consistent with a networks mechanism and instead about signaling that changes the perceived value of the location to firms and the flow of customers to neighboring retail businesses (demand pooling).14 If this is the case, then we would expect the Starbucks benefits to be highly localized in retail sectors.

Other agglomeration effects are theoretically possible (e.g., pooling of suppliers or workforce), but we consider those to be not of first order at the neighborhood level.

4.6. The Effect of Starbucks on Nearby Neighborhoods We consider a different type of evidence of a network effect. So far, we have studied the impact of Starbucks on the number of new startups in the census tract where that café opens. But visitors to a Starbucks are also likely to be from other nearby tracts, creating geographically localized spillovers. It is well established that such proximity effects, when occurring through networks and in-person interaction, dissipate quickly with distance. This pattern also holds for entrepreneurship. For example, when considering Midtown Manhattan, Rosenthal and Strange (2005) and Arzaghi and Henderson (2008) show that these networking benefits are non-existent above a distance of one mile. Manhattan, however, is more urban than anywhere else in the U.S.

After examining the Bay Area, Kerr and Kominers (2015) show that citations between patents 21 fall quickly beyond a 15-minute drive. Across the whole U.S., Rosenthal and Strange (2003) see proximity benefits dissipate with 10 miles. In contrast, local effects on entrepreneurship that are not knowledge-based, such as the ability to access employment and capital, dissipate more slowly (for example, according to the Census Bureau, the average commute time in New York is 35 minutes). If the Starbucks effect is due to networks, rather than signaling, then we would expect to see geographic spillovers that decrease rapidly with distance.

Table 7 exhibits changes in neighborhood entrepreneurship for census tracts that also did not have coffee shops but had a Starbucks open in a nearby tract, based on the distance between the tracts’ centroids (geographic center). To avoid double-counting treatments, as in the case where a neighborhood has multiple Starbucks open nearby over time, we limit our analysis to the first Starbucks that opens within 10 km from the tract, so that each tract can be treated by a neighbor opening only once. We also limit this analysis to neighborhoods that never received a Starbucks themselves.

Ideally, we would want to consider distances below 1 km. However, the distance between the centroid of most neighboring tracts is higher than that. Because there are few neighboring centroids less than 1 km apart, estimates based on that threshold are too noisy (column 1).

Columns 2 through 4 exhibit the results for neighborhoods that have a Starbucks opening within 1-2 km, 2-5 km, and 5-10 km. We observe a positive effect of Starbucks opening on these nearby neighborhoods. This effect is smaller in magnitude, and it decays with distance, as expected. Our starting point is a distinction in the entrepreneurship literature between two types of firms. One, the majority of firms, is those small businesses that, even if important for neighborhoods or their owners, tend to remain small and are unlikely to create significant employment or productivity growth. The other has been called high-growth (Guzman and Stern 2020), innovation-driven (Botello et al. 2023), or transformational entrepreneurship (Schoar 2010), and represents those firms that introduce innovative ideas into the market, create traded goods across regions, and have outsize outcomes that drive economic growth.17 Recent work has shown that a firm’s potential for high growth is partly predictable from its business registration information. For example, firms that are likely to grow will register as Delaware corporations, since Delaware’s jurisdiction and legal form allow complex financing contracts and appropriate governance (Guzman and Stern, 2020). In this section, we take advantage of these registration characteristics to evaluate whether Starbucks cafés contribute to high-growth entrepreneurship.

23 4.8 Other Types of Third Places As a final analysis, we expand our approach to consider the coffee shop effect relative to that of other potential social establishments. Table 9 has the same format as Table 3 but considers the opening of two other types of food establishments, bars and restaurants. We do not see an impact of bars on local entrepreneurship. This effect is different from the historical work in Andrews (2019), which was based on entrepreneurship during Prohibition. We speculate that one possibility is that the social structure of the U.S.—and the use of third places—has changed in a few ways between the two periods. In particular, whereas historically bars in the U.S. used to be venues for highly-organized social activity where multiple social movements and civil rights actions began, today those activities may be less common in U.S. bars relative to purely social drink. In this respect, they may lack the continued social significance that, say, British pubs appear to maintain. The effect of restaurants, in contrast, is positive. This finding is also consistent with a network benefit mechanism, as sharing meals over business activities is a common practice.

5. Conclusion Networks are important for economic activity, including entrepreneurship. Yet, the ability to form networks is mediated by space. We present evidence that the introduction of a new Starbucks café, intended to create a “third place” for community interaction, increased entrepreneurship in U.S. neighborhoods.

The effects are consistent with a network mechanism. They are limited to neighborhoods without prior coffee shops, and do not occur with other large coffee chains that do not offer a third-place experience. The effects are larger for Starbucks with more visits and with a higher square footage. They decrease quickly with distance. In contrast, we do not observe evidence that they are consistent with a signaling mechanism.

It is important to note that our estimates incorporate the full “causal pathway” of the impact of Starbucks on local activity—they estimate the change in startup formation after a Starbucks opens. However, there are several reasonable methods through which new third spaces promote networks and subsequent entrepreneurship. For example, a Starbucks café can both influence the behavior of current residents and attract new ones to the neighborhood, simultaneously strengthening and diversifying its social fabric. These interactions can promote entrepreneurship 24 directly, but also increase the local incidence of supporting organizations such as banks, credit unions, and community development organizations. These institutions, in turn, may additionally evaluate prospective loans differently based on the perceived evolution of the neighborhood. The impact of these spaces on artistic activities, as explored by Jeong (2023), further illustrates their multifaceted role. Therefore, a clear understanding of how space shapes local business activity, including its potential to improve underserved neighborhoods, requires far more investigation.

Appendix B. Industry Tagging Algorithm This section is based on the methodology developed by Engelberg et al. (2024), which we quote as below: “Our firm registration data does not include industry codes. To assign firms to industries we develop an industry tagging algorithm based on the words in firm names. Our approach proceeds in three steps.

“First, we consider all firms with a primary NAICS code assigned in a large firm dataset provided by Infogroup USA.1 We count the number of times a word appears in firm names for each NAICS two-digit industry. Second, we define word quotient as the number of times a word appears in an industry divided by the number of firms in an industry - we scale the word frequency to avoid industries with many firms dominating the classification. For example, words like ‘mining’ or ‘biotechnology’ are highly relevant to industries with relatively few firms. Third, we assign each word to an industry if (i) it has the highest word quotient and (ii) the quotient is at least twice as high as the next highest one (quotient ratio ≥2). Firms are then linked to industries if the words in their names are assigned to a specific industry.

“Words with the highest quotient ratio (i.e., those that are most closely associated with specific industries), include ‘wharehousing’(NAICS 49), ‘mining’ and ‘quarry’ (NAICS 21), and ‘winery’ and ‘panaderia’ (NAICS 31).

The median value of the quotient ratio is 8.5. Words around this value include ‘attorneys’ (NAICS 52), ‘volkswagen’ (NAICS 44), ‘key’ (NAICS 56), ‘powerwashing’ (NAICS 23), ‘abstract’ (NAICS 54), and ‘cooling’ (NAICS 23).

“In total, we have 5,507 words which tag about 54.6% of companies in our regression sample. We exclude N55 and N99. Within these tagged companies, 81% are assigned to exactly one industry, 17.2% to two, and 1.8% to three or more. Many of the companies tagged in two industries are those that span multiple sectors, such as ‘Commercial Properties Magazine, Inc’, which is tagged as NAICS 51 (Information) and 53 (Real Estate), or ‘Stella Kids Yoga’ which is tagged as NAICS 61 (Educational Services) and 62 (Health Care and Social Assistance).

“In our main analysis, we assign a firm an industry as long as it is tagged to that industry, i.e., a firm can be tagged to multiple industries. In untabulated results, our findings are robust to assigning a firm an industry when the firm is tagged to only one industry.”

1Infogroup USA dataset includes firms covering the majority of the U.S. economy (similar to Dunn & Bradstreet).

Our research utilises extensive microdata in combination with telephone interviews with over 200 start-up companies in Stockholm, Sweden. Our ﬁndings indicate that access to third places has a signiﬁcant impact on the number of new high-tech start-ups (both by entrepreneur place of residence and work) in their vicinity. This suggests that third places play a demonstrable role in innovation and economic growth.

KEYWORDS third places; entrepreneurship; innovation; high-tech start-ups; start-up ecosystems JEL L26, R12, R23 HISTORY Received 22 August 2022; in revised form 14 December 2023 1. INTRODUCTION Cities are typically perceived as serving two roles. On one hand, they are viewed as centres of economic activity, that is, as places for employment, innovation and productivity (Jacobs, 1969; Lucas, 1988). This stems from their increased density and diversity, their clusters of ﬁrms, their human capital, the economic assets they bring together, and their ability to create robust innovation and start-up ecosystems. On the other hand, cities are also centres of consumption (Glaeser et al., 2001) that provide access to amenities such as bars, restaurants, gallery spaces, cafés, nightclubs, theatres, concert halls and ﬁtness/health centres such as yoga, gyms and dance studios (Clark et al., 2002; Lloyd & Clark, 2001; Silver et al., 2010, 2011).

These two dimensions of city life come together through a unique set of organisations that sociologists have dubbed ‘third places’ – places where people come together that are neither home nor work but blend elements of both (Oldenburg, 1989; Oldenburg & Brissett, 1982). Third places work to connect the productivity and consumption sides of cities, enabling people not only to enjoy each other’s company but also to share information and knowledge and to build networks and business relationships. As such they serve as critical components of the connective ﬁbre crucial to the innovative capacities of cities. Saxenian (1994) highlighted the importance of such CONTACT Kevin Credit Kevin.credit@mu.ie aNational Centre for Geocomputation, Maynooth University, Maynooth, Ireland bSOFI, Stockholm University, Stockholm, Sweden cJönköping International Business School, Jönköping, Sweden dRotman School of Management and School of Cities, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada spaces to the face-to-face social interactions that enable knowledge spillovers. She identiﬁed the role played by the Wagon Wheel, a bar in Silicon Valley, where engineers and entrepreneurs from different companies would connect after working hours, dubbing it the ‘Fountainhead of the Semiconductor Industry’. Recent research ﬁnds that accessibility to bars, restaurants, hotels and coffee shops facilitates social interactions that generate knowledge spillovers and promote innovation (Roche, 2020). Furthermore, urban economists and economic geographers have long noted a connection between urbanisation economies and entrepreneurship (Acs et al., 2011; Audretsch et al., 2015; Tavassoli et al., 2021). However, when it comes to the mechanisms of the relationship, research has often referred to the black box of knowledge spillovers. A stream of studies has sought to unpack the various components or dimensions of innovation (Roche, 2020), or start-up ecosystems (Kenney & Florida, 2000; Saxenian, 1994). While the role of third places in such contexts has been suggested in the qualitative literature, additional empirical research is needed to identify more precisely the role played by such third places in entrepreneurship and innovation dynamics (Fang et al., 2022).

Our research contributes to this literature by analysing more closely the role of third places – particularly bars, restaurants and cafés – in promoting the formation of entrepreneurial high-tech start-ups in cities. The central Supplemental data for this article can be accessed online at https://doi.org/10.1080/00343404.2023.2297083 © 2024 Regional Studies Association 2226 Kevin Credit et al.

question we pose is to what degree does access to third places increase the likelihood of high-tech start-ups. The intuition behind this question is twofold: (1) if people live or work close to places with higher accessibility to third places, they should be more likely to meet other people and exchange knowledge and ideas. The importance of face-to-face interaction for knowledge transfer – even in highly digitalised environments and industries – has been demonstrated in the literature for some time (Battiston et al., 2020; Cowgill et al., 2009; Roche et al., 2022). However, we are also interested in (2) the less examined role that third places play in the actual planning of the start-up itself, as coffee shops, bars and restaurants can function as a kind of ‘quasi’-ofﬁce for early stage startups. In either case, the link between third places and startups is particularly relevant today as cities strategise for downtown recovery stemming from the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, and the shift to remote work, which have left many downtowns with less activity than before the pandemic.

To examine more closely the role of third places in start-up formation, our research focuses on the municipality of Stockholm, which provides a useful case study for this question as it ranks as one of the world’s leading start-up ecosystems. The Stockholm labour market is home to approximately one-fourth of the country’s population, but approximately 35% of all engineers, 46% of all computer scientists (Mellander & Florida, 2007) and 76% of all venture capital investments, 90% of which went to ﬁrms located in the city centre (Adler et al., 2019). Stockholm is home to many successful start-ups, such as Spotify, Skype, Minecraft and Candy Crush. It is also home to great universities, such as Stockholm University, Karolinska Institute, The Royal Institute of Technology and Stockholm School of Economics. It is a centre for urban amenities, teaming with third places of wide appeal.

Our analysis includes a mix of microdata and phone survey data to examine the connection between third places and start-ups. We ﬁrst map everyone who started a high-tech ﬁrm in Stockholm between 2010 and 2019.

We identify both their place of residence and their place of work (within 250 m2 grid cells) the year before the actual launch of the new ﬁrm. We then analyse the relationship between spatial access to third places and the number of start-ups while controlling for several grid characteristics which can relate to entrepreneurship. All estimations include neighbourhood ﬁxed effects to account for the heterogeneity of neighbourhoods in Stockholm. In addition, we conducted a telephone survey of over 200 entrepreneurs in Stockholm in October 2020 to better understand their perceptions regarding the role of third places in fostering their business ideas and start-ups.

Our key ﬁndings conﬁrm that third places play a role in high-tech business formation. Indeed, access (proximity) to third places is signiﬁcantly associated with new business creation across all model speciﬁcations, with a slightly larger impact based on the entrepreneur’s place of residence than place of work (although both are signiﬁcant). At the same time, 24% of surveyed entrepreneurs indicated REGIONAL STUDIES that they even planned the formation of their ﬁrm primarily in third places such as restaurants and bars, compared with 25% at home and 40% at the ofﬁce. In addition, 20% of entrepreneurs indicated in an open-ended response that third places were ‘very important’ to the early stages of the start-up to meet and discuss issues related to the business, compared with 21% in the ofﬁce and 15% online.

Taken together, these ﬁndings provide suggestive evidence of the importance of third places in entrepreneurship, particularly for planning in the early stages of ﬁrm formation.

We believe our results can be generalised beyond the context of Stockholm to other large cities and urbanised areas with high densities of third places. The remainder of this paper is organised as follows.

The next section provides a deeper overview of the relevant theoretical framework. We then turn to our data, identiﬁ- cation strategy and empirical methods. We include a section where we descriptively discuss the location of third places as well as start-ups in Stockholm. Following that, we present and analyse the key results from the regression analyses and the phone survey we conducted. The last section discusses these results and their salience relative to prior research and ongoing studies about cities, amenities and innovation.

2. THIRD PLACES, KNOWLEDGE-SHARING AND ENTREPRENEURSHIP Our research probes the role of third places not just as spaces of consumption but in spurring the knowledge sharing that motivates innovation, and entrepreneurship.

Innovation and entrepreneurship in cities are usually seen as the products of density, diversity, and the hard economic or technological assets of cities such as hightech ﬁrms, highly educated human capital, university research and venture capitalists. More recent research points to the role of face-to-face interaction and so-called ‘buzz’ in accelerating the ﬂow of knowledge exchange and information in cities (Asheim et al., 2007; Currid & Williams, 2010; Storper & Venables, 2004).

Research on entrepreneurship dates back to Schumpeter (1934) whose work very much focused on the entrepreneur and their abilities to perceive new technological and economic emerging out of innovation. A huge literature builds on these basic insights on the role of innovation and entrepreneurship in driving economic development (Aghion & Howitt, 1990; Griliches, 1957; Grossman & Helpman, 1991; Nelson & Winter, 1982).

Jacobs (1969) long ago argued that innovation and economic development are processes that occur just as products of innovative large and small ﬁrms. Cities function to attract a diverse set of actors, talented and skilled people who drive economic development. Lucas (1988) formalised Jacobs’ ideas with the construct of ‘human capital externalities’ which serves as the fundamental mechanism of innovation and economic development. The connection between human capital and economic growth has been widely documented in research, at both the national (Barro, 1991) and regional levels (Berry & Glaeser, 2005; Florida, 2002b; Glaeser, 2000; Rauch, 1993). Other research has documented the link between why skilled cities grow faster than low-skilled cities due to higher levels of productivity (Glaeser & Saiz, 2003; Rauch, 1993).

Urban economists and geographers have also long identiﬁed that such innovation and entrepreneurship is not just the province of ﬁrms per se but occurs in geographical clusters (Acs et al., 2002; Anselin et al., 1997; Jaffe et al., 1993). A large and growing body of studies identiﬁes the mechanism driving innovation and entrepreneurship in such clusters to be knowledge spillovers (Anselin et al., 1997; Audretsch & Feldman, 2004; Jaffe et al., 1993). Related research documents the geographical proximity for interactive learning and innovation (Balland et al., 2015; Boschma, 2005; Fritsch & Kublina, 2018).

Storper and Venables (2004) break down face-to-face interaction into four main features that create ‘buzz’ in a place: (1) it is an efﬁcient technology for communication; (2) it helps solve incentive problems; (3) it facilitates both learning and socialisation; and (4) it provides psychological motivation. Buzz in cities makes people more productive and creates more cross-fertilisation between different sector networks, such as science and tech, creative and cultural industries, ﬁnance and business, and/or the power and inﬂuence sectors. Guiso and Schivardi (2011) ﬁnd that knowledge spillovers happen more efﬁ- ciently in areas with many entrepreneurs and thus the probability that individuals develop entrepreneurial skills is higher. Andersson and Larsson (2014) show that the presence of entrepreneurs in a neighbourhood inﬂuences the emergence of new entrepreneurs in the area, arguing that it is due to social interactions among people in the neighbourhood. Sorenson and Audia (2000) suggest that if an area is highly entrepreneurial, residents might be more motivated and have higher self-conﬁdence that they can also make it if they start their ﬁrm. Minniti (2005) argues that social interactions between established entrepreneurs and people who want to start their ﬁrms lower the uncertainties about the start-up process. These studies highlight the role of social interactions in motivating the knowledge spillovers which underpin innovation and start-up formation.

A growing body of research focuses on the consumption side of cities in the clustering of talent and in spurring increases in innovative and creative output. Glaeser and Saiz (2003) show that high-skill workers tend to cluster around consumption opportunities. Kolenda and Liu (2012) ﬁnd that advanced, fast-growing creative industries and their employees are more likely to locate in city cores.

Other research examines the role of amenities and ‘scenes’ in creative output (Clark, 2003). Silver et al. (2011) suggest that scenes and technology industry clusters are contextually joined together.

Our research builds on these contributions to focus on the role of third spaces such as bars, cafés, restaurants, galleries and music venues in fostering the knowledge spillovers that shape innovation entrepreneurship (Jacobs, 1961; Oldenburg, 1989). Their role is especially important to interaction and knowledge sharing in the creative Third places, the connective ﬁbre of cities and high-tech entrepreneurship 2227 industries (Currid, 2007; Storper & Venables, 2004).

Fang et al. (2022) ﬁnd that proximity to coffee shops is signiﬁcantly related to start-up formation. Furthermore, third places play a critical role in bridging the production and consumption functions of cities. Most research in urban economics and urban geography sees innovation and start-ups as outcomes of the production side of cities.

Third places are typically bundled with a set of amenities that form the consumption side of cities. But they also play a crucial role in mobilising face-to-face communication and social interaction which is central to knowledge spillovers (Landry, 2000). As their very name implies, third places are arenas that are neither work nor home per se, but support elements of both. We thus hypothesise that they play a key role in fostering social interaction and knowledge-sharing, which motivate innovation and startup formation. They are a critical element of the human connectivity that shapes innovation, entrepreneurship and economic development in cities.

3. DATA, IDENTIFICATION AND METHOD To get at these issues and questions, we use register geocoded data from Statistics Sweden. We ﬁrst identify those who started a new high-tech ﬁrm and the exact location of their workplace and their place of residence within 250 m2 grid cells during the period 2010–19. We can also calculate their geographical proximity to cafés and restaurants as a proxy of all types of third places in the municipality of Stockholm the year prior to the start-up. Our unit of analysis is the 250 m2 grid squares, which addresses the very localised nature of knowledge spillovers through social interactions (Arzaghi & Henderson, 2008). The dependent variable is therefore the number of ﬁrms started by individuals working and/or residing in each 250 m2 grid square. Following the prior literature, we expect that accessibility to meeting places increases the face-to-face interactions between individuals working (living) in the same square.

Our independent variable of interest, Third place Access, is created by calculating a spatial access score for each grid cell using the Access package (v.1.1.3) in PySAL (Saxon et al., 2021). The idea of the access score is to provide a more realistic measure of weighted spatial accessibility to a given type of amenity – based on the fact that accessibility decays with distance rather than being a hard cut-off at the arbitrary grid cell boundaries (Isard, 1960). Moreover, empirical literature has also shown that social interactions are very local (Andersson & Larsson, 2014; Arzaghi & Henderson, 2008). We therefore calculate the Euclidean distance from each grid cell i centroid to the 10 nearest grid cell centroids j that contain third places, discounted by a distance-decay factor (negative exponent) of 0.25.

Each decay-discounted ij link is multiplied by the number of associated third places at j; these weighted distances to nearby third places are then summed by grid cell origin (i) to provide an aggregate measure of high accessibility to nearby third places from each grid cell. In this way, we estimate how the number of new ﬁrms in time t + 1 depend on REGIONAL STUDIES 2228 Kevin Credit et al.

accessibility to third places in time t. Since all squares are of equal size, this variable becomes a density measure. Empirically, we should be aware of the issue of omitted variable bias. Economic activity and entrepreneurship might be simultaneously determined in speciﬁc areas of the city, for instance, in the city centre. These areas, in turn, may be also attracting people who are more entrepreneurial to begin with. There is a large literature, starting with Florida (2002b), arguing that more creative individuals are also more likely to be in areas characterised by more amenities. Following Roche (2020), we attempt to address this issue by including neighbourhood ﬁxed effects. This way we can hold the unobservable characteristics of a neighbourhood such as culture or access to different amenities constant. Neighbourhoods in our case are regional statistical areas (RegSO). Statistics Sweden introduced RegSO as a deﬁnition of neighbourhoods designed speciﬁcally to facilitate the statistical analyses of socio-economic segregation. RegSO is a good geographical unit for analysing neighbourhoods because it accounts for demographic conditions based on speciﬁc geographical borders, such as streets, waterways and railways, representing real neighbourhoods rather than arbitrary administrative areas.1 The identiﬁcation comes therefore from within the neighbourhoods. These calendar ﬁles, which functioned as a ‘telephone directory of the time’, contain detailed information about the inhabitants of Stockholm including the address where they lived and their occupation. While it was not compulsory for the individuals to register in the address calendar, we have about 16,500 individuals in the dataset, which corresponds to around 10–15% of the whole population of Stockholm at the time.

To deﬁne the cultural workers, we use the occupations mentioned in the codebooks. In many cases, the occupation is no longer available today, and in these cases, we have tried to match it to the occupation closest to today’s labour market. For example, a horse driver has been transferred into being a taxi driver. We deﬁne cultural workers as people working in a cultural (‘bohemian’) occupation, such as a musician, singer or dancer. Assuming that there is some path dependency in places which are considered as ‘creative’, we argue that the location of the cultural workers in 1882 should be correlated with where the third places are located today. Figure 1 also Third places, the connective ﬁbre of cities and high-tech entrepreneurship 2229 shows the parts of Stockholm in which they were living.

It is worth noting that the city of Stockholm was much smaller in the late 1800s. Therefore, the geographical extent of the city then would be considered the inner city of the region today – all of which are now highly expensive neighbourhoods with many third places. However, according to an analysis of distribution of population by occupation, the cultural workers were less segregated than other groups of the society such as individuals working for the royal court, nobility, ﬁshing and farming occupations, and university graduates. Moreover, a vast body of literature discusses the correlation between creative, third places and bohemian culture, suggesting that they thrive in similar environments – both historically and today (Currid-Halkett, 2009; Florida, 2002a; Florida & Mellander, 2009; Markusen & Schrock, 2006; Seigel, 1999).

While the inclusion of ﬁxed effects combined with the use of IVs helps with identiﬁcation issues, claiming causal effects is always cumbersome in the absence of exogenous variation in the identiﬁcation strategy. 4. ACCESSIBILITY TO THIRD PLACES Figure 1 shows the spatial distribution of third place access and entrepreneur locations across the Stockholm municipality. The top left panel shows the distribution of average yearly (2009–18) third place access scores (the independent variable of interest). The top right panel shows accessibility to the 1882 proportion of cultural class employment (the IV), while the remaining two panels show the average yearly (2009–18) number of high-tech4 entrepreneurs by workplace location (bottom right) and residence location (bottom left), the dependent variables of interest.

In general, the highest concentration of third places is in the central parts of the city, including Gamla Stan, Södermalm, Norrmalm, Östermalm and, to a slightly lesser extent, Kungsholmen. These localities make up the inner city of Stockholm and are parts of the municipality that to a large extent compose the historical area of the region. Today they are home to an extensive number of bars, cafés, nightlife venues and retail shopping stores.

The top two panels of Figure 1 indicate that they are also the areas most favoured by entrepreneurs. Interestingly, entrepreneur workplace locations tend to be concentrated in the very centre, for example, Östermalm and Gamla Stan, while residence locations tend to be on the ‘periphery’ of that centre, in places such as Kungsholmen and Södermalm. However, the pattern of third place access is not descriptively much different between these two locations.

Beyond the centre, we ﬁnd a secondary concentration of third places and entrepreneur workplace locations in Kista, in northern Stockholm. While slightly further away from the city centre, this pattern is not surprising, since in recent years Kista has become one of the largest information and communication technology (ICT) clusters in Sweden, informally referred to the Silicon Valley of Stockholm. High-tech ﬁrms such as Ericsson, IBM, Samsung and Nokia are located there, which have attracted a lot of high-skilled workers into this area.

While Figure 1 suggests a clear spatial relationship between third place access and the residence and workplace locations of entrepreneurs, a more detailed empirical REGIONAL STUDIES analysis is required to see whether this relationship holds while controlling for other related factors (including density and employment in creative occupations).

5. RESULTS AND ANALYSIS As previously discussed, to establish the importance of third places for high-tech entrepreneurship, we combine quantitative empirical models together with a qualitative survey of Swedish high-tech entrepreneurs. We look ﬁrst at the quantitative data.

5.1. Accessibility to third places and start-ups Table 2 shows the effects estimations for the start-ups in high-tech industries from the 250 m2 grid cells where people work (columns 1–3) and where they live (columns 4–6). In columns (1) and (3) neighbourhood ﬁxed effects are not included.

The accessibility to third places estimates shows a positive and statistically signiﬁcant relationship in all the estimates. This provides suggestive evidence for the importance of third places in the start-up process of high-tech ﬁrms. These results indicate that access to third places is positively related to the number of hightech start-ups. The positive and signiﬁcant relationship holds when looking both at the place of work and the place of residence of the entrepreneur. The variable is signiﬁcant also when we control for employment density, creative workers in the square, age structures, income, gender composition in the location and access to universities.

In effect, accessibility to third places increases the number of newly started high-tech establishments from people who live or work in the vicinity. When looking at the size of the coefﬁcients, the estimations in Table 2 show that a 1% increase in access to third places increases high-tech entrepreneurship by about 0.04% in both estimations. To help with the interpretation of the magnitude, it is easier to discuss in terms of standard deviation change rather than percentage change. For the work model, a 1 SD increase in accessibility to third places is associated with a 0.09 SD increase in entrepreneurship.

This is a similar magnitude for both estimations. There may be a few mechanisms at work behind this observed relationship, though they are difﬁcult to pinpoint from the quantitative analysis. First, it might be that third places provide an increased opportunity for face-to-face interactions and exchanging thoughts and ideas. This would be in line with the well-developed theory of agglomeration economies previously discussed in this paper. When individuals are close to each other, the possibility of exchanging knowledge and information becomes easier. Duranton and Puga (2004) consider this as learning, where they see those processes aiding the generation and diffusion of knowledge accumulation. Learning is often associated with such face-to-face interactions, created through the ﬂow of knowledge across skilled individuals (Lucas, 1988; Jovanovic & Rob, 1989). To take into account the issue of spatial concentration of entrepreneurs within each grid cell and the relative rarity of the start-up event, we test a speciﬁcation in Table A6 online that uses a spatial empirical Bayes (SEB) estimator to smooth the dependent variable. The basic concept of the SEB smoother is that it shrinks the rate observed in a given grid cell towards the mean rate of the surrounding grid cells (in this case, the eight nearest neighbours) based on the variance of the rate in this spatial neighbourhood (Anselin et al., 2004; Clayton & Kaldor, 1987; Credit, 2019). There is not a clear central business district with only companies and no people living around there. Last, Table A8 online shows the results where we have excluded the top 95th and 99th percentiles to ensure that it is not a few squares at the top of the distribution that are driving all the results.

As discussed above, it is still difﬁcult to establish whether the third places affect or cause entrepreneurship or if we are dealing with a selection issue. It could be the case that people working in places characterised by higher accessibility to bars and restaurants would start high-tech ﬁrms anyway. Thus, the relationship between third places and entrepreneurship would be spurious and driven by simply working or living in the city centre rather than speciﬁcally having high accessibility to places which facilitate face-to-face interactions. For this reason, below we combine the regression results with an IV approach as well as relying on a phone survey with high-tech entrepreneurs from Stockholm.

5.2. Instrumental variable (IV) estimations To take care of this issue with selection and that high-tech ﬁrms possibly select themselves in the city centres where also the bars are located, we use an IV approach which was described in more detail above. We re-run the analysis in Table 2, but now also include our instrument (access to bohemian, cultural workers in Stockholm in 1882 to instrument the existence of bars and restaurants today).

The accessibility score is calculated in the same way as for the bars and restaurants. However, there is one caveat with using historical variables such as this: Stockholm was smaller in 1882 than today. Therefore, the areas outside the centre of the city Third places, the connective ﬁbre of cities and high-tech entrepreneurship 2233 (today) will show up with very low accessibility to 1882 cultural workers simply because the size of the city itself was different, which might then affect the IV. For this reason, we run the IV estimations only on those neighbourhoods located in the centre of the city (i.e., those within Stockholm in 1882): Gamla Stan, Kungsholmen, Långholmen, Norrmalm, Riddarholmen, Skeppsholmen, Södermalm, Vasastaden, Östermalm and Djurgården.

The results are shown in Table 4. However, in Table A9 in Appendix A in the supplemental data online we also show the results with all the neighbourhoods for the municipality of Stockholm, which are consistent with the main results of the paper.

The third place access variable remains positive and signiﬁcant when we include the instrument, both with and without control variables. This suggests that there is a signiﬁcant relationship between access to third places and high-tech start-ups. Note, however, that the magnitude of the coefﬁcients for the IV are larger than those of the OLS, especially in the ﬁrst two columns. While there can be several reasons for the observed difference in coefﬁcient size (e.g., Card, 2001), it could indicate that the behaviour of a subpopulation is being shifted due to the instrument as the IV and OLS measure slightly different effects. However, the value of the F-statistics is reassuring in all the columns given that it is above the usual threshold of 10, indicating that we do not have a problem with weak instruments. The second-stage results for the control variables is shown in Table A10 in Appendix A in the supplemental data online.

In general, the survey results show that while access to meeting places was not crucial for the development of an idea to start a ﬁrm (which might be difﬁcult to remember exactly how it happened), entrepreneurs in general, and serial entrepreneurs more speciﬁcally, see them as important in the start-up formation process. Somewhat counterintuitively, we might interpret these survey results as supporting the importance of third places primarily in the formal (i.e., planning) rather than the informal (i.e., ideation) stage of the start-up process. This is interesting because the idea that places outside of the home or work could form part of the crucial infrastructure for formal start-up activities is currently under-theorised. Most of the existing literature assumes the entrepreneurial beneﬁts from third places come from fostering informal interactions and that lead to knowledge spillovers (e.g., Jacobs, 1961, 1969), but these theories were largely developed in a time before it was possible to conduct much of the formal work of planning and organising a ﬁrm online using a laptop at a café or restaurant. It is certainly possible that this paper’s empirical results are supporting an alternative mechanism through which third places foster entrepreneurship, that is, as ‘free’ quasi-public venues for formally planning and organising the ﬁrm in its early stages. This certainly deserves to be studied more in future work.

But does this mean that the ﬁrms where the meeting places were of higher importance perform better as well? We have two indirect measures of performance in the survey: whether the ﬁrm is still active in 2020 (at the point in time when we conducted the interview) and the size of the ﬁrm. The results are shown in Figures 5 and 6.

REGIONAL STUDIES The results show that meeting places were more important for those entrepreneurs who still have an active ﬁrm in 2020 (86% of the respondents). We also see a similar pattern on the size of the ﬁrms; the ones whose ﬁrm is the largest, the importance of meeting places looks to be of higher levels. These are of course very descriptive results, and do not necessarily imply that the ones who state that meeting places are important for the start of the ﬁrm perform better. However, the results seem to support that argument.

6. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS This paper provides a detailed empirical assessment of the role of third places in high-tech start-up formation in cities. We argue that third places constitute a critical piece of the innovation infrastructure, knowledge exchange and connectivity of cities. We use detailed geocoded register data between 2010 and 2019 to observe the relationship between third places and start-ups over time in Stockholm. To deal with identiﬁcation issues, we rely on neighbourhood ﬁxed effects and IV estimates, and we complemented the results from the register longitudinal data with a telephone survey providing further conﬁrmation of the ﬁndings.

Our empirical results provide suggestive evidence that third places such as cafés, bars and restaurants facilitate knowledge spillovers among people and provide a kind of supportive quasi-public start-up infrastructure for new ﬁrm founders, which in turn leads to a higher rate of start-ups. This supports the ﬁndings of other recent research in this area (Fang et al., 2022). Our primary ﬁnding is that third places play a key role in supporting innovation and entrepreneurship within cities, particularly in Third places, the connective ﬁbre of cities and high-tech entrepreneurship 2237 Figure 5. Importance of meeting places for starting the ﬁrm by whether the ﬁrm is still active in 2020.

the planning stages of the ﬁrm (as shown in the survey results). While this result is somewhat counterintuitive from a theoretical perspective, given the focus of the existing literature on the role of third places in fostering informal knowledge spillovers, we think that it provides an interesting opportunity to develop a stronger theory of the role of third places on start-up activities that include the relatively recent ability for entrepreneurs to conduct a vast amount of formal start-up planning activities online from a local coffee shop or bar. However, it is worth noting Figure 6. Importance of meeting places for starting the ﬁrm, separated by ﬁrm size.

that this paper does not say anything regarding the potential substitutive role that other types of places where people can conduct business and discuss ideas in a face-to-face environment, such as libraries and community centres, might play. That is another interesting avenue for future research on this topic.

While the identiﬁcation of a direct causal effect of third places on the aggregate level of entrepreneurship in this case is difﬁcult, these ﬁndings are useful to policymakers at both the local/regional and national levels.

REGIONAL STUDIES 2238 Kevin Credit et al. From an urban spatial planning perspective, attracting entrepreneurship to particular areas – whether or not an aggregate increase is observed – is an important policy objective for a number of reasons, including increasing compact development, reducing spatial inequality and encouraging reinvestment and redevelopment. At the same time, in the context of agglomeration and knowledge spillovers, we might expect secondary (aggregate) beneﬁts to innovation and/or entrepreneurship based purely on creating a denser spatial pattern of start-ups within the city, which could help accomplish national economic development goals related to innovation and economic growth. In that way, our results suggest that planning policies encouraging the establishment of third places in particular areas might also be used to help generate an innovative infrastructure for new high-tech business creation within cities.

Our ﬁndings may have special relevance for cities that are crafting strategies to revitalise their downtown areas that were hard hit by the COVID-19 pandemic and the shift to remote work it motivated (Barrero et al., 2021).

This not only led to a reduction of ofﬁce space but also impacted many of the third places, such as restaurants, cafés and bars in these areas which were closed for a while and in some cases have been slow to reopen. It may be that cities would be better off focusing on repositioning their downtowns and business areas more around third spaces and their connectivity functions as they strive to revitalise their downtown areas.

Some work (Barrero et al., 2021; Delventhal et al., 2022) suggests that the pandemic has resulted in a new way of working, where more people will work from home. This could in turn have an impact on the demand for downtowns and third places. However, a series of recent research shows how those who have the greatest ability to work from home are also individuals with a preference for high-density neighbourhoods (Brueckner et al., 2023; Veuger et al., 2023), which may be an effect of the demand for urban amenities and social interactions outside of the home. Similar results have been found in the case of Stockholm (Correa, 2023).

In any event, our research strongly suggests that third places – as joint arenas for production and consumption – play a key role in supporting innovation, start-ups and economic development in cities.
