The Journal of Technology Transfer (2023) 48:240–291 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10961-021-09906-w Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems Francesco Perugini1 Accepted: 14 November 2021 / Published online: 4 January 2022 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2022 Abstract Entrepreneurial ecosystems (EEs) are viewed as the combination or interaction of elements producing shared innovative and cultural values that support entrepreneurial activities within a territory. The literature has mainly taken a static view of the concept and has analyzed these ecosystems at national or at NUTS-2 regional level. This paper proposes the NUTS-3 provincial level as a spatial unit for measuring EEs in a dynamic perspective and focuses on the Italian case using data for the 2000–2018 period. The choice of NUTS-3 provinces is supported by theoretical arguments and it is confirmed by empirical results, which show some degree of heterogeneity in the level of EEs across provinces and some spatial patterns that would have been ignored using larger spatial units. The temporal dimension also reveals some intra-distribution mobility in the cross-sectional values of the provincial EE index. The paper contributes to advancing the research on EEs, has implications for policymakers and practitioners, and suggests directions for future studies.

Keywords Entrepreneurial ecosystem · Spatial analysis · Distribution dynamics · Italian provinces JEL Classification L26 · R11 · O47 1 Introduction In recent years the concept of entrepreneurial ecosystem (EE) has received increasing attention by researchers and policy makers, as demonstrated by the growing number of scientific articles, books, and literature reviews (see, for instance, De Brito & Leitão, 2021; Cao & Shi, 2020; Cavallo et al., 2019; Malecki, 2018; Wurth et al., 2021, among others).

Stam, (2015, p.5) defines an EE a “set of interdependent actors and factors coordinated in such a way that they enable productive entrepreneurship within a particular territory”. The EE concept emerged as a framework to better understand the nature of places in which entrepreneurial activity and innovation prospers, however it still lacks a shared analytical basis to clearly identify its definition, determinants, and effects. Several issues remain * Francesco Perugini f.perugini@univpm.it 1 Centre for Innovation and Entrepreneurship, Università Politecnica Delle Marche, Via Brecce Bianche 12, 60131 Ancona, Italy 1 3 Vol:.(1234567890) 241 Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems﻿ controversial (Alvedalen & Boschma, 2017). For instance, part of the literature criticizes the inconsistent use of the term ecosystem and its vague definition that adds no additional value to the scholarly discourse, to existing concepts like cluster, regional innovation system, triple-helix initiatives or public–private partnerships (Brown & Mason, 2017; Stam & Spigel, 2018). Others argue that the concept is under-theorized and conceptually fragmented (Alvedalen & Boschma, 2017). Still others that it is not always clear in what way proposed elements are connected in an EE (Stam, 2015), or which interactions matter most (Ács et al., 2014). The specific mechanisms through which ecosystems influence entrepreneurs are also not well-defined (Roundy & Fayard, 2019).

Despite the large amount of research devoted to investigating these issues, one still unaddressed aspect is a closer examination of the spatial content as well as the dynamic relationships that characterize an EE (Spigel, 2017). Researchers have criticized the EE literature because it proposed a static point of view that describes relationships within an EE without considering its evolution over time (Alvedalen & Boschma, 2017). Moreover, it is not clear which level of analysis the literature is targeting, e.g., city, region, or country (Stam, 2015). In a recent analysis, Lange and Schmidt (2020) argued that EE should be viewed as a bridging concept that not only opens a communicative trans-disciplinary exchange but also allows to integrate novel dynamic temporal and spatial elements to otherwise rather strict spatial boundaries of the concept.

We believe that these gaps should be addressed to improve our understanding of EEs, given that most of the factors that characterize EEs originate at local level and evolve over time. In other words, the paper answers the following questions: how does the dynamic analysis and increased granularity of measurement improve our understanding of EEs?

How relevant are local factors for understanding EEs and their evolution? To answer these questions the paper (1) proposes a rigorous spatial unit for analyzing EEs, (2) measures EEs at this spatial scale level and in a dynamic perspective, (3) analyzes how EEs and the conditions that make up the EEs evolve over time and across spatial units, and then (4) assesses the sensitivity of the EE index to changes in the scale of the spatial unit, i.e., whether it is more appropriate to measure and examine the EEs at NUTS-3 provincial level or NUTS-2 regional level.1 In the paper, we adopt the following strategy. Regarding the unit of analysis, we propose the NUTS-3 provincial level, which we believe is the most appropriate unit to identify and measure EEs. To measure EEs, we follow the framework proposed by Stam (2015) and construct an index of EEs by modifying the version of Iacobucci and Perugini (2020a, 2020b), adjusted to account for the temporal dimension of the data, which goes from 2000 to 2018. We use Stam’s framework not for theoretical reasons, but mainly because it allows to overcome the problem of data availability at this spatial scale while preserving a way, out of other possible, to conceptualize and theorize EE. We also examine the dynamics and the spatial dimension of the EE index and its components by employing the mean and the standard deviation, while to look at 1 NUTS (Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics) is the geocode standard for referencing the subdivision of countries for statistical purposes, adopted by the EU. The NUTS hierarchical classification divides territories into three levels, where the NUTS 1 level identifies larger socio-economic regions, the NUTS 2 level indicates basic regions, often considered in the definition of regional policies, and the NUTS 3 level identifies the smaller regions, which can be considered for specific analyses (https://​ec.​europa.​eu/​ euros​tat/​web/​nuts/​backg​round). In the rest of the paper, we refer to NUTS-1 as “geographical macro-areas”, NUTS-2 as “regions”, and NUTS-3 as “provinces”. Moreover, we use the generic term “local” to define a small area, a limited place, a place generally within a city or a province.

1 3 242 F. Perugini its spatial pattern and to assess the heterogeneity across provinces and over time we compute the Theil index (Theil, 1971). Moreover, we apply the distribution dynamic approach developed by Quah (1993, 1996, 1997) in order to assess the extent of how far the provinces moved along the cross-sectional distribution of the EE index over time. Finally, for the analysis of the spatial correlation of the EE index and to assess the sensitivity of the EE index to changes in the scale of the spatial unit, we compute Moran’s I statistic (Moran, 1948) and rely on regression analysis.

The paper makes several contributions to advancing the research on EEs. First, the paper provides a measure for assessing how the conditions that shape EEs develop.

This is a relevant issue given the heterogeneity and complexity of EEs, thus allowing comparability. The paper also propose the NUTS-3 provincial level as unit of analysis. This is a novelty in the EE literature. Indeed, researchers have considered the lack of studies at a smaller scale unit than the national level as a weakness in the EE literature, given that most of the factors that characterize EEs, vary largely between regions, provinces and, in some cases, cities. Providing a measure of EE at a low level of spatial disaggregation is extremely relevant given that most of the factors that characterize EEs, such as regulations, institutions and norms, infrastructure, city amenities, access to finance, demand, etc., vary largely between regions, provinces, and in some cases cities. Moreover, as the literature suggest, the nature of entrepreneurship is mainly local (Autio et al., 2014; Bosma & Sternberg, 2014; Cunningham et al., 2019; Fritsch, 2013; Sternberg et al., 2019; Tsvetkova, 2015).

The paper tells us more about the dynamics of the EEs, how they evolve, and how the relative strength of components changes, all issues that are less explored in the literature. The paper also provides further insights into whether the dynamics and evolution of EEs in one location is influenced by the EE endowment and development in neighbouring locations. Combining the spatial with the time dimension is necessary because as EE evolves in both directions (i.e., time and space), the importance and relative strength of components changes, and so do the policies necessary to sustain these systems over time (Alvedalen & Boschma, 2017; D. B. Audretsch et al., 2019; Brown & Mason, 2017; Mack & Mayer, 2016; Spigel, 2017).

The analysis carried out for the Italian case is also a novel contribution to the theoretical and empirical literature. This is particularly interesting given that Italy is characterized by a persistent economic dualism, which has historically resulted in a considerable disparity among the Northern and Southern regions and provinces in terms of economic development (Toniolo, 2013).

Finally, the paper contributes to the policy-making decision process. Indeed, empirical findings reveal that EEs are spatially heterogeneous and therefore targeted interventions are essential to foster and stimulate the conditions that shape the EE and entrepreneurial activities at sub-national level. Moreover, the EE literature has recognized that the causal mechanisms and actors involved in entrepreneurship activities occur at different spatial levels of analysis (D. B. Audretsch et al., 2019). Thus, findings may provide useful information for coordinating policy interventions at provincial, regional, and national level.

The paper is organized in the following sections. Section 2 provides a discussion of the literature that deals with the geographical and dynamic aspects of EEs. Section 3 defines the EE index, its measurement and the methodology used. Section 4 provides the empirical results. Section 5 discusses the implications while Sect. 6 describes the limitations of the paper. Finally, Sect. 7 draws the main conclusions.

1 3 243 Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems﻿ 2 The geography and the dynamics of EEs In this section we highlight the most recent advancement in the debate regarding the spatial dimension of EEs and what the recent literature considers the main difficulties for defining a proper spatial boundaries. We also addressed why the recent literature on EEs regard the time dimension a relevant issue for better understanding EEs.

2.1 The spatial dimension Apart from single case studies and some analysis of emerging ecosystems at city level (Cohen, 2006; Mack & Mayer, 2016; Motoyama & Knowlton, 2017; Pugh et al., 2019; Spigel, 2017), EEs are usually measured at national level (see, for instance, Ács et al., 2014; Isenberg, 2011; Stangler J. Bell-Masterson 2015). More recently, there have been some attempts to measure EEs at NUTS-1 (REDI), NUTS-2 regional (Guzman & Stern, 2020; Stam, 2015; Sternberg et al., 2019) or provincial level (Stam, 2018).

Researchers considered the lack of studies at smaller scale unit than the national level as a weakness of the literature on EEs, given that EE is a spatially bounded entity that follows a strong spatial logic. The potential and the need for a geographical dimension of EE at provincial or regional level is extremely important in those contexts where large territorial differences emerge in terms of start-ups and business growth, but also in terms of socioeconomic, organizational, and technological endowment, as is the Italian context, which is analyzed in this paper. Indeed, as we will see in the rest of the paper, most of the EE dimensions are not evenly distributed across space, so EE may vary not only between Northern and Southern Italian regions, as commonly expected, but also between adjacent provinces.

However, defining the spatial boundary of an EE is a difficult task for several reasons. First of all, the outputs and outcomes of EEs are the result of a complex set of actors and factors such as human capital, networks and institutions that occur in a temporal and varying regional setting (Leendertse et al., 2020). For instance, social networks play a crucial role for entrepreneurs to get access to resources like knowledge, finance and human capital (Stuart & Sorenson, 2005). This means that the spatial context could be a city, a region or a country, or it can also be other systems less strictly defined in space that create opportunities for firm creation and growth (Stam and van de Ven 2021).

Moreover, some of the elements that make up the EE, such as finance or the quality of human capital, can be defined at a regional or provincial level, while others, such as regulations or investment in physical infrastructure, can be designed on both regional and national levels (D. B. Audretsch, Heger, et al., 2015; Audretsch, Link, et al., 2015).

One criterium to define the spatial boundary of the EE is to delimit the surrounding area where firms and individuals operate and interact. For instance, for entrepreneurs it could be the Local Labour Systems (LLS), i.e., geographical units delimited based on daily commuting of people for work reasons (Sforzi, 2009), or the same municipality when entrepreneurs interact with local banks. It is also possible to delimit the spatial context depending on the role assumed by the actors who operate within the EE. For civil servants it will be a particular administrative region, province, or municipality, for human capital a municipality or province where the university is established, for entrepreneurs it may be a municipality, a region, or even a country (Stam and van de Ven 2021).

1 3 244 F. Perugini Secondly, the definition of the spatial context is challenged by the presence of a multilevel context where formal and informal institutions interact at local (i.e., provincial in the Italian case), regional, and national level (Bosma et al., 2018). For this reason, some authors believe that although some level of spatial unit needs to be chosen for research purposes, multi-level methods are often the most appropriate ones for explaining entrepreneurship when considering sub-national spatial units (Hundt & Sternberg, 2016).

Thirdly, there is also the fact that although entrepreneurship is a local event, distant resources can be critical especially for new firms that are “born global” (Mahroum, 2016), but equally important is the firms’ ability to integrate global knowledge and become successful in their home EE (Malecki, 2011). At the same time, multinational corporations are perceived to attract skilled employees to that territory, upgrade managerial skills of local firms, operate as a source for spin-off firms and provide business opportunities for firms to access global markets (Mason C.& Brown 2014). Moreover, digitalization and globalization increase entrepreneurs’ opportunities to be exploited outside a cluster, causing entrepreneurship to lose its local dimension (Autio et al., 2018).

Finally, the choice of the spatial level of EE is constrained by data availability. Indeed, “there is often a disconnect between the theoretical definition of a region as integrated contiguous space and the political and census geography for which data are readily available” (Feldman & Lowe, 2015, p.1785). This limitation has so far constrained researchers to use data at national level or to conduct case studies analysis of specific high-tech places like the Boulder County and Phoenix in the US, Waterloo, Calgary and Victoria in Canada, and Lancaster in the UK (Cohen, 2006; Mack & Mayer, 2016; Pugh et al., 2019; Spigel, 2017).

2.2 The temporal dimension The theoretical and empirical literature have also addressed the need for integrating the temporal dimension in regional studies of EEs (Alvedalen & Boschma, 2017; D. B.

Audretsch et al., 2019; Brown & Mason, 2017; Mack & Mayer, 2016; Spigel, 2017). This perspective is necessary because EEs are complex and dynamic systems that evolve in space and over time. The EE components can also change and so do the institutions and the policies that are necessary to support these systems. A static analysis tends to miss the importance of institutional changes (Lowe & Feldman, 2017), and the type of support firms utilize through their own growth stages, from start-up to survival, growth, and exit (O’Connor & Reed, 2015).

To better understand the interdependencies between EE components and their evolutionary dynamics, scholars have proposed an industry lifecycle perspective, where the inherent dynamics lead to the birth, growth, maturity, decline, and re-emergence of EEs (Cantner et al., 2021; Mack & Mayer, 2016), or they have looked, based on a specific city’s empirical setting, on how EEs are shaped by different governance designs, which create network interactions and relationships with local actors to support entrepreneurship (Colombelli et al., 2019). Other studies have also focused on case studies to shed light on the micro mechanism underlying the EE formation and evolution over time. This is the case of Ryan et al. (2020) who examined how multinational enterprises in the Irish city of Galway created and developed an EE. These studies go in the right direction of uncovering the relationship and the mechanisms that enable the formation of new ventures in a dynamic perspective, but they are confined to case studies. By contrast, there is a lack of research that provides quantitative empirical evidence on the complex dynamics of EEs. Also, in order 1 3 245 Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems﻿ to capture the diversity and evolution of EEs more recent studies have started to use bigdata approaches (Schwab & Zhang, 2019; von Bloh et al., 2020).

Following the above arguments, it is therefore important to assess how EE and its components change over time because it reveals how the dynamics of people, processes, and places encourage entrepreneurial behaviour, but also why some EEs fail to develop while others prosper. The time dynamic perspective is also relevant because it can provide useful insight about the cross-sectional distribution of the EE index, if for instance the EE levels in poorer (with a low endowment of the EE index) provinces catching up in relative terms with the those in the richer ones (with a high EE index endowment), but also if geographical proximity plays a role in explaining why EEs in some provinces are more dynamic than in others. Such analyses would help policy-makers to implement proper and adequate interventions.

3 Measuring the entrepreneurial ecosystem Taking into account the research gaps opened at theoretical and empirical level, in the rest of the paper we aim to answer the following research question: how can EEs be measured at more granular level of analysis? To this purpose, in this section we first propose (1) a measure of EE, then (2) we examine the dynamics and spatial dimensions of the EE index and its components; (3) we explain the methodology used to assess to what extent provinces have moved along the cross-sectional distribution of the EE index over time; (4) and we assess the extent to which the conditions that make up an EE are geographically located, whether these are spatially correlated and how these are affected by changing the territorial unit of analysis.

3.1 Data The composite index used in this paper to measure EE is made up of 11 variables/components. Variable selection followed the framework proposed by Stam (2018) to measure EE at the Dutch provincial level, but we also take into account how EE is measured in other studies that used data at national level (see, for instance, Ács et al., 2014; Isenberg, 2011; Stangler J. Bell-Masterson 2015). Despite the scarcity of data at NUTS-3 provincial level, we select variables that embody those domains and features characterizing an EE, as suggested by this literature. The 11 variables selected are the following: (1) Social capital; (2) Entrepreneurship Culture; (3) Physical Infrastructure; (4) Value Added; (5) Finance; (6) New knowledge; (7) Business services; (8) Firm survival; (9) Human capital; (10) Migration flow; (11) Population structure. The index is a modified version of Iacobucci and Perugini (2020a, 2020b), adjusted to account for the temporal dimension of the data. Table 1 provides details on the variables used and on the source of the data, while a detailed description of the selected variables is in the Appendix.

Regarding the spatial level of analysis, our EE index is measured at the Italian NUTS-3 provincial level, the most disaggregated territorial level in relation to data availability.

This is especially true for the Italian case where, as we will see in the next section, the conditions shaping the EE varies across adjacent territories. The data used for the analysis cover the 2000–2018 period.

3.2 Methodology 3.2.1 The temporal and spatial dimension of the EE Based on the arguments provided in the previous sections, we use two statistical measures to examine the dynamics and the spatial dimension of the EE index and its components (point 1), that is the mean and the standard deviation. We also look at its spatial pattern and, to better assess the heterogeneity in the EE index at provincial level and over time, we compute the Theil index (Theil, 1971), a well-known measure of inequality that can be decomposed into between and within-group inequalities. In our case, groups are associated to NUTS-2 regions. The analysis is carried out for the EE index and for its components.

The visual inspection of the geographical distribution of the EE index or the synthetic measures of inequality and dispersion provide only a partial understanding of the evolution of the EE index over time and across space. This is because, persistent inequality in EEs across provinces is compatible with unchanging dispersion in the distribution of the EE index where, for instance, rich provinces (those with a higher endowment of the EE index) stay rich and the poorer provinces (with a low endowment of the EE index) stay poor, but it can also be consistent with marked changes in intra-distribution of individual provinces where the poor becomes rich, and the rich becomes poor. Intermediate cases, such as polarization or club-convergence (with two or more groups of provinces) in the distribution of the EE index can also be unnoticed through the empirical analysis of the Theil 3 In 2011, the National Institute of Statistics classified 611 LLS with an average population of 97 thousand (ISTAT 2014).

1 3 248 F. Perugini index or other statistical measures of dispersion, such as the sigma convergence measure used in classical growth convergence analyses (Barro & Sala-I-Martin, 1992). Indeed, the studies that rely on the sigma (and the beta) convergence can only provide a summary of statistics for the evolution of distribution but not the details of mobility of provinces, and hence identical summary statistics can be derived from two distributions with entirely different mobility.

As a result, to assess the extent that provinces have moved along the cross-sectional distribution of the EE index over time (point 2) we apply the distribution dynamic approach developed by Quah (1993, 1996, 1997). This approach focuses the attention on the external shape of the distribution and on the movement within the distribution of the EE index over time (Fingleton & López-Bazo, 2003). As for external shape, it could be that over time the distribution of the EE index collapses to a single point, implying a convergence process by poorer provinces approaching the level of EE index of the rich ones. Or the external shape of the distribution might indicate an increase of dispersion of the EE index over time. The external shape might also remain unaltered (e.g., poor provinces become rich and vice-versa), thus the focus on intra-distribution mobility might reveal how provinces transit from any point in the distribution to any other point at a future time (Calcagnini & Perugini, 2019b).

The distribution dynamic approach requires estimating the probability of a province to staying poor or becoming rich. An estimate of the external shape typically involves nonparametric estimation of the density function via the kernel method (Silverman, 1986), while intra-distribution dynamics can be analyzed through the estimation of a stochastic kernel (Stokey et al., 1989) for the distribution of EE index over the period under analysis.

The stochastic kernel is merely the counterpart of the transition probability matrix where the number of states (the values taken by the EE index) tends to infinity. The stochastic kernel can be drawn in a two dimension contour plot with the probability density function of EE at time t + s on the x-axis and at time t on the y-axis. It can also be drawn in the corresponding three dimensional plot with the conditional density estimated, i.e., the stochastic kernel, on the vertical axes for each pair of points in the t and t + s space. In the three dimensional plot for each value of EE at time t it shows the probability density s periods ahead, conditional on the density of that value at t. That is, it provides the probability of a province starting with any value of the EE index at t ending up at any of the values after s years.4 When most of the probability density function, as represented by the two dimensional contour plot, is concentrated along the diagonal, there is a lack of mobility in the variable of interest. In contrast, a tendency towards convergence would be signaled by a counterclockwise movement around the center of the 45-degree line. Complete convergence is represented by a concentration of most of the graph around the vertical 1-value of the time t + s axis and parallel to the time t axis (the 1-value represent the average level of the EE index). Finally, the formation of two (or more) separate modes is a signal of a tendency toward polarization.5 The stochastic kernel can also be used to describe movements between two distributions, i.e., an actual unconditional distribution and a conditional distribution (Quah, 1996).

In this case, when the mass of probability lies along the main diagonal the conditioning factor is not responsible for the variation in the actual distribution. In contrast, when a factor is responsible for most of the dispersion, conditioning out its effect will result in a kernel parallel to the unconditional distribution (so that provinces share similar values of the EE index when the effect of the factor is removed, regardless of their position in the original distribution).

To determine if geographical factors may explain provincial EE intra-distribution dynamics, it is possible to compare the initial unconditional EE distribution with the end of period space conditioned distribution. To this purpose, it is necessary to pre-filter the data to take out the influence of the conditioning variable before the analysis. In our case we are interested to see if geographical proximity influences the distribution of the EE index.

Therefore, to determine the space conditioned distribution, we compute the EE of a province relative to the average of its geographical neighbours. As we have seen above, there are two distinct clusters of provinces, one in the North of Italy, where rich provinces tend to be close to other rich provinces, and one in the South of Italy, where poor provinces tend to be close to other poor provinces. Therefore, it is interesting to see how the spatial conditioning factor influence the distribution and the transition dynamics of the EE index. The conditional distribution can be interpreted as the part unexplained by geographical proximity. If no differences exist between the unconditional and the conditional distribution, then one may conclude that geographical proximity does not matter for the transition dynamics of the EE index.

3.3 Robustness check: spatial and regression analysis As for the analysis of the spatial correlation of the EE index and the choice of the spatial unit of analysis (point 3), we compute Moran’s I statistic (Moran, 1948) and rely on regression analysis. Moran’s I compares the value of the observed variable at any location with the value of the same variable at neighboring locations.6 The values of Moran’s I statistic can also be plotted in a diagram, with the four different quadrants of the scatter plot identifying four types of local spatial associations between a province/region and its neighbours: going clockwise from top right we have HH (High-High), LH (Low–High) LL (Low-Low), and HL (High-Low). For instance, in the HH quadrant, the Moran scatter plot represents the high EE provinces/regions that are surrounded by high EE neighbours. Similar logic follows for the other quadrants. The spatial correlation in the EE index is measured at both the NUTS-3 provincial level and at the NUTS-2 regional level so we can compare to what extent the degree of spatial correlation varies when the scale and the shape of the spatial unit of analysis change.

In the literature the sensitivity of statistical results to the modification in the shape and the size of the geographical units is known as the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP) (Fotheringham & Wong, 1991). 4 Empirical results 4.1 Spatial and time dimensions In Fig. 1 we plot the average value of the EE index and its standard deviation from 2000 to 2018. The tendency for both measures to increase until the start of the recent financial crisis in 2008 and then to gradually decline up to more recent years is can clearly be seen.

This suggests that over the last two decades there has been a general deterioration of the conditions that make up the EE but also less dispersion in the value of EE index among provinces.

Looking at the single variable composing the EE index, the mean values of “Firm survival”, and “Population structure” followed the same path of the EE index, while other variables such as “Business services” and “Entrepreneurship culture”, registered an opposite trend, that is their values have been gradually increasing since 2008 (Table 2). A steady improvement of the mean values is observed for “Human capital”, “New knowledge”, “Migration flow”, and to a lesser extent, “Social capital”.

A deterioration of the mean values is instead observed for “Value Added” and “Finance”, i.e., the EE components more directly influenced by the financial crisis. In terms of standard deviation, it is also interesting to note that since 2008 and in contrast to what has been observed for the overall EE index, the degree of dispersion increased for “Population structure”, “New knowledge”, and “Human capital”. For “Value Added”, and “Finance” instead we observed less heterogeneity among provincial values, with the standard deviation falling to lower levels in 2018. This might suggest a possible convergence process towards lower mean levels for these variables. Similar paths have been followed by “Social capital” and by “Firm survival”. Indeed, since 2008 the degree of dispersion has reversed its trend and decreased. By contrast, from 2008 New knowledge, Human capital, and Population structure were the variables that contributed more to amplify the dispersion of the provincial EE index, which is measured by the standard deviation. Overall, since the financial crisis the EE index has deteriorated, but some of its components have improved.

Most importantly, the analysis at the NUTS-3 provincial level highlighted some results that would have been ignored at the NUTS-2 regional level of analysis. Indeed, we found that over time EE variability decreased across provinces but increased within regions.

To further analyze the spatial pattern of the EE index we now evaluate the degree of spatial correlation using data at NUTS-3 level and see how its magnitude changes when using data at NUTS-2 level. We first compute Moran’s I statistic (Moran, 1948) and then we estimate the model in Eq. (1). For both analyses, we select the year 2013 since data for 1 3 263 Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems﻿ the dependent variable, i.e., the EEBR, the employer enterprise birth rate, in the regression analysis discussed below are not available for more recent years. However, results do not show major changes when a different year is selected.

The Moran I test shows positive spatial autocorrelation of the EE index as most of the observations are in the HH and LL quadrants and are concentrated along the linear fit, for both the provincial (Fig. 9a) and regional (Fig. 9b) level data.16 This means that provinces/regions with very relatively high/low EE values tend to be located near other provinces with high/low EE values more often than would be expected as a result of purely random factors. However, the spatial correlation is higher at provincial level (0.773) than at regional level (0.552), suggesting that clusters with similar values of EE index are spatially correlated at a more disaggregated geographical level. Similar differences in the spatial correlation emerge when considering a different year.17 The result of the Moran scatter plot can also be represented in a map as in Fig. 10a (at provincial level) and in Fig. 10b (at regional level). These maps show provinces/regions with a significant Moran statistic classified by type of spatial correlation: red for the HH association, blue for LL. When the Moran statistic is not statistically significant the provinces/regions are coloured in light grey (Anselin, 1995). Overall, the two maps in Fig. 10 show that the two spatial correlated clusters are located one in the North of Italy, with provinces/regions characterized by a high value of the EE index, and the other in the South of Italy, where provinces/regions with lower level of the EE index are surrounded by provinces/regions with low EE values. The maps also show that the appearance of statistically significant clusters is more dependent on the selection of the spatial unit. For instance, in the South of Italy the Low-Low cluster from the provincial level is geographically more widespread than what is observed at regional level, while in the North of Italy the High- High cluster observed at regional level disappears in some provinces but appears in others.

This is evidence of a higher degree of spatial correlation in the EE index when considering NUTS-3 provinces than at NUTS-2 regional level. We now estimate model (1) to quantify the spatial dependency that has been identified by Moran’s I and possible spatial spillovers at both NUTS-3 provincial and NUTS-2 regional level. Table 6 shows estimation results at different levels of spatial aggregation when the dependent variable is the EEBR, the employer enterprise birth rate: column 1–4 provides estimates at NUTS-3 provincial level, while column 5–8 at NUTS-2 regional level.18 When we estimate the model with no controls other than time dummies, the choice of the scale aggregation of the data matters. Indeed, the EE index has a larger impact on firm birth at provincial level. However, the MAUP effect diminishes when we include the control variables and when we estimate the spatial models. The elasticities calculated on the EE coefficients are similar to the provincial and regional data, although in the former case these are of larger magnitude. These spatial spillovers are slightly larger in the case of NUTS-3 provinces than in the NUTS-2 case, thus partially confirming the higher spatial correlation detected through Moran’s I with smaller geographical units.

Interestingly, the values of the coefficients of the spatially lagged error terms (λ) are higher when the SEM is estimated with regional data, suggesting that other explanatory variables, which have been omitted from the model, could be relevant for firm growth when we consider larger spatial units. Still, the EE elasticities have similar magnitude in both NUTS-3 and NUTS-2 cases.

Overall, the robustness exercise provides evidence of strong spatial correlation and statistically significant spatial dependence in the data. It is well-known that the presence of spatial dependence should be taken into account in model specifications because it invalidates linear regression via OLS estimation (Anselin, 2002). Besides this methodological issue, from a theoretical point of view these results emphasize the spatial concept of EE as a set of interconnected actors and may explain why in certain places the conditions that promote entrepreneurial activities are more favorable as they are also affected by spatial spillovers. A number of studies have explored regional variation in entrepreneurship activity based on the hypotheses that the conditions that stimulate such activities differ between locations (see for instance Armington & Acs, 2002; Iacobucci & Micozzi, 2014). However, spatial dimensions have not been incorporated into empirical studies that look at the determinant of EE or how an EE may impact on entrepreneurial activities.

The above results also reveal that these conditions are more spatially correlated at NUTS-3 provincial level but as observed by Arbia (2012), this may be also due to statistical reasons, i.e., the level of spatial correlation generally increase with smaller spatial scale units. However, this argument is controversial in the literature. Studies on agglomeration economies (Burger, M.J. van Oort, F.G. van der Kamp 2010) or on regional economic growth (Dapena et al., 2016) found results to differ across geographical scales mainly 1 3 265 Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems﻿ Fig. 10 a Moran’s cluster map on EE index in 2013 at NUTS-3 provincial level b and at NUTS-2 regional level because the interactions among socio-economics variables and actors vary at different spatial units, so further investigation is also needed in the EE field.

5 Discussion We believe that the findings have important implications and may contribute to advancing the research on EEs for several reasons. First, the paper provides a measure for assessing how the conditions that shape EEs develop. Indeed, measurement is the most relevant and preliminary question that needs to be answered before conducting any analysis on EEs (Audretsch et al., 2021; Credit et al., 2018; Sternberg et al., 2019). Measurement should involve both EE dimensions, i.e., spatial and dynamic (Bruns et al., 2017; Sternberg et al., 2019) and be made with standard means that allow to overcome EEs heterogeneity and complexity (Shwetzer et al., 2019) while enabling comparative analysis. This can advance our understanding of what constitutes EEs and their impact on entrepreneurial behaviour and economic development and vice versa.

The paper also takes the analyses at a low level of spatial disaggregation, i.e., the NUTS-3 provinces. This is a novelty in the EE literature. Some of the previous studies identified and measured EEs mainly at national level (see, for instance, Ács et al., 2014; Isenberg, 2011; Stangler J. Bell-Masterson 2015), although in recent years there have been some attempts in the direction of implementing the national measures to smaller scale.

For instance, the GEM NECI (National Entrepreneurship Context Index) from the GEM (Global Entrepreneurship Monitor) or the REDI (Regional Entrepreneurial Development Index) from the national GEI (Global Entrepreneurship Index), but these indicators refer to regions (NUTS-1 or NUTS-2) or countries.19 Other measures of EEs at NUTS-2 level 19 For more details see http://​www.​gemco​nsort​ium.​org/​images/​media/​gem-​neci-​backg​round-​notes-​16137​ 53990.​pdf for the GEM NECI and https://​thege​di.​org/​regio​nal-​gedi/ and Ortega Argiles et al., (2014) for the REDI.

The only exemption is Stam (2018), who builds an EE index for the Netherland provinces, which however is equivalent to the NUTS-2 according to the EU classification, and Guzman and Stern (2020) who provide a framework for assessing the EE at the US national and state level.

More recently, Sternberg et al., (2019) developed an EE index based on survey data at NUTS-2 regional level for Spain and Germany following the EE concept of Stam (2018).

There are also single case studies and some analysis of emerging ecosystems at city level (Cohen, 2006; Mack & Mayer, 2016; Motoyama & Knowlton, 2017; Pugh et al., 2019; Spigel, 2017), but their diversity creates serious limitations in terms of EE comparison.

Researchers considered the lack of studies at a smaller scale unit than the national level as a weakness in the EE literature, given that most of the factors that characterize EEs, vary largely between regions, provinces and, in some cases, cities. As noted by Sternberg et al.

(2009, p.215) “entrepreneurs need the primarily regional, informal network of friends, former colleagues and bosses, relatives and first customers to be able to realize their start-up idea at all, particularly at the first attempt. It is regional or even local institutions such as banks, chambers industry and commerce and heads of business incubators who give “entrepreneurs-to-be” the decisive stimuli in this early phase of the entrepreneurial process”. Indeed, the existing literature has recognized EE as a spatially bounded entity that follows a strong spatial logic. It is argued that close geographic proximity fosters network formation and knowledge exchange (Glückler, 2007) and that entrepreneurial activity cannot be seen as independent from the environment within which businesses operate; rather the community and the culture of a given place can have a significant impact on entrepreneurship (Autio et al., 2014). For instance, universities and research centres with their traditional mission of knowledge transfer and knowledge spill-over play a relevant role for the development of EE.

The university’s entrepreneurial role based on third mission is also important to disseminate knowledge especially in the surrounding area where universities and research centres are located (Baldini et al., 2015; Bolzani et al., 2014; Chiarello et al., 2021). The articles in a recent special issue provide important insights regarding the ways in which knowledge transfer takes place in Italy (Grimaldi et al., 2021). For instance, Villani and Lechner (2021) argue that universities can create a community of specialized and complementary actors and form a supportive network in the local ecosystem, while Barbini et al.

(2021) explore the ways universities promote student entrepreneurship. The university’s entrepreneurial role is also analysed by Sciarelli et al. (2021), as they focused on university spin-offs in the South of Italy. Therefore, the role of local institutions, organizations, universities, and the connections between the elements that compose an EE matter (Motoyama & Knowlton, 2016). Indeed, the term ecosystem has become prevalent among researchers to describe the interactions between economic agents and their environment (Acs et al., 2017). The literature also acknowledges that regional agglomerations of local factors and resources and certain mechanisms that shape the EE exist outside its boundaries, and that spatial spillovers in terms of knowledge, institutional policy, social interactions, and networks of entrepreneurs are facilitated through geographic proximities (D. B. Audretsch et al., 2019). There is also empirical evidence that the level and type of entrepreneurial activities varies systematically across different EEs, which in turn differ in several elements among clusters of spatial units (Content et al., 2020). As a result, the analysis at a lower level of spatial disaggregation is extremely important.

Third, the paper contributes to the literature by examining the dynamic components of the EE. Different indicators, proxies, and measures, such as the GEM or the REDI have 1 3 269 Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems﻿ been used to explore the time evolution of EEs. The problems with most of these country level or NUTS-1 level indices is that they rely heavily on the availability of data and ignore the specificities needed to analyse EEs on a smaller spatial scale (Brown & Mason, 2017). Studies at city level have tried to overcome these limitations, by offering a detailed description of how entrepreneurial activities take place, however they mainly take a static view of the concept, and their diversity creates serious limitations in terms of EE comparison (Sternberg et al., 2019). Spigel (2017) observed that, in an EE, elements can develop simultaneously and reinforce each other, though they can never replace one another completely. Others claim that the elements of EEs will shift in importance and in their connections as they evolve (Mack & Mayer, 2016). In this paper we try to reconcile the need to measure EEs at a small spatial scale unit with the necessity to understand how EEs evolve over time.

Fourth, the analysis is carried over by focusing on the Italian case, thus it provides a contribution to the arguments advanced in the literature for explaining the heterogeneous entrepreneurial performance (Iacobucci & Micozzi, 2014) and differences in economic growth observed at the Italian provincial level. Indeed, the analysis for the Italian case showed that on average the conditions that make up the EE and that foster productive entrepreneurship are unevenly geographically distributed and have deteriorated after 2008, especially among the richer (with higher values of the EE index) provinces, which are mainly located in the North of Italy.

The paper also contributes to the design and implementation of the policy-making process. Indeed, local authorities may contribute to shape and promote the EE, given that their policies may directly or indirectly impact on the EE components. Moreover, the EE index may complement other statistical tools such as the Regional Innovation Scoreboard (RIS) and help policy makers to target policies designed at fostering innovation at regional or provincial level. In the Italian case, provincial authorities have a limited importance in the administrative structure, however they are responsible for implementing decentralized policies in relevant sectors such as health, education, transport, culture, energy policy and environmental protection, which are functional in promoting and sustaining the economic environment and in creating the necessary conditions for firms, universities, and entrepreneurs to implement entrepreneurial activities (Calcagnini & Perugini, 2019a; Veneri & Murtin, 2016). Indeed, policy measures on land-use, transportation, human capital, and housing, may be designed and implemented in different ways within the same region or province.

Therefore, the adoption of targeted measures aimed at expanding the quality and the quantity of infrastructures and business services, at increasing the supply and accessibility of finance and investment in R&D, and at fostering the endowments of social and human capital are essential for enhancing firm competitiveness and for reducing the divergence that exists between the North and the South of Italy in terms of EE conditions, entrepreneurship growth rates, and economic development (Calcagnini & Perugini, 2019a; Iacobucci & Micozzi, 2014; Putnam, 1993; Toniolo 2013).

6 Limitations The paper has some limitations, which give rise to several opportunities for future research. First, the quantification of the EE has been constrained by data availability. More direct measures of EEs in terms of entrepreneurial attitudes, abilities, and aspirations have not been taken into account because they are hardly measured at provincial level. Therefore, 1 3 270 F. Perugini it would be interesting to complement the measuring of EEs with survey data to capture these features.

A second limitation is in the use of variables able to capture technological innovation, which has an increasing and profound impact on entrepreneurship and venture creation.

Only recently has the EE paid more attention to describing and understanding how digital technologies may influence the nature and interactions among actors and the components of the EEs.

A third limitation of the paper concerns its nature, which is mainly descriptive. However, this may represent an avenue for future research, for instance to examine how EEs contribute to explaining performance differences across territories in terms of creation of firms and economic growth. A related interesting issue would be to assess how, and through which channels, EEs may impact on other entrepreneurial variables, linked for instance to the creation of high-growth firms or the industrial structure of the territories.

Indeed, the causal relations between EEs and entrepreneurship have not yet been studied sufficiently (Alvedalen & Boschma, 2017; Stam & Spigel, 2018). Another interesting issue would be to analyse how the various components of an EE interact with each other and what is their impact on entrepreneurial activities. The use of longitudinal data would help researchers to investigate these issues with a more efficient empirical instrument.

7 Conclusions Interest in the concept of an entrepreneurial ecosystem (EE) has been growing in recent years. An EE can be defined in several different ways, but most of them highlight the combination or interaction of elements producing shared innovative and cultural values that support entrepreneurial activities within a territory (Cao & Shi, 2020; Cavallo et al., 2019; De Brito & Leitão, 2021; Malecki, 2018; Wurth et al., 2021). Even though the concept has quickly gained popularity and despite the growing number of published works, there is a lack of studies that measure EE at regional or provincial level and combine the spatial and the dynamic view of EE (Alvedalen & Boschma, 2017; Stam and van de Ven 2021; Sternberg et al., 2019). To date, scholars have mainly considered EEs as a static concept and have primarily proposed the analysis at national level (see, for instance, Ács et al., 2014; Isenberg, 2011; Stangler J. Bell-Masterson 2015). Some qualitative case studies combined both the spatial and the time dimensions (Cohen, 2006; Mack & Mayer, 2016; Pugh et al., 2019; Spigel, 2017), however, although they are useful to understand the interconnections and the role played by certain actors in a single EE, their diversity creates serious limitations in terms of EE comparison.

The paper tries to fill these gaps, i.e., (1) it proposes a rigorous spatial unit to analyze EEs, (2) it measures EEs at this spatial scale level and in a dynamic perspective, (3) it analyzes how EEs and the conditions that make up the EEs evolve over time and across spatial units, and then (4) it assesses the sensitivity of the EE index to changes in the scale of the spatial unit, i.e., whether it is more appropriate to measure and examine the EEs at NUTS-3 provincial level or NUTS-2 regional level.

1 3 271 Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems﻿ The analysis considers the 2000 to 2018 period, and it is carried out at the Italian NUTS-3 provincial level, which we believe is the most appropriate spatial unit to identify and measure EEs. Indeed, our findings support the theoretical arguments advanced in the EE literature about the need to analyze such ecosystems at a more disaggregated territorial level than the regional or the national level. To measure EEs, we follow the framework proposed by Stam (2015) and construct an index of EEs, which is a novelty at the Italian NUTS-3 provincial level, by modifying the version of Iacobucci and Perugini (2020a, 2020b), adjusted to account for the temporal dimension of the data.

To examine the evolution of EEs across time and space the paper proposed statistical tools and regression analysis. These were used to assess inequality in the EE index through the Theil’s entropy measure (Theil, 1971), which also allowed to determine the contribution to inequality by considering the level of EEs in the neighbouring provinces, that is provinces that belongs to the same NUTS-2 region. We also explored the time dimension of the data and assessed how the degree of heterogeneity in the EE index has changed over time but, most importantly, what is the dispersion of the provincial EE within the larger NUTS-2 region. Statistical evidence was also provided in terms of spatial correlation and spatial dependence in the data to assess whether the spillover effects are more relevant at provincial or regional level, thus providing an indication of which measure of spatial unit is more adequate to account for the strength of the interconnections that exist between the EE components. Only recently has the entrepreneurship literature recognized the relevance of incorporating spatial modelling techniques for such analysis (Plummer, 2010), however to our knowledge these have not been applied in the EE context yet.

Spatial analysis and spatial models are necessary because the existence of spatial dependence renders ordinary least square estimation inappropriate. In addition to the spatial analysis, the paper proposed an analysis on the time evolution of the cross-sectional distribution of the EE index, which is investigated through the distribution dynamic approach developed by Quah (1993, 1996, 1997). This approach provides useful insights to whether the value of the EE in a province has changed, if there has been a convergence process of the EE index across provinces, i.e., if the EE levels in poorer (with a low endowment of the EE index) provinces are catching up in relative terms with those in the rich ones (with a high EE index endowment), or if the convergence occurs within two or more clusters of homogeneous provinces, i.e., if the distribution of the EE index is polarized. Like the spatial analysis approach, which is extensively used in the regional science literature, the distribution dynamic approach has not been employed in the EE literature yet but offers a different perspective to understand how the provincial EEs evolved over time but also across the entire EE distribution, and to evaluate how specific factors, such as for instance geographical proximity, may have an impact on the transition dynamic in the value of the provincial EE.

1 3 272 F. Perugini Results show the existence of a heterogeneous geographical distribution of the EE index with two distinct spatially correlated clusters, one located in the more developed Northern part of Italy, with provinces characterized by high values of the EE index, and the other in the South of Italy, where provinces with lower levels of the EE index are surrounded by provinces/regions with low EE values. This feature does not disappear over time, although there is a tendency for an overall deterioration of the mean value of the EE index toward lower levels. Findings also support the choice of selecting NUTS-3 province as a spatial unit of analysis and confirm the theoretical arguments typically advanced in the literature that view EE as a complex system that emerges and evolves at local level. Indeed, results reveal an increasing within regional variability in the EE index, spatial correlation in the data, and some spatial patterns in the EE index that would have been ignored using larger spatial units.

The dynamic perspective adopted in the paper also shows some intra-distribution mobility of provinces (the poor provinces becoming richer and the rich provinces becoming poorer) that produced a convergence process toward the mean value of the EE index and the disappearance of the polarization pattern that emerged at the beginning of the period.

Results also show that geographical proximity is a factor that has limited the extent of this convergence process. In this paper we addressed two main shortcomings in the EEs literature that are at the center of the recent debate and that deals with the measurement and the evolution of EEs, i.e., the spatial dimension and the time dimension of EEs, so we hope this paper could encourage scholars to further investigate these weakness in a future research agenda on EE.

Stam’s (2018) framework is focused on the conditions of a region to promote and sustain EEs. Accordingly, the EE is viewed as the interaction of systemic conditions and framework conditions. The former, such as networks of entrepreneurs, leadership, finance, talent, knowledge, and support services, are at the heart of Stam’s (2018) EE, while the latter entail a social context (informal and formal institutions) that enables or constrains human interaction.

Iacobucci and Perugini (2020a, 2020b) applied this framework to the Italian case and built the EE for the year 2011. In this paper we extend this analysis to the 2000–2018 period and build the EE following the conditions selected by Stam (2018). However, in the construction of the index we also take into account how the domains and features characterizing EEs have been selected by the literature (Isenberg, 2011; Mason C.& Brown 2014; Ortega Argiles et al., 2014; Stangler J. Bell-Masterson 2015; Sternberg et al., 2019). For instance, we include the “Firm survival” condition in our EE index. The conditions are: (1) Social capital; (2) Entrepreneurship Culture; (3) Physical Infrastructure; (4) Value Added; (5) Finance; (6) New knowledge; (7) Business services; (8) Firm survival; (9) Human capital; (10) Migration flow; (11) Population structure. Due to data availability, we dropped formal and informal institutions from Stam’s (2018) selection. To proxy these variables/ conditions, we gathered data from different sources (see Table 1 in the paper).

(a) Description of the selected variables (1) Social capital The literature on social capital and its positive impact on economic development, innovation, productivity, well-being and other socio-economic aspects of life is extensive (see, for 1 3 279 Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems﻿ instance, Bjørnskov, 2006, among others). More recently, studies have provided evidence of a beneficial effect on entrepreneurial activities. Indeed, social capital, which includes personal relationships, trust, and civic norms, allows entrepreneurs to benefit from positive externalities (Dana et al., 2019; Pittz et al., 2019; Theodoraki et al., 2018). It is argued that formal or informal relationships with family and friends, or networking between groups of people is particularly important in providing intangible resources and competencies of various kinds, such as technological, commercial, administrative and organisational capabilities, to nascent entrepreneurs (Romano et al., 2017). Also, relations with the community and the territory are equally important because they can facilitate the procurement of financial resources, through mechanisms such as, for instance, crowdfunding (Giudici et al., 2018). The literature also shows that a stable environment, in which trust is an essential element, is favourable to the transfer of knowledge and capabilities among members (Iansiti & Levien, 2004; Theodoraki et al., 2018). When relationships are based on trust, members are more willing to cooperate and exchange information, thus facilitating entrepreneurial activities. Moreover, to build trust within an ecosystem, shared norms of behaviour are also a powerful tool (Thomas & Autio, 2014).

Social capital is defined and measured in various ways (Bourdieu, 1986; Coleman, 1988; Putnam, 1993). For these reasons a precise and widely accepted definition is still not available (Adler & Kwon, 2002). The lack of a common definition of social capital has given rise to different measures and a variety of applied empirical works. Generally, these studies classify social capital into several dimensions, which are then reduced to a single index. In this paper, we construct a measure of social capital taking into account those dimensions that have been identified in the literature to be relevant elements for promoting entrepreneurial activities. More specifically, we normalize using the min–max method and aggregate with the arithmetic mean three variables that are proxy for social networks, civic norms, and trust respectively: a) the number of employees in social cooperatives over total employees; b) the percentage of municipal waste object of separate collection on total municipal waste; and c) the number of protests on ordinary bills, drafts and bank checks over the resident population.20 The source of this data is ISTAT.

Even though our selection was constrained by the lack of data at NUTS-3 provincial level for the period under observation (2000–2018), the geographical distribution of the obtained social capital index shows the expected results, i.e., provinces located in the North and the Centre of Italy have a greater endowment of social capital than Southern provinces. This result is in line with previous findings (Cartocci, 2007; Micucci & Nuzzo, 2003). For instance, the Spearman rank correlation coefficients of our social capital index and the social capital index computed by Cartocci (2007), a widely cited work in the social capital literature, is 0.69. For robustness exercise we also compute the social capital index with the principal component analysis. Results do not show sensible changes.

2) Entrepreneurship Culture This variable measures the degree to which entrepreneurship is valued in society (Stam, 2018). The literature often used the share of small businesses or average firm size as a proxy for the entrepreneurial climate (Armington & Acs, 2002; Lee et al., 2004). We use 20 For more details on the methodology used to construct the social capital index see Section b) Index construction and robustness, in this Appendix.

1 3 280 F. Perugini the number of start-ups per thousands of inhabitants. Data are from Movimprese, which is a regular survey of the demography of Italian companies conducted by the Unioncamere, the Italian Chamber of Commerce.

3) Physical infrastructure The important role of transport infrastructure for economic development has been widely investigated in the literature (see, for instance, Audretsch, Heger, et al., 2015; Audretsch, Link, et al., 2015; Spiekermann & Wegener, 2006). It is generally argued that areas with better access to the locations of input materials and markets will be more productive, more competitive and hence more successful than more remote and isolated areas. Our measure of physical infrastructure is an accessibility index. The index takes into account transport infrastructure such as total length of roads, motorways and rail lines in the province itself, but also the connectivity of transport networks, i.e., activities and opportunities that can be reached by the network itself. In other words, we also consider how easily destinations can be reached in terms of travel time, cost or inconvenience. A recent measure of accessibility index for the Italian provinces, which is used in this paper, is provided by Messina (2007).

4) Value Added The spatial dimension of market location is an influential factor that has an impact on entrepreneurial activities. The relevance of the market may also vary in relation to specific products (Sternberg et al., 2019). Stam (2018) measures demand as a composite index consisting of per capita disposable income, population, and an indicator of potential market demand. In this paper we use per-capita Value Added. Value Added at provincial level is from ISTAT and it is measured at current prices. To deflate Value Added we use the consumer price index, which is measured in the main cities of provinces and in regions.

5) Finance The supply and accessibility of finance for firms is vital for firms’ growth and survival (Ortega Argiles et al., 2014; Parker, 2004). Without a large and efficient credit market to supply firms, some entrepreneurs will face a financial barrier making it impossible to seize opportunities. We use the amount of loans to households and firms as a share of Value Added. Data are from the Bank of Italy and ISTAT.

6) New knowledge Investments in new knowledge are an important source of entrepreneurial opportunities (Mason C.& Brown 2014). New knowledge can be measured in different ways, from patents, innovation projects or expenditure in R&D. The indicator of new knowledge used in this paper is the capital stock of R&D by public and private firms over Value Added. The National Institute of Statistics (ISTAT) provides only data on R&D expenditure at regional level. To construct the stock of R&D expenditure at provincial level we first update the time series of regional capital stock of R&D from Bronzini and Piselli (2009), using the perpetual inventory method. At regional level, this time series is highly correlated with other economic variables such as the Value Added, the number of graduated students, and 1 3 281 Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems﻿ the number of firms in high tech industries. In the worst case, that is in the case of the number of graduated students, the correlation coefficient with the stock of R&D is above 0.65. Therefore, we use the province average shares of these three variables to apportion the regional data of the R&D capital stock. Data on expenditure in R&D at regional level are from ISTAT.

7) Business services Business services are an important driver of the knowledge-based economy and a key element for establishing enterprises (Feld, 2012). The growing trend in outsourcing has increased the demand for business services, especially for some core activities such as the recruitment services, ICT development, and administrative activities. The availability of such specific intermediate business services can lower the barrier to firm creation (Stam, 2018). We measure intermediate services as the percentage of active firms in the professional, scientific and technical activities (that are within the M section under the Nace Rev.

2 classification of economic activities) and in the administrative and support service activities (N) in the population of active firms in the business service sector (G-O). Data are from Movimprese.

8) Firm survival The capacity of a firm to survive within a defined area is another important element that shapes an EE. Indeed, the empirical literature shows that if firms belong to a vibrant ecosystem than it increases its odds of survival (Ahmad & Hoffman, 2008). We use the survival rate, which is defined as the percentage of start-up firms at time t-3 that survived at time t and the number of start-up firms at time t-3. Data are from ISTAT.

9) Human capital A relevant explanatory factor of the entrepreneurial activity is to possess the skills and knowledge required to create new companies. The literature shows that these human capital outcomes are vital to discover and create entrepreneurial opportunities, and to assist in the accumulation of new knowledge and the creation of advantages for new firms (Marvel et al., 2016). In the literature it is common to measure human capital with the number of graduated students or with the educational attainment of the resident population. However, work experience it is also assumed to be an important element for entrepreneurial activities. Therefore, in this paper we combine these two elements, and we construct a measure of human capital by considering both formal education and work experience of the resident population. For this purpose, we used the earnings functions of education proposed by Mincer (1974) and estimate the returns to investment in education as follows: logWi = 훾Si + ψ1T1 + ψ2T2 i 1 3 282 F. The parameters γ measure private returns from investment in education while ψ1 , ψ2 the return from the accumulated labor experience.21 The calculation of years of schooling ( Si ) is obtained by the number of years required to reach a certain level of qualification, weighted by the relative province educational qualifications.22 With regard to labor experience ( Ti ), we follow the specification provided by Bils and Klenow (2000): Ti = (Agei −Si −6)(1 −ui).

On average these migrants have higher educational attainment and work experience than the population of origin, so migration flows had profound implications for the economy of the local territories (Piras, 2013). Entrepreneurial activities can also take advantages of migration flows, especially if these are of qualified human capital, because it is another way of increasing the pool of capable entrepreneurs. Moreover, migration flows, by providing a mix of people and ideas, help to strengthen entrepreneurial vitality (Florida et al., 2008).

1 3 283 Space–time analysis of entrepreneurial ecosystems﻿ 11) Population structure Another element that may foster an entrepreneurial ecosystem is the presence of an innovative and entrepreneurship culture. The literature suggests that young people have higher motivation and attitudes for entrepreneurship than older people (Minola, T. Criaco, G. Cassia 2014). However, data on the age of entrepreneurs are not available from ISTAT. Therefore, we use the share of young population, i.e., those aged within the 24–39 bracket, over total population, to proxy how the entrepreneurship culture is spread at provincial level.

Data are from ISTAT. b) Index construction and robustness. Once the suitable variables have been selected, we define the normalization process, the weights, and the aggregation methods in order to construct the composite EE index.

First of all, to ensure comparability and given that the variables have different measurement units, data have been normalized on a 0–10 scale using the min–max method, with higher values representing better performance: ( xp −min(x) xp = max(x) −min(x) ) ∗10 where xp denotes the observed value of the variable in province p. In the second step, the 0–10 variable scores are averaged using equal weight to obtain an aggregate index of EE.

For more comparability of provincial rankings, we further normalize the EE index using the min–max method so that the range of the EE index varies between 0 and 10. For robustness check we also use the standardization method, which converts the variables to a common scale with a mean of zero and standard deviation of one. Indicators with extreme values thus have a greater effect on the composite indicator. However, results do not show substantial changes. The Spearman rank correlation coefficients with our base EE index is 0.97.

We then select the weighting method using equal weights on the variables. It should be noted that no consensus exists on this issue. The selection of the weights implies that a judgement should be being made in terms of the relative importance of each indicator.

Equal weights have some limits that can be mainly associated to its simplicity. However, equal weight is the most common scheme used in the development of composite indicators.

This is especially the case when there are no statistical or empirical grounds for choosing different weights (Nardo et al., 2005). Moreover, equal weights might be a valid approach compared to other alternative weighting schemes that are based on statistical methods, such as the principal component analysis, or on subjective judgement, where weights are assigned by the researchers or by a participatory methods that involve various stakeholders, experts, citizens or politicians (see Nardo et al., 2005). Indeed, the former has some limitations especially when the variables are not highly correlated, like for some variables in our cases, while the latter requires the involvement of experts and stakeholders and the collection of their opinion on the importance of each variable. For these reasons we use equal weights to aggregate our variables.

We then proceed with the aggregation of the variables. To this purpose we choose the arithmetic mean, which is the most used aggregation method. However, we perform some robustness check by calculating the index with the geometric mean, which rewards those provinces with higher scores. Results show that changes in provincial rankings across weighting schemes are very small. The Spearman rank correlation coefficient with our base EE index is 0.98.̂ 1 3 284 F. Perugini We perform some robustness check on the final EE index. More specifically we focus on the dimensionality issue, that is we assess to what extent the final EE index is sensitive to the inclusion/exclusion of a single variable (Nardo et al., 2005). To this purpose, given that our EE index derived from the aggregation of k dimensions (k = 11), we construct k EE index by excluding one dimension at a time. The analysis shows that in all cases the Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient with the original EE index is above 0.95, suggesting that the EE index is well-balanced in all dimensions.

Finally, we compare our EE index with a previous index calculated at the Italian NUTS-1 level, i.e., the REDI (Regional Entrepreneurial Development Index) from the national GEI (Global Entrepreneurship Index).23 For the Italian administrative classification NUTS-1 corresponds to 4 geographical units: North-West, North-East, Centre, and South and Islands. When we aggregate our index at this spatial scale level the correlation coefficient with the REDI index calculated in the year 2007 is very high, 0.93. Also, the Spearman rank correlation coefficient is high, 0.80. This results suggests that our EE measure is well-defined.

This approach works in two steps. First, the probability density function of the EE index is estimated by using a kernel function (Silverman, 1986). Let xi, … , xn be a sample of n independent and identically distributed observations on a random variable X . The density value ̂ f(x) at a given point x is estimated by the following kernel density estimator: n ∑ K nh i=1 (∥x −xi ∥ ) (2)̂ f(x) = 1 h where ̂ f(x) the density estimation of the variable x , h is the bandwidth (smoothing parameter) of the interval around x, and K(∙) is the smooth and symmetric kernel function integrated to unity. Finally, ∥∙∥ is the Euclidean distance. The kernel estimator assigns a weight to each observation in the interval around x with the weight being inversely proportional to the distance between the observation and x. The density estimate consists of the vertical sum of frequencies at each observation. The resulting smooth curve allows us to visualize the shape of the distribution of provincial per-capita income and detect the presence of convergence clubs represented by modes.

Second, the dynamics of the distribution and intra-distributional mobility of provinces is estimated by the stochastic kernel, which maps the density of a random variable at one point in time into the density in a subsequent period, where the density functions have been calculated through kernel density estimators (Stokey et al., 1989). In other words, the stochastic kernel describes the law of motion of a sequence of distributions and it serves to retrieve the evolution of the probability distribution of a random variable along time.

Assuming that the frequency of the distribution follows a first order Markov process, in a transition probability matrix M each element indicates the probability that a province that was in state i in period t ends up in state j at t + 1. Therefore, given the distribution of the EE index across provinces at time t (EEt ) then the evolution of EE can be described by the law of motion: EEt+1 = M ∗EEt.

Accordingly, the ergodic distribution allows to analyze the longrun tendencies of provincial EE assuming that the observed dynamics continue to hold.

This long-run equilibrium distribution plays a central role in the analysis of provincial convergence. At any point of time, the distribution ft+s (xt+s ) may reflect disequilibrium due to short-run external shocks. In the long-run, however, the ergodic distribution, (xt+s ) , remains invariant and all transitionary effects disappear. Moreover, a tendency of f∞ f∞ (xt+s ) towards a unique mode, means distributional convergence. On the other hand, a divergent tendency of f∞ (xt+s ) towards bimodality (or multimodality), means polarization (convergence clubs) (Galor, 1996).

Finally, the stochastic kernel can also be used to describe movements between two distributions, i.e. an actual unconditional distribution and a conditional distribution (Quah, 1996). The latter is the distribution that prevails when other variables affect future values of the EE index. In this case, when the mass of probability lies along the main diagonal the conditioning factor is not responsible for the variation in the actual 1 3 286 F. Perugini distribution. In contrast, when a factor is responsible for most of the dispersion, conditioning out its effect will result in a kernel parallel to the unconditional distribution (so that provinces share similar values of the EE index when the effect of the factor is removed, regardless of their position in the original distribution).
