Given the sensitivity of these types of strategic decisions, the interactions they entail between government and other regional actors with their own vested interests and the little experience of regional governments in prioritisation, new questions emerge around the roles that evaluation can play. In particular, there is potential to inject collective strategic intelligence into decision-making, a very speciﬁc need for regional governments with limited capabilities and capacities for prioritisation in an experimental context. Yet for such strategic intelligence to be considered robust and legitimate, the governance processes under-pinning the production and use of that intelligence warrant attention.

Governance of evaluation is often neglected in the evaluation literature. Debates have traditionally been focused on the external/internal evaluator issue with little emphasis on the process of governance itself. However, moving from individual policy evaluation to policy-mix evaluation highlights the importance of evaluation governance.

Innovation policy mixes are normally designed and implemented by diﬀerent government actors operating at diﬀerent administrative levels (Magro et al., 2014). While some coordination in policy design and implementation is often achieved, a systemic coordination of evaluation is a more complex task, due in part to the sensitivity surrounding ‘being evaluated’. In the context of smart specialisation strategies these challenges are particularly acute. There are multiple actors with a stake in research and innovation policy, both within government (diﬀerent levels of governments impact regional strategies as do diﬀerent departments and agencies), and outside government (in the other ‘helixes’ of business, research and civil society). These actors both engage in the governance process setting the direction of the strategy and are subjects and/or objects of evaluation of the policy-mix supporting the strategy.

That raises potential conﬂicts of interest, as engagement in strategy shapes actors behaviour and that behaviour interacts with the policymix, which needs to be monitored and evaluated for policy learning purposes.2 It is this link between behavioural change and governance of evaluation that remains unexplored in the literature.

The key contribution of this paper is to present a concrete view on the emerging governance needs of evaluation in the context of new place-based innovation strategies. It does so by dissecting characteristics of innovation policy mixes that are particularly important in the context of smart specialisation strategies; their verticality, their directionality and their capacity to foster experimentation. The paper then develops a conceptual framework for analysing the governance of policy-mix evaluation as an integral part of placed-based innovation policy. The framework is oriented to better understanding the conditions under which evaluation is able to provide collective strategic intelligence and contribute to the development of the government capabilities needed in smart specialisation strategies. These arguments are explored through the example of the Basque Country in Spain, which serves as an illustration of the diﬀerent elements to be taken into account for establishing a collective, strategic evaluation process in a complex setting of institutions and actors.

2. Innovation policy mixes in the context of new place-based policies Recent years have seen a general increase in attention aﬀorded to the concept of policy-mix. This is evident in what has been called the third generation of policy-design theories (Howlett and Rayner, 2007, 2013; Howlett et al., 2015), in the innovation policy literature in general (Flanagan et al., 2011; Borrás and Edquist, 2013; Magro and Wilson, 2013; Lanahan and Feldman, 2015; Flanagan and Uyarra, 2 It is also worth noting that policy learning itself is usually not a shared purpose of all actors, so there will be asymmetries of interest.

2 2016; Martin, 2016), and in literature on sustainable transitions speciﬁcally (Kivimaa and Kern, 2016; Kern et al., 2017; Rogge and Reichardt, 2016). This interest has been fairly rapidly passed onto policy-makers, at least at a superﬁcial level, as can be seen in the increasing usage of the term policy-mix in policy documents. The European Commission’s 2012 Guide to Research and Innovation Strategies for Smart Specialisation (Foray et al., 2012), for example, is explicit in establishing the ‘deﬁnition of coherent policy mix’ as one of six steps towards a smart specialisation strategy, and this has helped the terminology to become widespread among regional innovation policy-makers.

The analysis of policies seeking to foster sustainable transitions is an area where the signiﬁcance of place is particularly evident, as seen in literature on the geography of sustainable transitions (Coenen and Truﬀer, 2012; Hansen and Coenen, 2015). Coenen et al. (2012: 968), for example, highlight the “institutional embeddedness of socio-technical development processes within speciﬁc territorial spaces”, working alongside “an explicit multi-scalar conception of socio-technical trajectories”. This is in line with Truﬀer’s (2016: 12) identiﬁcation of the need to disentangle complex multi-level geographical relationships so as “to better understand who plays a central role in the core processes and how policies may be deﬁned that are able to intervene in these complex interaction patterns.” Complexity of relationships between a wide range of diﬀerent interested actors is indeed a common theme in analysis of place-based sustainable transitions (Hodson and Marvin, 2010, 2012; Loorbach and Rotmans, 2010; Maassen, 2012; Shove and Walker, 2010), and highlights the absolute importance of understanding the governance context in which strategy and policy decisions are made.

2.1. Smart specialisation and innovation policy-mixes The place-based nature of sustainable transitions implies strong synergies with emerging theory and practice in the latest generation of regional innovation policies, so-called smart specialisation strategies. A coming together of science, technology and innovation (STI) policy with new industrial policy (Aranguren et al., 2017a; Radosevic, 2017a), these regional strategies provide a policy framework that follows the shift in literature and practice from spatially-blind to place-based innovation (Barca, 2009; McCann and Ortega-Argilés, 2015). Smart specialisation strategies are being implemented across Europe with impetus from the European Commission (including structural funding conditionality that insists all regions have a Research and Innovation Strategy for Smart Specialisation or RIS3). Rooted in previous placebased innovation policies, they shift the focus towards the explicit prioritization of activities based on regional capabilities. In many regions this prioritisation has been linked explicitly or implicitly to sustainable transition as a grand societal challenge (Capello and Kroll, 2016).

While in one sense smart specialisation strategies are an evolution of the regional innovation systems approach and acknowledgement of the desirability of a strongly place-based innovation policy, they have also been inﬂuenced by arguments for new industrial policies in which prioritization of activities is determined not by government, but by a nexus of private-public cooperation (Rodrik, 2004). Thus two distinguishing characteristics of smart specialisation strategies can be highlighted. Firstly, like industrial policies or mission-oriented STI policies, they are directional; they imply making choices. Secondly, they rely on new governance processes for making those choices; they are rooted in an experimental ‘entrepreneurial discovery process’ (EDP) involving a wide range of regional stakeholders from the quadruple helix of government, business, research and civil society (Foray, 2013, 2015).

It is the notion of an EDP that provides the key novelty of smart specialisation strategies. It implies that the governance process through which regional stakeholders identify the areas in which the region should specialise and build new paths becomes a central anchoring E. Magro, J.R. Wilson Research Policy xxx (xxxx) xxx–xxx point for innovation policies. As such innovation policies become necessarily rooted in evolutionary approaches. Although still very much a black box, how to build a sound EDP has been the object of increasing attention (Aranguren et al., 2018; Gianelle et al., 2016; Marinelli and Perianez Forte, 2017). Most critically for understanding policy mixes, an EDP implies a new governance conﬁguration underpinning regional innovation strategy and policy. It transforms them into territorial, rather than government, strategies and policies. This new governance is a highly pluralistic context (Lynn, 2012; Howlett and Ramesh, 2014; Jarzabkowski and Fenton, 2006) in which building shared vision requires navigating through a range of diﬀerent interests and potential conﬂicts among actors. As such, Morgan (2017: 569) has argued that it “places unprecedented demands on public sector bodies”.

Another key feature of smart specialisation strategies is their treatment of research and innovation as transversal elements, inﬂuenced by and impacting on government policy from the whole spectrum of government departments. Developing a coherent policy mix, roadmaps and action plans to promote regional priorities is one of the six steps promoted by the European Commission (Foray et al., 2012). Yet policy-mixes in the smart specialisation context have tended to be considered more a portfolio of instruments from which to pick and choose, than a policy setting that might be strategically used to aﬀect the directionality of innovation, fostering a structural transformation of the economy through experimentation. This is somewhat incongruent given the aim of smart specialisation strategies to generate structural transformation through targeting speciﬁc innovation activities over others.3 There is indeed little reference to new innovation policy instruments or new combinations of instruments in the smart specialisation literature, and Veugelers (2015) and McCann and Ortega-Argilés (2016) ﬁnd relative homogeneity of policy mixes across Europe. Moreover, very little emphasis has been placed on the link between the government role in designing and implementing an appropriate policy-mix and the dynamic, pluralistic EDP process through which strategic direction should emerge. Directionality through experimentation, which is at the core of the EDP, tends to materialise in practice through the selection of projects to fund. How the dynamics of that project selection are linked to policy-mixes remains underexplored in two ways. The ﬁrst is in terms of how prioritised projects are supported by policy-mixes. This relates to neoclassical failures, where policy can rely on classical incentive mechanisms. The second is in terms of how policy-mixes might themselves contribute to generating experimentation spaces. This relates to coordination failures, implying that policy-mixes should include ‘softer’ instruments (Rodríguez-Pose and Wilkie, 2017). In practice, however, the experimental approach to smart specialisation strategies has been conﬁned to the selection phase, and implementation is recurring to traditional instruments (Radosevic, 2017b). This poses a particular policy-mix challenge given acknowledgement that the EDP should be continuous and present throughout the implementation of smart specialisation strategies (Marinelli and Perianez Forte, 2017).

2.2. Dissecting the innovation policy mix There are several deﬁnitions of the policy-mix concept, some of them stressing the complex nature of the term (Flanagan et al., 2011), and others focused on the issue of which elements should be combined in a policy-mix (Borrás and Edquist, 2013). Rogge and Reichardt (2016) propose a holistic view of the term and highlight that a policy mix is not only made up of concrete elements (instruments), but also by processes (policy-making) and their characteristics (mainly consistency of elements, coherence of processes, credibility and comprehensiveness).

3 In this sense the rapid uptake of smart specialisation strategies provides a great example of the ubiquity of use of the policy mix term with little depth of understanding around what it could imply.

3 Howlett et al. (2015) propose a typology of policy mixes ranging from simple cases in which there are single instruments from single policies and one single government, to more complex ones (multi goals, multi policies and multi-level governments). Regional innovation policy is in this respect considered a complex setting (Magro and Wilson, 2013), in which we can ﬁnd diﬀerent instruments from diﬀerent policy domains that respond to diﬀerent rationales, target diﬀerent actors, and are designed and implemented over time by governments at diﬀerent levels.4 However, one of the main criticisms to the regional innovation policy literature – including the European Commission’s Smart Specialisation Guide (Foray et al., 2012) – is that it tends to list innovation policy instruments as options from a portfolio that policymakers can choose from, contradicting the notion of ‘one size doesn’t ﬁt all’ (Todlting and Trippl, 2005). There is little explicit reﬂection about the rationales of each instrument, the policy goals they can be addressing, or the overall policy strategy they respond to. This is especially problematic given consensus in policy design literature that Tinbergen’s rule of a one-to-one correspondence between instrument and policy goal no longer holds. Thus one instrument may address several targets or several instruments address the same target. Additionally, policy mixes are built over time and normally result from incremental changes that introduce modiﬁcations to existing instruments or add new ones to the previous mix (Flanagan et al., 2011; Streek and Thelen, 2005). This is reﬂected in the often little room for manoeuvre policy-makers have to introduce changes to historicallyrooted practices (Howlett and Rayner, 2007).5 To further dissect the innovation policy mix concept in the context of smart specialisation strategies, it is particularly relevant to consider three dimensions in greater detail; their verticality, their directionality, and their capacity to facilitate experimentation.

2.3. The verticality of policy-mixes for smart specialisation The multi-level reality for regions has strong implications for the consistency of policy-mixes. The absence of contradictions among policy objectives, the presence of synergies among instruments and the alignment of the instrument mix to the evolving regional innovation strategy become even more complicated questions when the administrative boundaries of policy-mixes are blurred. Thus the capacity of regional actors to generate coordination mechanisms between government levels becomes critical.

On the one hand contradictory objectives could come from diﬀerent policy interests; e.g. national goals to champion certain activities by investing in large infrastructures versus regional goals to promote the activities coming from the local EDP. On the other hand the type of instruments integrated into the policy-mix is likely to depend on both the geographical scale at which policies are designed to impact and the level of government responsible. There are some instruments that are considered tools for national governments and have hence been neglected in the place-based policy literature, although they are included in the portfolio of possible instruments to be implemented by regional governments. The use of public procurement for boosting innovation is a good example of this (Uyarra et al., 2017). Network or cluster policy instruments, on the other hand, are most commonly implemented at regional level, due to their lower cost and their reliance on proximity relations.

The directionality of policy mixes for smart specialisation Policy-mix directionality is an issue that has not been much considered in either the general literature on policy design or that on innovation policy. While the focus of the policy-mix concept tends to be put on maximising the complementarity between instruments (Howlett et al., 2015), how to address directionality is often forgotten. Indeed, European regions had a ‘menu’ of instruments in the RIS3 guide (Foray et al., 2012) according to diﬀerent taxonomies, but there was no clear indication about the directional or neutral nature of the instruments to be implemented. Regions therefore face the challenge of building consistent policy-mixes as described by Rogge and Reichardt (2016) that explicitly target prioritised activities through experimentation.

Many regions have followed a ‘patching’ path (Howlett and Rayner, 2013), essentially modifying existing instruments in order to address new challenges or just keeping the traditional ones, which minimise the experimental nature of smart specialisation strategies (McCann and Ortega-Argilés, 2014). Although Howlett et al. (2015) suggest following this strategy in established and complex environments, it can be risky in the framework of smart specialisation strategies. In lieu of a more comprehensive re-design of the policy mix, there is a danger that patched policies may simply be supporting projects or activities labelled as ‘prioritised’ by actors in order not to lose previous support, leading to opportunistic behaviour. In addition, it is diﬃcult to address certain speciﬁc problems faced in many smart specialisation strategies with this approach; for example the problem of reducing scaling-up problems in certain key enabling technologies, like nanotechnologies, that are important for the development of new innovation paths from other priority areas.

An alternative solution is to design tailored instruments for each priority and priority goal. Yet this generates high administration costs and may not yield high additionality. It is here therefore where real concern with policy-mix could add a lot to the strategic design of policies to support smart specialisation; for example through a policy-mix design for each priority area that combines neutral instruments for the whole economy with tailored instruments addressing speciﬁc failures.

This would require eﬀective coordination mechanisms to guarantee coherence. Moreover, the dynamism inherent in the EDP and the plurality of interests contained within that process makes it critical that there is strong strategic intelligence around how this policy-mix is working and evolving to meet new needs.

2.5. The challenge of experimentalism Building on the above arguments it is clear that the practical challenge of policy-mix design and implementation in the context of regional smart specialisation strategies goes beyond improving previously existing mixes of instruments. Innovation policy mixes to support smart specialisation strategies should be composed of directional and horizontal instruments (from various domains and administered by different government levels) that promote speciﬁc innovation investments, but that also facilitate processes of experimentation (Magro and Wilson, 2013; Reid and Maroulis, 2017; Rodríguez-Pose and Wilkie, 2017). Yet smart specialisation literature frequently identiﬁes as a major obstacle the lack of regional capabilities to develop an experiment-based regional policy (Foray, 2017; Marques and Morgan, 2018; Radosevic, 2017b).

The remainder of the paper explores how the strategic intelligence and learning provided by appropriately governed evaluation processes might be part of the solution to boosting regional capabilities, both with respect to experimental processes and with respect to eﬀectively managing the aforementioned challenges of policy-mix verticality and directionality. A key argument is that new place-based innovation policies convert policy-mix evaluation from an operational to a strategic issue; it becomes a collective intelligence process that is central for avoiding coordination failures among diﬀerent policy levels, for 4 eﬀectively navigating decisions around strategic direction, and for fostering meaningful experimentation. This in turn opens a series of questions around the governance of policy-mix evaluation.

3. Evaluation governance for smart specialisation policy-mixes Despite an adoption of the policy-mix language within the innovation policy-making community, there has been little analysis of how the singular characteristics of policy-mixes for place-based innovation that are analysed above shape evaluation practices and vice versa.

Monitoring and evaluation clearly has large potential to contribute to understanding the behaviour and performance of policy-mixes, going beyond accountability purposes to focus on learning. While the results of policy learning will diﬀer depending on the object and subject of learning (Bennett and Howlett, 1992), the timely injection of monitoring and evaluation knowledge will be a key input. However, innovation policy-mix learning requires a shift from fragmented evaluation of the eﬀectiveness of individual instruments (Martin, 2016) to more holistic evaluations accounting for interactions among instruments in a complex policy context (multi-rationales, multi-level, multiactor) (Magro and Wilson, 2013).

In the context of smart specialisation strategies policy learning around the directionality of policy instruments should be a prime concern (Magro and Wilson, 2015), as should learning related to the eﬀectiveness of experimentation processes and to vertical policy coordination. Yet while monitoring and evaluation is acknowledged as important for smart specialisation – featuring strongly in both of the Commission’s guides (Foray et al., 2012; Gianelle et al., 2016) – the emphasis on how they can contribute to strengthen the critical link between implementation of the innovation policy-mix and the dynamic, experimental nature of an EDP is largely missing. In practice only very conservative approaches employing traditional indicators to monitor smart specialisation strategies tend to be found (McCann and Ortega- Argilés, 2016).

It is argued here that concern with the appropriate governance of policy-mix evaluation in highly pluralistic contexts is likely to be central to its usefulness as a strategic intelligence tool that can boost oftenlacking regional capabilities and guide both the EDP and the dynamic design and implementation of the innovation policy-mix.6 In particular, the new governance arrangements embodied in the notion of a territorial EDP should be extended to evaluation. This marks a signiﬁcant change for an activity that is usually conceived as a governmentcentred (and relatively closed) process of gathering and analysing information; it requires “fourth generation” evaluation practice in Guba and Lincoln’s (1989) classiﬁcation.

3.1. Changing the paradigm: evaluation as social learning Del Río (2014), pleading for a better deﬁnition of policy boundaries in order to assess the success of a given policy-mix distinguishes between horizontal (single-level) and vertical (multi-level) mixes. While the vertical dimension is the most complicated for assessing policymixes (Stame, 2004), the horizontal dimension also has potential to be a source of vested interests among diﬀerent regional actors, particularly in the context of a pluralistic EDP. Tackling this complexity requires changes of evaluation paradigm that are only possible through social learning (Bennett and Howlett, 1992). Indeed, following Del Río (2014), and also Kulhman’s (2001) arguments on vested interests (winners at a superior administrative levels might lead to losers at inferior levels), it can be argued that a framework for evaluating policymixes in the context of smart specialisation strategies should be 6 This is in line with the arguments of McCann and Ortega-Argilés (2016) around the importance of learning by evaluating in place-based policy experiments, and reﬂects the emphasis on experimentation in much of the literature on sustainable transitions.

Such an approach might ﬁnd conﬂict with the European Commission’s primary concern with ‘accountability evaluation’ of the funds invested in smart specialisation strategies, leading to un-useful evaluation practices (Amanatidou et al., 2014). Moving beyond this dichotomy requires working on the complementarities of the diﬀerent approaches and appreciating how evaluation evidence of diﬀerent kinds, when embedded in appropriate governance arrangements (Howlett and Rayner, 2013), can generate collective, strategic learning.

In particular, it implies recognising the signiﬁcance of behavioural additionality in terms of promoting experimentation and uncovering appropriate strategic direction, alongside the more traditional evaluation measures of input and output additionality.

As such a better understanding of innovation policy-mixes for placebased policies doesn’t only depend on ﬁnding appropriate evaluation methods, but also on how evaluation is governed. Recent literature on monitoring and evaluation of smart specialisation strategies puts emphasis on governance structures such as evaluation committees as a passive mechanism for evaluating progress (see Gianelle and Kleinbrinck, 2015). It doesn’t consider how governance processes interact actively with the evaluation of smart specialisation strategies and their policy-mixes, shaping actors behaviour. Yet literature on evaluation emphasises not only on the formative role of evaluation for policy learning, but also the importance of people for understanding change (Pawson and Tilley, 1997) and for making evaluation useful (Patton, 2012). Indeed, the principles of empowerment evaluation, namely training, facilitation and advocacy (Fetterman, 1994), integrated into emerging smart specialisation governance arrangements, could constitute a powerful source of change and contribute to promote social learning capabilities.

3.2. Towards a conceptual framework for policy-mix evaluation governance Among the dimensions that make innovation policy-mixes quite singular in the context of smart specialisation strategies and related sustainable transitions, the analysis of the previous section highlighted verticality and directionality in an experimentalist context. In this extreme pluralistic context (Gil and Pinto, 2017) the vested interests of multiple actors at diﬀerent levels are likely to be present, and a sophisticated network governance solution will be required to navigate these interests. This governance situation will also condition the evaluation of policy-mixes, leading to diﬀerent answers to the questions of ‘why evaluate?’, ‘what to evaluate?’, ‘how to evaluate?’ and ‘who should be responsible for evaluation?’. Indeed, the collective results and usefulness of evaluation will depend on the forces of the diﬀerent private and public actors embedded in the EDP and with vested interests in the evaluation outcomes.

In less complex innovation policy situations, the main purpose of evaluation is likely to be accountability and control, as policy decisionmaking is principally within-government. This may lead to fairly traditional evaluation processes (the ﬁrst and second generations of evaluation practices following Guba and Lincoln, 1989), which rely on either internal or external evaluators conducting evaluations based on the impacts and cost eﬀectiveness of the mix of instruments being employed (including their interactions). However, the plurality of agents involved in the policy process surrounding smart specialisation strategies alongside the particular sensitivity of directionality, where conﬂicts in interest are likely, changes the requirements. Given the sensitivity and subjectivity of certain evaluation information – e.g.

around the ‘success’ of following certain innovation pathways over others – it will be very important that all parties buy into the evaluation process and that it is governed in a way that is seen as legitimate. Only under those circumstances is evaluation likely to be accepted as impartial strategic intelligence that can legitimately inform speciﬁc decisions on both the policy-mix and the overall strategic process in which 5 agents are engaged through the EDP.

This assumption does not imply a rejection of more traditional evaluations for individual instruments with a purpose of accountability (for example evaluation of smart specialisation strategies to fulﬁl the European Commission’s requirements), however, but rather an integration of those into systems evaluations in which other evaluations are more learning-oriented (Arnold, 2004). Nevertheless, evaluation of innovation policy-mixes in the context of smart specialisation strategies should move from being primarily about accountability to being a strategic learning tool at diﬀerent levels. This implies a focus on learning about the contribution of policy-mixes to the directionality of the strategy, but also the capacity to detect changes in actors’ behaviour towards a more experimental or entrepreneurial character, in essence evaluating the EDP itself.

Approaches like stakeholder-evaluation (Hansen and Vendung, 2010) are more suitable for such governance contexts than other traditional evaluation approaches. Yet, the main unresolved issue does not rely on the speciﬁc methods to be used in discrete evaluation tasks but on the overall governance of the process. That means not only involving stakeholders in the evaluation, but turning it around to put them at the core of the process, following principles of empowerment evaluation (Fetterman, 1994). The ‘owners’ of the policy instruments that compose the policy-mix, the beneﬁciaries of those instruments and other related stakeholders essentially shift from being object of evaluation to protagonists. The objective is to facilitate collective strategic intelligence and learning that leads to changes that improve decision-making and experimentation processes related to the smart specialisation strategy.

These ideas are illustrated in Fig. 1, which depicts three possible governance modes for the evaluation of innovation policy-mixes. These move through diﬀerent scenarios of policy-mix complexity, which are argued to shape the governance requirements of policy-mix evaluation.

The last scenario corresponds with the characteristics of smart specialisation strategies – in particular the signiﬁcance of directionality, verticality and the need for experimentation. It is important to note, however, that the three types of evaluation and their associated governance modes could co-exist – and indeed are likely to co-exist – in the framework of a systemic evaluation (Arnold, 2004) that brings together diﬀerent pieces of evidence in a strategic learning framework.

4. The Basque country smart specialisation strategy: an illustration of policy mix evaluation governance challenges 4.1. Background to the case The Basque Country, a region of two million people in the north of Spain, has been object of analysis for many innovation scholars in recent years due to what is usually seen as successful industrial transformation and innovation upgrading. It is one of the few European regions considered as a ‘real’ regional innovation system (Cooke et al., 2000) and one of the few that already had an incipient smart specialisation strategy even before the term was conceived (Aranguren et al., 2016). In addition, the Basque Country holds strong regional competences on innovation policy which exist alongside limited national competences and signiﬁcant sub-regional competences. Thus the region can be deﬁned as a policy space in which innovation policies from diﬀerent levels are being felt (Uyarra and Flanagan, 2010), as a consequence of which innovation policy and its derived instruments are embedded in a complex, multi-level policy framework.

Each industrial sector has its own historical and operational dynamics, so joining visions, steps and strategies requires a really intensive-cooperation driven process. Even in the public area, and although the Department of Economic Development and Competitiveness is leading the process, there are clear links to other departments, institutions…” (Aranguren et al., 2016 p. 46).

This complex environment is reﬂected in both the governance of the EDP surrounding this priority (see later analysis), and in the speciﬁc policy-mix for addressing the priority, which are mainly instruments from the regional government, although instruments from diﬀerent administrative levels are also included. They are principally designed and implemented by two of the main regional government departments: the Department of Economic Development and Competitiveness (DEDC) and the Department of Education.

Other innovation policy instruments at sub-regional levels that impact in the region include those implemented by the Provincial Councils of Bizkaia and Gipuzkoa, among which we can highlight tax incentives for R&D. In addition, there are city-level economic development initiatives, for example from Bilbao city council, which are mainly related to the use of urban spaces and encouraging cross-fertilisation across activities. At the supra-regional level, also, there are some national and European STI policies (for example the H2020 programme) that impact on ﬁrms and knowledge infrastructures related to advanced manufacturing in the region. Thus there is a strong verticality to the Basque innovation policy mix for advanced manufacturing, with at least ﬁve diﬀerent administrative levels involved.

Analysis of the directionality of the policy mix is less straightforward. While the smart specialisation strategy by deﬁnition introduces directionality into the strategy for innovation, it can be argued that the Basque policy-mix for advanced manufacturing is composed of a mix of instruments that exhibit diﬀerent degrees of directionality. There are some neutral instruments with no explicit directionality, such as those that support non-technological innovation in ﬁrms. There are also instruments that are directional per se, such as those that support scientiﬁc and technological agents focused on speciﬁc domains and technologies.

Finally there are instruments that have been ‘made’ directional to serve the strategy after a patching process. This last group warrants further explanation. The Basque Country has always been characterised by a high degree of support to industrial ﬁrms based largely on subsidies. One of the characteristics of these support mechanisms has been their lack of directionality. However, in recent years and especially as a consequence of the implementation of the smart specialisation strategy, the Basque Government has introduced as criteria for eligibility to subsidized projects that they have to be conducted in one of the ‘prioritised domains’ of the strategy. In that sense, advanced manufacturing projects will be prioritised over projects that fall outside of this domain. Although the instrument is not directional by deﬁnition, the introduction of these criteria in a patching process has introduced directionality.

4.3. New governance arrangements for smart specialisation The degree of verticality and directionality of the policy mix in this case pleads for a new governance model based on experimentation in 7 See Aranguren et al. (2016) for more detail.

7 which the actors embedded in the EDP play a bigger role in the governance of the innovation policy mix and its evaluation. The response of the Basque smart specialisation strategy in terms of generating new governance arrangements can be split into two: ‘hard governance’ arrangements in terms of the regional government’s oversight of the implementation and evolution of the strategy (and associated policy mix); and ‘soft governance’ arrangements in terms of the wider engagement, alongside government, of business, research and civil society in a socalled ‘entrepreneurial discovery process’. Both respond in diﬀerent ways to the network governance challenges posed by innovation policymix verticality, directionality and experimentation in a smart specialisation context.

The key novelty in the ‘hard governance’ arrangements or governance structures has been the establishment of an interdepartmental committee to coordinate the implementation of the strategy across the diﬀerent government departments implicated and also to act as a focal point for vertical, inter-institutional coordination (Aranguren et al., 2016). This committee is composed of representatives of seven regional departments alongside the Presidency department, and its main role is setting milestones and supervising the strategy process by providing a meeting point to share what is happening in the development of the diﬀerent priority areas. It is in this space where a shared vision is being built within government, an aspect that is particularly important for policy-mix purposes as it includes representatives from the diﬀerent ‘owners’ of the instruments. The potential for improved communication and coordination between government departments around the innovation policy mix is recognised by those involved, and the discussions here also form the basis for stronger coordination with government institutions at diﬀerent levels through an inter-institutional committee that meets after each inter-departmental meeting (Aranguren et al., 2016). Therefore, it could be argued that these new ‘within-government’ governance arrangements in response to the demands of the smart specialisation strategy governance favour better policy-mix governance in the region.

In terms of the ‘soft governance’ arrangements, the key novelty is the establishment of so-called ‘live processes for the development of the priority areas’. In practice these are organised through ‘steering groups’ as spaces that bring together the key public and private agents, and form a focal point for the establishment of relevant thematic working groups to explore and develop each of the priority areas. In the case of the advanced manufacturing priority, for example, the composition of the steering group includes representatives from the Basque Government (Department of Economic Development and Competitiveness-DEDC and its agency-SPRI), from cluster associations and ﬁrms (automotive, machine tools, energy and ICT clusters), from knowledge and technology agents (technology centres and universities) and from intermediate agents.

In theory these soft governance arrangements should provide directionality and discovery of new activities based on experimentation over time, by identifying and exploring opportunities based on the competences and knowledge of the diﬀerent agents involved.

Government involvement in the steering groups and their reporting back to the interdepartmental committee should enable this directionality to feed into the innovation policy mix. In the case of the advanced manufacturing priority, almost all the regional actors with vested interests in developing an advanced manufacturing strategy are involved.8 However, there is no direct representation from some of the key public agents that design and implement instruments included in the policy-mix, such as the regional department of education or the subregional representatives. Eﬀective transmission of the emerging directionality to the diﬀerent departments and levels of government involved in implementing relevant policy instruments thus depends on 8 Indeed, there is an argument that the presence of the most dominant actors crowds out the involvement of small companies or entrepreneurs.

E. Magro, J.R. Wilson Research Policy xxx (xxxx) xxx–xxx the connection between these soft governance arrangements and the hard governance arrangements of the interdepartmental and interinstitutional committees.

4.4. Evaluation context and challenges Monitoring and evaluation has traditionally been considered one of the weaknesses of the Basque innovation system and policies (OECD (2011); Morgan, 2013). In recent years, however, the region has sought to push forward in this area and advances have been made in the evaluation framework established around the smart specialisation strategy. Evaluation of the smart specialisation strategy is conducted by Innobasque, the regional innovation agency, which has established a framework for evaluation that includes three diﬀerent lines: 1 Monitoring the current strategic objectives and their evolution; 2 Assessing the contribution of individual instruments to the strategy (an exercise based on the monitoring system implemented by SPRI, the Basque Business Development Agency); 3 A comparative analysis of the Basque innovation system.

While this evaluation framework is in the early stages of implementation, by way of illustration it is interesting to assess it against the arguments made in the previous section. There we argued that innovation policy-mix in the context of smart specialisation strategies places diﬀerent requirements on evaluation processes given the plurality of agents (public and private) involved in the policy process and the sensitivity of the directionality issue. More concretely, we suggested that the evaluation process itself should be governed in a way that is seen by all parties as being valid and leading to impartial strategic intelligence. This would imply moving from traditional evaluation methods to others such as stakeholder-driven evaluation, in which empowerment principles are present. In the context of this case, such a process could be an important tool for ensuring that the link between the soft governance and hard governance analysed above are eﬀective and would feed the strategy with a learning loop.

While the monitoring of current strategic objectives and the comparative analysis of the Basque innovation system (objectives 1 and 3) are useful to understand where the region is in terms of overall direction and benchmarking with others, only the second objective of the framework can truly be termed a policy evaluation exercise. Moreover, it is fairly limited in terms of analysing the policy-mix as it is currently being conceived over one speciﬁc subsidy programme designed at the regional level. This implies that it will not easily be able to address verticality and directionality issues.

Indeed, the evaluation framework has been established for the strategy as a whole, as a Science, Technology and Innovation Policy, but there is not yet a consensus-built framework for each of the speciﬁc priorities, such as advanced manufacturing. Such a general approach has some disadvantages. First of all, evaluation will provide insights about general targets in the STI policy context (for example about R&D investments and their impacts), but little speciﬁc knowledge about how the policy is contributing to advance in each of the priorities and how the policy-mix contributes to the generation of experimentation and directionality in those areas. Secondly, the governance framework for evaluation will not take into account the speciﬁcities of each priority setting, missing an opportunity to take advantage of the dialogue spaces that are being established as part of the EDP to engage the diﬀerent stakeholders in evaluation as a strategic intelligence tool to their discovery processes.

In the speciﬁc case of advanced manufacturing, for example, the framework takes into account only one of the government departments and levels responsible for relevant policy-mix instruments (the DEDC), and users (cluster associations, ﬁrms, knowledge organisations,…) are the object of the evaluation but not taking part in the exercise as part of their engagement in the RIS3. Following our arguments above, with this 8 approach accountability purposes might be ﬁlled, but learning ones might be limited, inhibiting the strategic intelligence contribution of the evaluation to the regional smart specialisation strategy in general and to the articulation of a smart policy-mix in particular. There is, however, potential to promote consistency in the innovation policy-mix if evaluation governance evolves towards a new paradigm in which the diﬀerent agents embedded in the EDP of advanced manufacturing are empowered in a more stakeholder-centric evaluation approach.

Questions such as the coherence of the instruments with their goals and the strategy are already being discussed in a non-systematic way in the new forums created by the strategy. The inclusion of these issues in a more integrated evaluation mechanism would add legitimacy to the process, and contribute to the consistency and comprehensiveness of the policy-mix among the diﬀerent regional actors.

Summarising, governance of smart specialisation strategies in the Basque Country has evolved towards a new governance mode (see ﬁgure 3) but evaluation processes still follow governance mode 1 or 2.9 Evolving towards a governance mode 3 for evaluation in a way that complements other modes of governance will be a key step for generating collective learning about the contribution of policy-mixes to the evolution of the diﬀerent strategic priorities.

5. Conclusions and emerging challenges The notion of policy-mix has become very popular among innovation policy analysts and also among innovation policy-makers, where it has been given a boost by the rapid emergence of smart specialisation strategies as a new regional innovation policy framework. The key features of smart specialisation strategies make them extremely interesting laboratories for analysing policy mixes, in particular those geared towards promoting sustainable transitions Indeed, it can be argued that innovation policy under smart specialisation strategies, as with sustainable transition promotion, takes place in an extreme pluralistic governance context. Moreover, the emphasis in smart specialisation strategies on prioritization of activities as a result of an experimentation process (entrepreneurial discovery process) among private and public actors adds complexity in terms of the need for directionality of policy instruments in combination with neutral policy instruments and the active role of non-government actors in policy-making.

This new context for innovation policy-mixes creates demands for new governance arrangements and processes both within and beyond government. In particular, there is a need to ensure a well-functioning link between the diﬀerent government departments and levels that design and implement an appropriate innovation policy-mix and the dynamic, pluralistic EDP process through which regional innovation priorities should emerge. These new governance arrangements in turn place demands on evaluation processes and in particular on the governance of evaluation for policy-learning purposes, meaning shifting from an accountability role of evaluation to a formative, strategic one.

Indeed, where such a range of vested (and potentially conﬂicting) interests come together, it is important to ensure strategic intelligence through evaluation that is trusted and seen as legitimate by all parties.

Thus the verticality and directionality of policy-mixes in placed-based policies with an experimental approach, condition not only evaluation itself, as new evaluation frameworks should be established in order to respond to the mix sophistication, but also the governance of evaluation processes. In particular, to complement traditional evaluation approaches a focus on strategic learning is required, alongside the integration of evaluation issues into the new governance arrangements underscoring entrepreneurial discovery processes and their links into government policy decision-making.

9 The government is advancing towards a policy-mix evaluation and for that purpose is participating in an Interreg project called MANUMIX (www.interregeurope.eu/manumix/ ) E. Magro, J.R. Wilson Research Policy xxx (xxxx) xxx–xxx However, despite the smart specialisation agenda, the governance of policy-mixes in general and their implications for evaluation governance in particular, are still pending issues in regional-policy making.

Even in regions that have developed capabilities in innovation policymaking over time, such as the Basque Country, incipient changes in policy-mix governance are not yet reﬂected in evaluation governance.

Indeed, it is often naively assumed that once priorities are set through entrepreneurial discovery processes, governments will be able to choose from a menu of policies to guide innovation in those directions.

Thus new governance arrangements capable of truly linking the strategic and policy processes are not adequately developed. These arrangements would add consistency to policy-mixes in the framework of smart specialisation strategies. Stakeholder-based evaluation and principles of empowerment evaluation could be employed as strategic tools in this context, increasing policy knowledge (and boosting its legitimacy) among the pluralistic collective of actors that play a role in the entrepreneurial discovery processes shaping innovation policy mixes.

The illustration presented here shows a work in progress in this regard. New governance arrangements relevant for the policy mix have emerged in the context of the smart specialisation strategy – both ‘hard governance’ mechanisms within government, and ‘soft governance’ mechanisms beyond government – but there remains a missing link in terms of a sound and comprehensive approach for strategic intelligence through evaluation integrated within these new governance arrangements. While this is one regional example employed for illustrative purposes, we argue that it is symptomatic of a wider problem, where there is still a governance gap in new place-based innovation policies between policy-mix design and implementation and policy-mix evaluation. Thus the linking of governance structures and processes for evaluation is a key issue in the context of place-based policy mixes. It suggests the need for further research into this governance gap drawing on what is being experimented with in practice in diﬀerent regions as the implementation of their smart specialisation strategies takes form.

The Spatial Mismatch Between Innovation and Joblessness Edward L. Glaeser and Naomi Hausman NBER Working Paper No. 25913 May 2019 JEL No. O31,R11 ABSTRACT American technological creativity is geographically concentrated in areas that are generally distant from the country’s most persistent pockets of joblessness. Could a more even spatial distribution of innovation reduce American joblessness? Could Federal policies disperse innovation without significant costs? If research funding is already maximizing knowledge production, then spatial reallocation of that funding will reduce America’s overall innovation unless that reallocation comes with greater spending.

Without any spatial reallocation, the primarily inventive parts of innovation policy, such as N.I.H. grants, can potentially aid underperforming areas by targeting the problems of those areas, like widespread disability. The educational aspects of innovation policy, such as Pell Grants, work-study, vocational training, and Federal overhead reimbursement on grants, currently have multiple objective and could focus more on employability in distressed areas. Lifting the cap on H1B visas in poorer places could attract outside human capital to those places. Geographically targeted entrepreneurship policies, such as eliminating the barriers to new business formation near universities and in distressed places, could potentially enhance employment growth in those regions. Spatially targeted employment subsidies will increase the returns to labor-intensive innovation in depressed areas, but we know little about how much innovation will respond to such subsidies.
