doi:10.1016/j.regsciurbeco.2012.06.006 In this study, we evaluate the impact of the French Zones Franches Urbaines on economic activity. This publicfunded place-based program, comparable to US enterprise zones, exempts businesses from taxes for a period of at least ﬁve years. For the purpose of this evaluation, we merged several administrative datasets at the company level. This allows us to exhaustively observe business creations and stocks, as well as employment and ﬁnancial outcomes for companies at speciﬁc geographical locations. We focus on the second round of the program, during which treated territories were selected among a pool of deprived areas according to a known set of covariates. The way treatment was assigned makes the conditional independence assumption credible in our case. Overall, we ﬁnd signiﬁcant effects on both business creation and employment while the impact on companies that were located in the treated areas before the program is not signiﬁcant, regardless of the outcome. We also provide evidence of signiﬁcant negative spillovers of the program on neighboring areas.

© 2012 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. welfare. As these low-income neighborhoods cumulate deﬁciencies that could impact on the productivity of businesses, location-targeted tax incentives aim at displacing the optimal location decision of companies. If agglomeration effects play a prominent role on business location decisions (see for instance Combes et al., 2011), the level of local taxes can also modify these choices (Devereux and Grifﬁth, 2003; Rathelot and Sillard, 2008; Duranton et al., 2011). The motive behind the ﬁrst “Enterprise Zones”, ﬁrst in the UK in the early eighties followed by the U.S., was to use this ﬁscal tool to attract new businesses in some targeted areas.

In this paper, we evaluate a French program known as the Zones Franches Urbaines (hereafter ZFU). This initiative aims at boosting business births and facilitating relocations,2 as well as avoiding the exit of already settled establishments through placed-based tax exemptions. Being located within the limits of a ZFU allows a company to be totally exempt from business and corporate taxes, as well as social security contributions. Compared to similar programs in the U.S., the ZFU scheme is particularly generous, with a wide range of tax credits and almost no requirements other than location, although it is restricted to companies with a workforce of less than 50 employees 2 In this text, we distinguish business births (also called “pure creations”) from business relocations (also called “transfers”). The former refers to the creation ex nihilo of a business activity, the latter to the relocation of a business that was already existing somewhere else.

152 P. Givord et al. / Regional Science and Urban Economics 43 (2013) 151–163 (plus a less stringent criterion relating to total sales). As smaller companies tend to be more ﬁnancially constrained, they may be more responsive to tax incentives. This analysis could thus provide relevant elements, in particular regarding the optimal design of placed-based tax-exemption programs.

This paper contributes to an already vast but still inconclusive literature on this topic. While several articles indicate that spatial mismatch may explain a large part of urban unemployment,3 no consensus emerges on the effectiveness of place-based tax exemptions to foster economic development in deprived areas. The major part of the empirical evaluation literature ﬁnds that US Enterprise Zones have little or no impact on economic activity and employment (Bondonio and Greenbaum, 2007; Neumark and Kolko, 2010), while Busso and Kline (2008) provide opposite evidence for federal-level Empowerment Zones.4 In recent contributions, Ham et al. (2011) re-examine all US programs for a wider set of outcomes and ﬁnd more encouraging results for place-based policies. Krupka and Noonan (2009) show that the effect of these ﬁscal tools can be seen to some extent in housing prices, maybe by increasing local amenities (see also Landers, 2006). However, the ex-post evaluations of European place-based programs are scarce. Potter and Moore (2000) provide a positive assessment of the capability of the inwards investments created by the UK Enterprise Zones to generate local employment. Accetturo and de Blasio (2012) conclude that the Italian Area Contracts (Patti Territoriali) program was largely ineffective in fostering growth. Little evidence exists on the impact of the French program on economic activity.5 Besides, little is known so far on the issue of the externalities created by these place-based policies. They are often blamed in public debate for “cannibalizing” neighboring communities by causing a shift of economic activity within a city, from areas that do not beneﬁt from the program to areas that do. It is obviously an important concern for public policy to know whether a revitalizing program spurs the development of one area at the expense of another.

As per Hellerstein and Neumark (2011), most existing evaluations of place-based programs face two kinds of issues. First, as the boundaries of treated zones do not necessarily coincide with administrative ones, a signiﬁcant proportion of the area considered as treated in most studies is not actually treated. This measurement error is likely to bias downwards the estimator of the impact. Second, the issue of which areas are considered as a valid control group is of paramount importance. Because of the quality of the data we use and because of the selection process of the ZFU, our paper provides a contribution to the international debate on place-based tax-exemption policies.

Our data make it possible to assess the impact of the program not only on treated areas but also on the untreated areas which are geographically close to the treated ones, providing evidence on the existence of spatial externalities created by such schemes.

We use exhaustive administrative panel establishment-level data with precise location during the period 2002–2007. For each establishment, its creation date, whether this creation corresponds to a birth or a relocation and its eventual date of bankruptcy are available. For each year, the number of employees, their wages, as well as several outcomes regarding the business' economic and ﬁnancial health (income, sales, cash ﬂow, debt, investment) are also measured. Therefore, we can 3 Gobillon et al. (2011) show that in the case of France, spatial differences contribute to explain more than half of the differences of individual unemployment spell durations. See Gobillon et al. (2007) for a review about spatial mismatch.

4 The controversy also involves Bondonio and Engberg (2000), Greenbaum and Bondonio (2004), Elvery (2009) or Lynch and Zax (2010) that ﬁnd no effect and Papke (1994), O'Keefe (2004) that do.

5 Gobillon et al. (2010) provide a complementary analysis on the impact of ZFU on local unemployment. They use public-employment-service data, at the level of municipalities, and ﬁnd that the ﬁrst round of ZFU brought about a very small drop of the number of job seeker in treated areas. Recently, Givord et al. (2012) provide analysis on the ﬁrst round and Briant et al. (2012) links the heterogeneity in estimated impact of the program with the geographical characteristics of areas.

assess the impact of the program on business entry and exit rates, economic activity, employment, as well as on the ﬁnancial strength of companies. We are also able to differentiate between businesses that settled before and after the implementation of the program. The decisive strength of our data is the access to the speciﬁc location of each establishment. This is particularly interesting as, like EZ in the U.S., ZFU borders do not coincide with the limits of pre-existing jurisdictions. We can therefore establish whether a given entity is located within or beyond the boundaries delimiting tax exemption.6 The implementation of the ZFU program occurred in three rounds, respectively in 1997, 2004 and 2006. In this paper, we focus on the second step as it beneﬁts from several desirable features for evaluation. In 1997, when the government deﬁned the 44 territories that were granted ZFU status for the ﬁrst round, 416 other territories were also labeled Zones de Redynamisation Urbaine (ZRU). The difference between the two programs in terms of the respective generosity of available exemptions is large (see infra for details). The 44 ﬁrstround ZFUs were identiﬁed as the most distressed areas, while the 416 ZRUs were regarded as slightly less deprived. In 2004, 41 new ZFUs were created, all chosen within the pool of the ZRUs. Our main strategy consists in comparing outcomes between ZRUs that subsequently became ZFUs and ZRUs whose status did not change by propensity score matching. Such a strategy must inevitably deal with selection bias. As ZFUs are supposed to be more economically depressed than ZRUs, companies may naturally choose to locate less frequently in ZFUs, regardless of any tax incentives. This would induce a negative selection bias on the impact of the program.

In practice, two elements may argue in favor of our strategy. First, the most distressed neighborhoods, which might have been difﬁcult to compare, were in principle turned into ZFUs in the ﬁrst round of the program. Statistical evidence shows that ﬁrst-round ZFUs are indeed more distressed than second-round ones. Second, the committee in charge of choosing which ZRUs would be granted ZFU status in 2004 had to follow precise guidelines: as determined by an index calculated using ﬁve local variables (total population, unemployment rate, tax revenues, proportion of youth, proportion of dropouts).7 As we were able to compute these variables and this index in particular, we found that the ZRUs chosen to become ZFUs proved to be quite similar to the areas that did not beneﬁt from the policy. As the summary statistics and propensity score estimation make it clear, the most crucial factor that determined which areas were selected in the second round was their geographical location: an area had more chance to be chosen if it was further from a ﬁrst-round ZFU and closer to another ZRU.8 We ﬁnd that tax exemptions provided by the ZFU program had a positive impact on the number of businesses located in the treated areas. Such impact is mainly driven by an increase in the number of new companies, both through births and relocations. In relative terms, the increase is mainly due to a surge in the number of businesses relocating. The program also had an impact on total employment in the area, measured in terms of both jobs and worked hours.

However, the scheme seems to have had no effect on establishments that already existed in 2002. While these existing companies were as eligible as new ones for tax exemptions on offer, their bankruptcy 6 To our knowledge, only Peters and Fisher (2002), Billings (2008), and Neumark and Kolko (2010) have used data at such a precise scale.

Finally, we ﬁnd that the ZFU program had signiﬁcant negative spillover effects at least during the ﬁrst three years, on the areas situated just beyond the ZFU boundaries.

Negative effects are observed on economic activity outcomes (number of establishments, creation rates, etc…) but not on employment outcomes. Spillovers can be quantiﬁed, on average, with the same order of magnitude as the impact of the program, meaning that the positive impact on treated areas is likely to be totally offset by negative effects on their immediate vicinity.

The following section introduces the institutional context and the features of the evaluated program. Section 3 presents the data as well as some summary statistics. In Section 4, we detail the methodology used. The results of the estimations — both the direct impact of the policy and some evidence about displacement effects — are provided in Section 5. Finally, in the last section, the main results are summarized and discussed from a policy perspective.

2. A brief description of the French Zones Franches Urbaines In France, sporadic outbursts of violence (as recently as 2005 for example) have called for revitalizing policies in poor suburban areas characterized by a high concentration of social problems. Since the early 1980s, the French government has taken a series of measures targeting these economically distressed neighborhoods,9 generically named Politique de la Ville (Urban Policy). Common features of these neighborhoods include high unemployment and poverty rates, limited access to public services and retail as well as relatively low property prices. The ﬁrst two development stages of French urban policy in the 1980s and early 1990s have not been evaluated. In many deprived neighborhoods, these measures have not been sufﬁcient to resolve issues.

The Pacte de Relance de la Ville (Urban Revival Pact), initiated in 1996, constituted the third stage. Stressing the need for economic revival in sensitive urban areas (ZUS) as a prerequisite for their social renovation, the pact listed several hundreds of priority neighborhoods and granted them tax exemptions to attract new business and raise employment levels. Three area categories were created.

First, 750 neighborhoods were labeled Zones Urbaines Sensibles (ZUS). In practice, the fact of being deﬁned as a ZUS alone does not grant any tax exemptions, but rather signals that local funding should be directed there as a priority. Then, 416 particularly distressed ZUS neighborhoods were declared Zones de Revitalisation Urbaine (ZRU), while the 44 most underprivileged were assigned to the ZFU program. In contrast to ZUS, businesses entering either a ZRU or a ZFU are entitled to tax rebates and exemptions.

The main objective of the ZFU and ZRU programs is to promote economic development in these areas. These schemes grant substantial tax reliefs to existing and new businesses, with a much higher exemption level in ZFUs than in ZRUs (see Appendix A for details).

ZFU-located companies with fewer than 50 employees beneﬁt from ﬁve-year exemptions from local business taxes, corporate income tax and property taxes. They are also exempt from employers' social security contributions for a period of ﬁve years on the fraction of salaries lower than 1.4 times the minimum wage. This aid is, however, limited in time, as the measures on offer terminates over a gradual three- to nine-year period, following the full-rate exemption for the ﬁrst ﬁve years. Ten years after its entry in the program, a company with fewer than ﬁve employees still beneﬁts from a 60% tax rebate.

Moreover, in practice, all ZFUs have been extended beyond the theoretical deadline and are still active as of today. 9 In what follows, a neighborhood has typically a population of 9000 to 30,000.

153 P. Givord et al. / Regional Science and Urban Economics 43 (2013) 151–163 French ZFUs share some features with similar programs, especially with U.S. schemes. 10 The U.S. scheme offers a number of tax credits to businesses located within the zone boundaries. U.S. authorities deﬁne eligible areas based on socio-economic criteria, such as high unemployment rate or low income levels (Bondonio and Engberg, 2000).

By contrast, the initial UK Enterprise Zones program focuses directly on areas witnessing the contraction or relocation of existing industries.11 The Italian program Patti Territoriali adopts a much more decentralized approach, as a broad set of regions are eligible, establishing a local agreement signed by both local governments and representatives of civil society to obtain public and private investments.

French and similar programs differ in many other respects. First, in the French case, the designation process does not require a strategic development plan, which is the case in some U.S. Enterprise Zones.

French ZFUs are tend to be generous in magnitude, but restricted in scope. They provide a wide range of tax exemptions, which can be sizable for eligible companies (see Givord et al., 2012, for an estimation).

While in most Enterprise Zones, the tax incentives granted to businesses are tied to speciﬁc requirements (e.g. a threshold for job creations or capital investment), such requirements are rather weak in France. For example, in the case of exemptions from payroll taxes that are applied to all employees of a business establishment located in the zone, the only requirement stipulates that one third of new hirings should be local residents. In contrast with the Enterprise Zone program, ZFU speciﬁcally targets very small businesses. Only those with less than 50 employees are eligible (with an additional restriction on sales). These small businesses are likely to be particularly sensitive to tax incentives, as their limited access to credit means that are ﬁnancially constrained.

The second round of ZFU creations occurred in January 2004, with 41 new ZFUs. These areas were selected out of the existing ZRUs. Ofﬁcially, the selection criteria were speciﬁed by a decree, and consist of a combination of 5 local indicators, namely: the total population of the area, the unemployment rate, the proportion of youth (under 25), the proportion of drop-outs with no qualiﬁcations and the tax potential of the municipality.12 The composite index was calculated as the product of the ﬁrst four elements, divided by the ﬁfth.13 In addition, it was speciﬁed that a ZFU should have more than 10,000 residents.

However, anecdotal evidence from conversations with ofﬁcials of the Ministry of Urban Affairs suggests that the main selection criteria used in the second round were clearly: (i) the metropolitan area in which the ZRU is located and (ii) its size.

The objective of the decision makers was to achieve a more even distribution of ZFUs at a national scale. While many major metropolitan areas (Bordeaux, Montpellier, Toulon, Nice…) had been allocated a ZFU in 1997, some important ones had not (Toulouse, Clermont- Ferrand, Nantes, Grenoble…). Fig. 1 demonstrates the uneven distribution of ZFUs at a national level. Further evidence relevant to this feature is given below, in the section which discusses the estimation of the propensity score.

3. Data Finally, in 2006, 15 new ZFUs were created from the remaining ZRUs. As we focus our analysis on the second round, we have removed 14 All variables presented in this ﬁgure are deﬁned in more detail in Section 3.

3.1. Data description The data we use come from several sources. The SIRENE directory (INSEE) contains exhaustive information on businesses in manufacturing, trade and services industries, in particular their location. The stock of businesses is reported yearly. New businesses are also reported, as well as their creation date and the business origin (whether a birth or a relocation). The bankruptcy ﬁle (INSEE) contains the records of all bankruptcy proceedings brought before a trade tribunal.16 15 For a recent analysis of this wave, see Givord et al. (2012).

16 A bankruptcy is characterized by insolvency, i.e. when a company is no longer able to repay its debts. Not all legal decisions to open bankruptcy proceedings (company ﬁling for bankruptcy as part of legal proceedings) lead to liquidation. In addition, bankruptcy does not give the whole picture in terms of discontinuance of business. A company can, for instance, put a stop to its activity because its owner decides to retire and his assets are not taken over.

Fig. 2. The ZRU (dotted line) and the ZFU (plain line) in Stains, in the Northern banlieue of Paris. The DADS (annual declarations of social security data) dataset (INSEE) contains exhaustive information on employment and salaries in these businesses. The ﬁscal records, called BRN and RSI, are provided by the tax administration. These ﬁles provide accounting information (balance sheet and income statement) as well as the amount of taxes paid by every business. These data are available and matched over the period 2002–2007, that is from two years before the introduction in the ZFU policy. We also use the 1999 Census (INSEE) to extract variables which characterize the socio-demographic situation of the areas under study. In particular, some of these characteristics are the criteria that were considered by decision-makers during the selection process.

These data allow us to evaluate the impact of the ZFU program over a broad range of indicators. We estimate the impact of the ZFU program on economic activity as measured by the stock of companies located within the boundaries of the targeted areas, on business demography (creations and bankruptcy), and on paid employment. We can also evaluate whether the tax subsidies result in the location of new businesses or affect the economic situation of previously existing ones. Because we have access to establishment-level panel data, we can isolate businesses with at least one employee which are eligible for tax exemptions (less than ﬁfty employees, total revenue under €10 million, not held by higher corporate), located in ZRUs in 2002. We follow the commercial outcomes for these establishments during the period, according to whether the ZRU in which they are located was granted ZFU in 2004 or not. As it is unlikely that these businesses anticipated receiving these tax concessions two years before the ZFU assignment, we can rule out possible selection issues due to businesses locating there later. We can therefore measure whether tax exemptions are effective in fostering economic development in existing small businesses.

As micro-businesses are often said to be confronted with ﬁnancial difﬁculties jeopardizing their survival, tax exemptions can improve their ﬁnancial situation. We measure the impact of the subsidies on a large number of outcomes, in order to evaluate whether businesses use the money to improve employment, investment, or their ﬁnancial situation (which may, in turn, have an effect on their risk of bankruptcy).

155 P. Givord et al. / Regional Science and Urban Economics 43 (2013) 151–163 We will therefore focus on several indicators of the economic and accounting situation: sales, current taxable income, debt, cash ﬂow, investment levels, as well as the share of bankruptcies in the area. We also measure whether the impact on employment is achieved at the intensive (with more worked hours per employee) or at the extensive margin (resulting in more employees).

Depending on their industries, businesses may respond differently to tax incentives. For instance, some industries may beneﬁt more from agglomeration externalities or may rely more on skilled labor. The economic activity can be located in places other than the business establishment (and so not be affected by the negative externalities of a distressed neighborhood). Finally, it appears essential to determine whether the impact of these geographically-targeted tax cuts is made at the expense of surrounding neighborhoods, which are themselves quite poor.

4. Estimation strategy Ideally, the effect we want to measure would be obtained by calculating the difference in the dependent variable between the units which are actually treated and the same units but in a scenario in which they would have not been treated. While we can directly observe the former, the latter is unobservable as the units in question have been treated. The ZFU program is granted to areas that have experienced economic and social problems. Therefore, direct comparison of all treated and all non-treated units could lead to spurious results, probably understating the true impact of the program. As detailed below, our empirical strategy involves choosing a control group of areas as close as possible to ZFUs in terms of their observable characteristics. The pool of ZRUs which were not assigned to the program is an obvious choice, given the assignment process of the second round. Our identiﬁcation assumption states that, conditional on characteristics observed before assignment, the affectation of a ZRU to the ZFU program is not related to the potential outcome.

Formally speaking, we can consider that any ZRU i has virtually two potential outcomes, at time t: one referred to as Yit 1, if it is located in a ZFU, and the other, referred to as Yit 0, if it is not. The impact of the ZFU program at time t on this area is equal to Yit 1−Yit 0, with t being after the formation date of the ZFU. It will never be possible to estimate this impact as we can never simultaneously observe both potential outcomes for the same unit at the same time. In order to obtain an evaluation of the counterfactual outcome, we use a conditional differencein-differences strategy.18 The identifying assumption states that conditionally to observable characteristics, all remaining differences (that could impact outcome) between the units are not associated with 18 Similar method have been used on related topics for instance in Billings (2011), Bernini and Pellegrini (2011).

the treatment. This is supported by the fact that we could use timedifferentiated outcomes, and thus eliminate potential systematic differences between the areas (see Heckman et al., 1998).

As shown by Rosenbaum and Rubin (1983), if the conditional independence assumption holds for observables X, it also holds for the propensity score, i.e. the probability of being treated conditional on these observables. In other words, hypothesis (1) implies it⊥Ti p Ti ¼ 1 ð jXi j Þ: ð2Þ In practice, the estimation is a two-stage process: the estimation of the propensity score followed by the matching itself. We estimate this propensity score using a logit model.

Many conditioning variables are introduced in the speciﬁcation of the propensity score. First, we include the variables used to build the composite index which was supposed to guide decision makers for the assignment of ZRUs to the ZFU program (see Section 2). Apart from the ﬁscal potential, measured in 2002, these variables are extracted from the census collected 1999. Then, we introduce two variables related to the relative distance of ZRUs from each other and of ZRUs with ﬁrst-round ZFUs. Next, a cubic of the total population, measured in 1999, is included. Finally, we use the number of businesses and employment, levels (in 2002) and in ﬁrst-differences (2002 minus 2001), to control for the diversity of local economic situations.

As expected by our descriptive analysis, the areas that turned into ZFUs in 2004 tend to have slightly more social issues than ZRUs, yet most of the coefﬁcients are insigniﬁcant (see Table 3). Only the share of youth is signiﬁcantly associated with assignment probability.

In spite of what appeared in descriptive analysis, population seems to play no signiﬁcant role, once other covariates are accounted for. In contrast, coefﬁcients related to distance variables are strongly significant. We argued in Section 2 that, for a ZRU in 2003, the distance to a ﬁrst-round ZFU and to another ZRU should affect positively the probability of being assigned to treatment. The former because it leads to a more even distribution of ZFUs at the national scale, and the latter because ZRUs could be merged in order to constitute a zone achieving the required size (10,000 inhabitants). Overall, the results of the propensity score estimation are compatible with our view, built on anecdotal evidence and summary statistics, indicating that selection bias should be of second-order. First, because it turns out that the most important predictor for the assignment to the treatment is the distance to another ZRU or to a ﬁrst-round ZFU. Second, because social covariates, even those which should have been taken into account by decision-makers, do not differ that much between treated and control groups. Even economic variables, like the number of businesses, are largely insigniﬁcant. Note that the results presented in the next section are robust to changes in the speciﬁcation that concern insigniﬁcant variables.

In the second stage, each treated unit is matched with untreated units with a similar propensity score. We used a kernel matching method: untreated observations are weighted according to their distance from the treated observation, the weights being determined by a (Gaussian) kernel.19 At the end of this matching process, the estimated effect of the treatment is obtained for each treated unit. The average effect of the treatment is then calculated by considering the average of individual differences. Because we want our results to be robust to variations in the speciﬁcation of the matching process, we also performed the analysis using nearest-neighbor matching, inverse probability weighting and inverse probability weighting with a control for covariates in a second stage. The results we stress in the next section are all qualitatively unaffected by these speciﬁcation changes.20 As demonstrated by Bertrand et al. (2004), the inference is biased by both group effects, as businesses in the same areas may experience joint shocks, and serial correlation in residuals. Our estimation is performed at the ZRU level, which reduces the extent of the former issue. Besides we use full bootstrap on ZRUs for inference to take into account serial correlation.

5. The impact of the ZFU program on the treated areas In this section, we report the results of our propensity-score matching estimations, on a large set of outcomes (company demography, employment, economic situation of preexisting companies) for each year between 2003 and 2007.21 It is important to stress that the program started, for the second round of ZFU, in 2004. Year 2003 thus constitutes a “falsiﬁcation test” in the sense of Manning and Pischke (2006): if the control group is a valid counterfactual for the treatment group then control and treated areas should not differ before the program is enforced.

This falsiﬁcation test can be considered as a test of our identiﬁcation assumption. For all the outcomes considered in this study, there is no significant difference between our treatment and (matched) control groups before the introduction of the tax exemptions (Tables 4–6).

The overall impact of the ZFU program on economic activity is positive from the starting date of the treatment until 2007 (Table 4). In particular, the growth rate of the stock of companies is 5 to 7 percentage points higher in the treated ZRUs than in the control group between 2004 and 2007. Such a positive effect could be explained in two ways.

At the intensive margin, the ZFU program could have helped preexisting companies not to exit. At the extensive margin, the program could have fostered company births or relocations to the treated areas.

When we focus on companies that were already present in the area in 2002, we observe a positive difference in favor of the treatment group in 2004, especially for the companies with less than 3 employees,22 but this effect is neither signiﬁcant nor persistent over 19 The kernel bandwidth is chosen with the rule of thumb: ﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃﬃ V ^p ð Þ p N−1=5 (where V ^p ð Þ is the variance of the estimated propensity score and N the number of observations). Table 5 presents the impact of the ZFU program on employment outcomes. Two outcomes are considered: the annual growth rate of the number of employees in a given establishment on December 31st, and the annual growth of the number of hours worked. Interestingly, the impact of the treatment is similar on both measures, which means that the program has no impact on the number of hours worked per worker.23 Overall, there is a positive effect of the program on employment, yet the effect is signiﬁcant only for year 2007. The magnitude of the effect of the ZFU program on employment ranges from 4 percentage points (insigniﬁcant) in 2004 to 12 percentage points (signiﬁcant at 5%) in 2007.

Is this relatively small effect on employment due to the formation of new companies or to the growth of pre-existing ones? When we restrict our sample to establishments which were already present in 2002, we ﬁnd no effect of the program on employment. Focusing on businesses with less than 3 employees in 2002, there are signiﬁcant and positive effects on hours worked in 2006 and on employment in 2007. On larger pre-existing businesses, no signiﬁcant effect is observed. In a nutshell, if the program had an impact on business creation, evidence on employment is more mixed. The impact on employment seems to be weak on pre-existing establishments, and, if anything, focused on small businesses.

6. Spatial externalities The relative importance of business relocations among the new businesses raises concern about the existence of negative geographical externalities of the ZFU program, at least in the short run. Spillovers could also have affected the location of business births: an entrepreneur willing to create a new establishment at a given locality may relocate the premises if a ZFU is created nearby and set up within the ZFU instead. If theory could predict such negative spillovers in the short run, the geographical concentration of a growing number of companies may also bring about, in the longer run, positive externalities due to agglomeration economies.

We do actually observe that the program produced signiﬁcant negative spillovers on economic activity within the close neighborhoods of the targeted areas during the period under study. More precisely, we address the issue of the existence of externalities by measuring the impact of the program not on the treated area itself but on a neighboring ring around the treated area. We build a 300-meter-wide ring of land around all the ZFUs (meaning surfaces of land which are comparable to that of the interior of a typical ZFU).24 Fig. 9 displays what the ring looks like in the case of the Stains ZFU. However, the issue here is somewhat different to that discussed in previous sections. We do not measure the impact of local tax subsidies on targeted areas, but the impact of being near some 24 The mapping technology used to build these areas is quite similar to that used in Neumark and Kolko (2010).

161 P. Givord et al. / Regional Science and Urban Economics 43 (2013) 151–163 areas beneﬁting from these tax subsidies. The control areas, for the sake of comparability, are similarly-built 300-meter-wide rings around the ZRUs which were not included in the ZFU program in 2004. The same setting as previously for the matching procedure: normal-kernel matching with caliper, and full bootstrap for inference. As the program assignment decision was based on the characteristics of the zones themselves, we match a treated ring and a control ring in terms of the propensity scores of the corresponding ZRUs if close enough.25 Summary statistics (see Table 9 in Appendix B) suggest that treated and control rings are very close in terms of characteristics prior the introduction of the ZFU policy. If there is a scale difference between rings around ZFUs and ZRUs, the former being on average twice as large as the latter, social indicators (measured in 1999) and business creation rates (measured in 2002) are almost identical. A falsiﬁcation test similar to the one used in the previous section, conﬁrms that the rings around untreated ZRUs are a plausible control group for the rings surrounding ZFUs. Using the propensity score matching for outcomes observed in 2003 we do not ﬁnd any signiﬁcant differences between treated and control rings (Table 8).

In contrast, we observe a signiﬁcant decline in the growth rate of the number of establishments located in the rings surrounding a ZFU, with respect to the rings surrounding ZRUs. We can also see a negative impact of the inﬂows of new establishments. This decline seems to affect slightly more the relocations than the births of new establishments. The evidence of direct effects on employment were rather tenuous, so are spillover effects. If most coefﬁcients are negative, only one, relating to the number of hours worked in 2004 is signiﬁcantly different from zero. Finally, we note that spillover effects on economic activity have more or less the same magnitude as direct effects. This suggests that most of the direct impact of the ZFU program is compensated by losses in the neighboring territories, just beyond the ZFU boundary.

Conclusions Overall, we observe a signiﬁcant positive impact of the Zones Franches Urbaines place-based tax-exemption program on economic activity, in contrast with part of the empirical literature dedicated to the evaluation of place-based tax-exemption programs. This impact is mostly due to the fact that new companies are created or relocated in the treated areas. These effects are heterogeneous across industries: services to businesses are the industry that beneﬁted most from the program. Somewhat surprisingly, the impact on preexisting companies is almost never signiﬁcant, despite substantial ﬁnancial transfers. Moreover, the policy has substantial negative spillovers on neighboring areas: the presence of a ZFU depresses the location of new businesses in the immediate vicinity of the treated area.

Despite a positive impact on economic activity overall, the policy seems to have missed part of its target: businesses which were located in the treated areas before the treatment started experienced no improvement whatsoever. While these establishments were as eligible as new ones for tax exemptions, their survival rates, their employment levels, as well as their economic situation were essentially unaffected by the program.

A possible explanation is that the potential positive impact of the program was offset by the increased competition induced by the creation of the new businesses.

This result is in line with evidences from the US: Greenbaum and Engberg (2004) observe that the average null impact of the Enterprise Zone resulted from the opposite effect on new and already existing establishments within the zone (see also Bondonio and Greenbaum, 2007; Ham et al., 2011).

explanations. Firstly, at the city-level, the net impact of policy minus its spatial externalities may be too weak to be detected. Second, more local jobs do not necessarily mean less local job-seekers. According to the results of a survey conducted in 2008 targeting local authorities and some companies located in the ZFU areas, companies declare major difﬁculties into hiring employees inside the area (and minor but not major difﬁculties, to hiring from outside the area) in more than two thirds of these areas. This fact could question the efﬁciency of local tax exemptions as a tool to reduce local unemployment, especially in areas where workers lack basic skills. One possibility could be to combine place-based tax exemptions to increase labor demand with place-based training programs to improve the quality of local human capital. Another possibility is to directly target individuals rather than businesses. The evaluation made by Gutirrez Romero (2009) of the ‘New Deal for Communities’ program implemented in the UK suggests that area-based ﬁnancial aids to residents of deprived neighborhoods can improve local employment.

Beside labor market aspects, the above-mentioned survey reports that companies complained about the lack of available land, and more speciﬁcally of commercial real estates. A shortage in real-estate supply could hamper the efﬁciency of the policy, as landlords, either by increasing selling prices or rents, may capture part of the money.

Finally, the relative failure of the policy could be due to a lack of information about the policy or uncertainty about the local application of ﬁscal rules, as emphasized by the local survey. Some companies would, for instance, waive their rights to tax exemptions in order to avoid tax inspection. As shown by Kolko and Neumark (2010), the way the areas are monitored by zone administrators can make a difference in the ﬁnal assessment of the policy.

Appendix A. Tax exemptions in ZRU and ZFU According to the 2007 ONZUS (Observatoire National des Zones Urbaines Sensibles) report, companies in ZFU and ZRU beneﬁt from the following tax exemptions: Local business tax: only companies with less than 50 employees and a total revenue of less than €10 million are concerned by ZFUs.

Businesses located in ZFUs are fully exempt for ﬁve years, within the limit of a taxable amount of €337,713 (2006) and €100,000 of cumulated aid over 3 years. In ZRUs, all businesses with less than 150 employees are eligible. However, the ceiling of the taxable amount is lower: it amounted to €125,197 in 2006.

Property tax on buildings: all buildings located in ZFUs belonging to companies liable for this tax are exempt for 5 years. ZRUs are not concerned. Corporate income tax: companies located in ZFUs with less than 50 employees and a total revenue of less than €10 million are exempt for 5 years, within the limit of €100,000 per year (increased by €5000 per new recruit). In ZRUs, this exemption is limited to newly created companies in the area, with no staff limitations. These beneﬁt from full exemption for 2 years and decreasing exemption for the next 3.

Corporate income tax exemption is limited to €225,000 per 36-month period. Employer contributions: companies located in ZFUs with less than 50 employees, a total revenue of less than €10 million and one third of whose staff live in the ZUS where the ZFU is located are concerned.

Employees with open-ended contracts or ﬁxed-term employment contracts of more than 12 months are exempt from employer contributions for 5 years, on the fraction of salary lower than 1.4 times the minimum wage (Smic). This measure concerns companies with less than 50 employees in full-time equivalent and is limited to a cumulated €100,000 over 3 years. In ZRUs, there is no staff or total revenue limitation for the company, but this exemption only relates to new recruits and lasts for 12 months (maximum of 50 jobs in full-time equivalent).

Rothenberg a ,∗, Yao Wang b , Amalavoyal Chari c a Syracuse University, United States of America b The Ohio State University, United States of America c University of Sussex, United Kingdom A B S T R A C T A R T I C L E I N F O JEL classification: R13 R58 O18 Keywords: Place-based policies Local taxes Informality 1. Introduction In developing countries, manufacturing firms are often characterized by small scale and persistently low growth. Such firms are constrained by restricted access to markets, capital, and technologies, as well as by unfavorable investment climates (Tybout, 2000). To spur industrial growth, many countries have established special economic zones, a particular place-based policy that provides tax incentives or reduced regulatory burdens for firms locating in specific places.

Such policies are common in the developing world; examples include China’s special economic zones (Wang, 2013), export processing zones in Bangladesh, Thailand, and Vietnam, and free trade zones in Honduras (Farole and Akinci, 2011). While some countries choose to establish these zones in favorable areas with good market access, others use them to attract investment to poorer regions.

If threshold effects and multiple equilibria are important features of economic growth, these policies may attract enough manufacturing activity to constitute a ‘‘big push’’ that generates large increases in productivity, improving welfare not only in the affected localities but also throughout the country (e.g., Rosenstein-Rodan, 1943; Murphy et al., 1989; Azariadis and Stachurski, 2005). Although place-based We study Indonesia’s Integrated Economic Development Zone (KAPET) program. Although firms in KAPET districts paid lower capital taxes, the program’s incentives neither stimulated entry nor increased output, and KAPET districts experienced similar development outcomes relative to non-treated districts. To investigate whether regional policies could be more optimally redesigned, we develop a quantitative spatial model where place-based capital tax cuts affect multiple sectors and impact a transfer system to finance local public goods.

We find that capital incentives in KAPET areas would have been more welfare and growth enhancing if they had been accompanied by additional place-based improvements.

tax cuts may be initially costly, they may also generate productivity spillovers for existing firms and encourage entry. This could create a self-sustaining, virtuous circle of development, with growth dividends that pay for the initial tax cuts.

However, the relative costs and benefits of place-based policies are difficult to discern. If workers are imperfectly mobile, place-based policies could encourage more productive reallocations of labor, but they may also just reshuffle economic activity from one place to another without increasing aggregate welfare (Bartik, 1991; Glaeser and Gottlieb, 2009; Kline and Moretti, 2014). Tax cuts could also make it harder for lower to middle-income countries to provide for public goods.

This paper investigates the effects of a large place-based intervention in Indonesia known as the Integrated Economic Development Zone (Kawasan Pengembangan Ekonomi Terpadu, or KAPET) program. This program, which began in the late 1990s, provided substantial capital tax-breaks for firms in certain districts in the Outer Islands of Indonesia, a country with large regional differences in per-capita income, a sizable informal sector, and a history of policies to promote inclusive growth.

To study this policy, we combine treatment variation with high quality $ Acknowledgement: We are grateful for financial support from Private Enterprise Development for Low-Income Countries (PEDL), United Kingdom, a joint research initiative of the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), United Kingdom and the Department For International Development (DFID), United Kingdom. A.D. Rothenberg et al. panel data on demographic outcomes, measures of regional growth, poverty, employment, informality, and manufacturing outcomes. Using a series of reduced form exercises, we estimate the average treatment effect of the KAPET program on treated districts for this rich set of economic outcomes.

When estimating the impact of place-based policies like the KAPET program, a central concern is that omitted variables influence selection into the program and also affect outcomes. Because Indonesia’s Outer Islands tend to be less developed than the Inner Islands (Java and Bali), we document that on average, program districts were poorer, further from Jakarta, and less populated than non-treated districts. This endogenous program placement creates a negative targeting bias, meaning that naive treated vs. non-treated comparisons may underestimate program impacts.

We adopt several approaches to improve identification. First, we restrict the non-treated comparison group to include only districts in the Outer Islands, which are more comparable to KAPET districts. Next, we combine a difference-in-differences design with an inverse probability weighting (IPW) approach that explicitly adjusts for potential ex ante differences between KAPET and non-KAPET districts. This approach uses propensity-score reweighting to adjust the contribution of nontreated district trends to the counterfactual in accordance with their odds of treatment. After implementing this IPW approach, we verify that pre-trend differences between KAPET and comparison districts disappear. As an alternative, we also use the synthetic difference-indifferences approach of Arkhangelsky et al. (2021), which combines attractive features of traditional difference-in-differences designs with the method of synthetic controls.

We find that along many dimensions, KAPET districts experienced no better development outcomes than their non-treated counterparts. We find no significant impacts on migration, population growth, employment outcomes, or consumption expenditures. We also find that the program was not associated with increased economic growth or nighttime light intensity, another commonly used measure of regional output (Henderson et al., 2012; Olivia and Gibson, 2013). To verify that our null estimates of the KAPET program are precise, we use a simulated power analysis to calculate the minimum detectable effect sizes that our estimators can reliably estimate. This analysis shows that for many outcomes, we can confidently reject effect sizes for similar policies estimated in the literature.

We also study the KAPET program using panel data on medium and large manufacturers, from Indonesia’s Industrial Survey. Importantly, we find that firms in KAPET districts paid significantly lower sales, license, building, and land taxes than similar firms in non-treated districts. This is reassuring, given that the KAPET program was designed explicitly to reduce formal taxes, and our effect sizes are similar to policy intentions. In spite of these tax cuts, we find no impacts on firms’ use of labor, output, value added, or productivity. Our quantitative null results validate other analyses of the KAPET policy, many of which are qualitative (e.g. Rahardja et al., 2012; Temenggung, 2013).

There are many possible reasons for the KAPET program’s lack of success. The program began around the time of the Asian Financial Crisis and its subsequent political upheaval, so firms may have been dissuaded from using the incentives. Moreover, because the program operated at the beginning of Indonesia’s decentralization program, heterogeneity in district administration may have undermined its effects (Soenandar, 2005). However, our findings are also consistent with literature suggesting that policies encouraging firms to locate in lagging regions may suffer from fundamental challenges, because those locations often have poor market access, unfavorable natural amenities, or low quality infrastructure.

To evaluate the welfare effects of the KAPET program, and to understand whether it could have been redesigned to encourage a more productive reallocation of economic activity, we specify a quantitative spatial model of Indonesian economic geography, based on Zárate (2022) and Henkel et al. (2021). In the model, workers choose a 2 Journal of Development Economics 176 (2025) 103503 location of residence and whether to work in the formal or the informal sector. Between districts, trade and migration are both costly, and workers value local public goods, which are paid for by local tax revenues and transfers from the central government.

Firms use labor and capital to produce goods, and they face input wedges (Hsieh and Klenow, 2009), a portion of which includes taxes paid by formal sector firms. Reducing taxes on capital inputs can encourage sector switching and increase firm entry. If tax cuts target places with greater potential for agglomeration economies, they could reduce spatial misallocation and lead to overall welfare gains.

At the same time, tax cuts in poorer districts with unattractive local fundamentals may not increase entry, and they could also constrain financing for local public goods, which reduces workers’ welfare. After calibrating the model, we simulate the impact of the KAPET program, and we conduct a series of policy counterfactuals to study how it might have been redesigned.

We first demonstrate that our reduced form estimates are similar to model-based analogs, using a counterfactual scenario where we remove the KAPET tax cuts entirely. Then, using the model to evaluate the KAPET program, we find very small effects: the program only increased national welfare by 0.01 percent and output by 0.09 percent. Although it increased KAPET districts’ formal sector employment by 0.62 percent, it also displaced informal workers and largely reshuffled economic activity without leading to growth. Because the KAPET program targeted districts that were poor and net recipients of central transfers, the tax cuts did not have a large impact on equilibrium local public goods.

Second, we find that the growth and welfare benefits of the KAPET tax cuts would have increased dramatically if they were combined with other local improvements that increased productivity and amenities, such as infrastructure that promotes communication or reduces commuting costs. This echoes findings from the literature on place-based policies suggesting that without other policies, tax incentives alone may be insufficient to stimulate investment (Duranton and Venables, 2021).1 Next, we use the model to evaluate alternative regional policies.

After simulating separate 50 percent capital tax cuts in every district in Indonesia, we find that fiscal incentives in larger, denser districts would have been far more welfare and growth enhancing than tax cuts in poorer areas with larger informal sectors. This finding supports ideas in the literature that firms tend to locate in cities that are too small from the perspective of maximizing social welfare (Henderson, 1974; Albouy et al., 2016).

Finally, we evaluate other place-based policies that could have targeted KAPET districts. Similar to our baseline findings, cutting labor taxes or reducing overall misallocation wedges alone would not substantially increase output or welfare. Instead, reducing formal entry barriers by promoting greater competition would lead to significant growth and welfare improvements. We also find that despite a long history of using fiscal transfers to improve local public goods (Lewis, 2001), increasing transfers to KAPET districts would have increased migration to those areas, but it would also encourage people to stay in less attractive places, reducing welfare (Henkel et al., 2021).

Literature Contribution. This paper contributes to a large empirical literature evaluating the benefits and costs of different place-based policies (Neumark and Simpson, 2015). Much of this literature focuses on programs implemented in the U.S. and Europe and finds decidedly mixed results.2 We also contribute to a growing literature that studies these policies in developing countries, and our work helps contextualize the findings of some reduced form papers in the literature.

1 On the need to combine fiscal incentives with other policies in designing place-based policies or special economic zones, see also Farole (2011), Frick et al. (2019), and Frick and Rodríguez-Pose (2023).

2 In particular, the evidence on enterprise zones in the U.S., which are similar in some ways to KAPET zones, is quite mixed, with results that often differ depending on the authors’ research design (c.f. Elvery, 2009; Ham et al., 2011; Lynch and Zax, 2011; Freedman, 2013).

A.D. Rothenberg et al. For example, many place-based policies enacted in India and China are actually combinations of fiscal incentives with other complementary policies. Shenoy (2018) finds when combined with infrastructure improvements, tax incentives and investment subsidies in Uttarakhand, India led to large growth in nighttime lights. Gallé et al. (2024) find that a combination of fiscal incentives, administrative benefits, and a unifying legal framework in India’s Special Economic Zone Act of 2005 led to significant employment and manufacturing growth. Lu et al. (2019) also find large employment, capital, and output effects of China’s SEZs, which combine fiscal incentives with discounted land-use fees and special treatment in securing bank loans. Our results suggest that tax incentives alone are unlikely to be impactful, and that the success of policies studied in the literature owes not just to the fiscal incentives themselves, but also to the infrastructure improvements, administrative streamlining, or other policies with which they were combined.3 Additionally, we build on a growing literature that uses structural models to study the welfare consequences of place-based policies (Fajgelbaum and Gaubert, 2020; Gaubert et al., 2021). Several papers on developing countries examine the effects of migration costs (Bryan and Morten, 2019), international trade and migration restrictions (Tombe and Zhu, 2019), pollution induced migration (Khanna et al., 2021), and the spatial allocation of educational investments (Hsiao, 2024), but few have looked at the effects of capital taxation in such settings.

Our model reflects key features of developing countries and distinctive characteristics of Indonesia. Prior work has emphasized the importance of the informal sector as a source of employment in many LDC settings (e.g., Hsieh and Olken, 2014; Rothenberg et al., 2016), and we follow Zárate (2022) to allow for informal employment. Placebased policies that cut formal sector taxes may encourage more entry, leading workers to transition out of informality and into the formal sector. This sector switching could broaden the tax base and increase revenues, enhancing the ability of the national government to provide public goods. Our model also specifies taxes as one component of input market distortions embedded in production wedges, as in Hsieh and Klenow (2009).

At the same time, tax cuts may instead result in lower tax revenue if the sector switching effects are not pronounced, and the revenue base on which to levy a reduced tax rate does not grow. Because tax revenues are pooled by Indonesia’s unitary central government and distributed to districts through a system of regional transfers, we follow Henkel et al. (2021) to formulate this transfer system, but do so in a model with both trade and migration frictions.

Finally, we incorporate capital as an input for firms, which was the explicit focus of the KAPET policy. In most quantitative economic geography models, firms only use labor for production (Allen and Arkolakis, 2019; Bryan and Morten, 2019), but we allow for capital supplied elastically on a national market, as in Khanna et al. (2021). Our general equilibrium evaluation of the KAPET program also complements recent work that adopts a reduced form, partial equilibrium approach to study the equity and efficiency of place-based policies (Siegloch et al., 2025).

The benefit of our general equilibrium modeling is to allow for the study of rich policy counterfactuals and non-marginal policy changes. 2. Regional policies in Indonesia and the KAPET program Spatial differences in the concentration of economic activity, employment, and output have long been a feature of Indonesia’s economy.

Some differences owe to natural resources, but in the early 17th century, the Dutch East India Company practiced an uneven development strategy, promoting extractive enclaves in the form of plantations and mines in Sumatra, Sulawesi, and Kalimantan while encouraging more 3 See also Wang (2013) on China’s SEZs, or Koster et al. (2019) on the opening of science parks in Shenzhen.

3 Journal of Development Economics 176 (2025) 103503 balanced, diversified growth in Java (Hill, 2000). Regional disparities in output and income have also strained internal relations throughout Indonesia’s history.4 After independence, Suharto’s New Order regime (1967–1998) enacted several policy initiatives to combat regional inequality (Soenandar, 2005). For example, Suharto’s first five-year development plan introduced several investment incentives to promote growth in the Outer Islands, including a tax holiday for firms locating outside of Java.5 Despite these efforts, regional inequalities have remained considerable. For example, in 1990, non-oil GDP per capita in the richest district (Kediri, in East Java) was more than 70 times that of the poorest district (Lampung Barat, in South Sumatra).

KAPET. After the mid 1980s when off-Java tax breaks were eliminated, efforts to promote growth in Indonesia’s poorer regions were limited until the creation of the Integrated Economic Development Zones (Kawasan Pengembangan Ekonomi Terpadu, or KAPET). The KAPET program, first announced in 1996, was designed to accelerate growth and development in Eastern Indonesia, which consists of the island groups of Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Maluku, Papua, and Nusa Tenggara.

By law, formal businesses locating in KAPET zones were eligible for several incentives that reduced corporate income tax. These measures included a partial tax holiday, with a 30 percent reduction of taxes on capital, expanded choices for depreciation and amortization of capital and losses, fiscal loss compensation for 10 consecutive years, and lower income taxes on dividends for foreign taxpayers.6 Other benefits included: (1) a corporate income tax exemption on imports of capital goods, raw materials, and other equipment; (2) a 50 percent reduction on building and land taxes for both new construction and expansion; and (3) additional benefits, including being able to deduct 50 percent of employee costs from corporate taxable income (Presidential Decree 9/1998, Article 22).

By using fiscal incentives, policymakers hoped that KAPET areas would attract investment and stimulate manufacturing and export growth. Planners also intended to promote growth and development for micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) to reduce the size of the informal sector. Growth in formal manufacturing would stimulate labor demand, creating jobs, raising wages, and reducing poverty and unemployment.

Presidential Decree No. 89 of 1996 created the KAPET program, building on earlier programs aimed at accelerating development in Eastern Indonesia. Apart from one KAPET zone created in Papua (which we ignore in our analysis because of data quality concerns), 12 KAPET zones were launched by presidential decree in January 1998, before Suharto resigned, and in September 1998, after Habibie became president. Table 1 lists the names and locations of the 12 KAPETs in our sample, the presidential decree that established them, and the year they started operation. Although one KAPET was established in Banda Aceh, in North Sumatra, the remaining 12 other KAPETs were located in Eastern Indonesia.

On paper, the KAPET program can primarily be thought of as a cut to taxes that firms pay on capital inputs. However, in practice, the program suffered from several implementation issues. First, many 4 For example, in the 1950s, violent separatist movements in Kalimantan and Sumatra, notably in Aceh, threatened to overwhelm Sukarno’s early presidency (1945–1967) and dissolve the Indonesian nation.

5 For an in-depth discussion of the history of regional policies and investment incentives in Indonesia, as well as some background on the KAPET program, see Temenggung (2013). Some policies that expanded in the late 1970s and early 1980s, such as Indonesia’s Transmigration program, were also designed in part to stimulate economic activity in unpopulated, underdeveloped regions (Bazzi et al., 2016).

6 Indonesian corporate taxpayers pay both corporate income tax, which apply to profits, and value added taxes, which are levied at a flat rate of 10 percent, with rebates for exports (Basri et al., 2021). The KAPET incentives mostly applied to corporate income taxes and not to value added taxes.

This list differs slightly from Soenandar (2005), who does not include KAPET Sabang in his analysis. In our empirical work, because of concerns about data quality, we drop Papua and KAPET Biak entirely from the analysis. The number of districts is based on 1990 district definitions. The determination of ‘‘well implemented’’ KAPET zones follows Soenandar (2005) and Financial and Development Supervisory Board (BPKP) (2003).

KAPET zones were created in early 1998, right before the Asian Financial Crisis and its subsequent political upheaval. Despite the tax breaks offered by the program, these contemporaneous political and macroeconomic events may have dissuaded investors from the region, especially during the early years of the program. However, in 2000, Regulation No. 20 offered some streamlining of the KAPET incentives and more flexibility to firms who would use them, and this signals the government’s intent to continue operating the program after the macroeconomic and political upheaval.

A second issue is that KAPETs were managed under a decentralized structure, and local governments had substantial authority over how to use program funds. In the early days of Indonesia’s ‘‘big bang’’ decentralization, there was considerable uncertainty over administrative authority and obligations. Local governments had trouble coordinating with the central government and often lacked the capacity to manage and implement many programs transferred to them (Hofman and Kaiser, 2004).

According to a report conducted by the executive director of the Development Council for the Acceleration of Eastern Indonesia and the Developing Body of KAPET, by 2003, only 6 KAPET zones had actually established transparent fiscal incentives for firms: (1) Sabang/Bandar Aceh; (2) Sanggau/Khatulistiwa; (3) Batulicin; (4) Minado-Bintung; (5) Pare-Pare; and (6) Bukari/Bank Sejahtera Sultra (Financial and Development Supervisory Board (BPKP), 2003, cited in Soenandar, 2005).

The remaining KAPETs struggled to do so because of coordination issues between the center and local administrative authorities. Table 1 lists this set of ‘‘well implemented’’ KAPETs, which we take as our main group of treated locations. However, for robustness, we also consider the full set of KAPET zones.

Fig. 1 presents a map of the districts treated by the program. Although 28 different districts were nominally treated by the program, it was only properly implemented in 17 districts.7 Districts were selected for the KAPET program according to several different criteria: (1) favorable geography; (2) potential for economic growth; (3) the presence of leading sectors capable of boosting growth in hinterland areas; and (4) potentially large investment returns. Each KAPET zone was established in a different province. Within provinces, it was hoped that KAPET zones would be growth centers, attracting activity from hinterland areas.

7 Note that based on legislation documents, 21 districts were fully treated by the program, but 7 districts were only partially treated, with incentives that just covered specific sub-districts. Because much of our data is coded at the district level, we ignore differences between fully treated and partially treated districts in our empirical work.

4 3. Data In this section, we first define districts, the spatial unit of analysis used in our empirical work. Then, we describe several key datasets used in the paper: (1) geographic characteristics and satellite data; (2) census data to measure demographic outcomes; and (3) data on economic and industrial activity.8 Districts. Throughout the paper, we use Indonesia’s districts (kabupaten) as the primary spatial unit of analysis. The district is the second administrative division in Indonesia, nested below the province, but above the subdistrict (kecamatan) and village (desa or kelurahan). Because many districts were divided and partitioned into new districts during the process of decentralization after the fall of Suharto, we aggregate the data back to 1990 definitions in order to achieve a consistent geographic unit of analysis.9 Our sample contains 290 districts, with a median land area of 1,877 square kilometers. This is similar to the size of U.S. counties, which have a median area of 1,595 square kilometers.10 Geographic Characteristics. We use the Harmonized World Soil Database (HWSD) and other sources to measure many agroclimatic features. These include measures of topography, such as elevation, slope, ruggedness, soil characteristics, and distance to rivers and the coast. We also construct measures of centroid distance to Jakarta, distance to major roads, and distance to major ports to proxy for market access. These variables capture aspects of districts’ natural amenities that may influence productivity, and they also proxy for the ‘‘favorable geography’’ criterion used to govern selection into treatment.

Demographic Characteristics. For the last 40 years, Indonesia’s Central Statistical Agency (Badan Pusat Statistik, or BPS) has collected high quality decennial population censuses. We use IPUMS extracts of the 1990 Census and unit-level data from the 2000 and 2010 Censuses to measure district-level demographic characteristics. Our data includes the size of the total population, the percent of the population with different levels of educational attainment, and measures of migration flows.

We also use data from the World Bank’s Indonesia Database for Policy and Economic Research (INDO-DAPOER), which contains population and social indicators at the district-level, including annual data on district populations as well as measures of infrastructure.

8 More information on these variables, including precise details on how various outcome measures were calculated, can be found in Appendix B. 9 Until the late 1990s, district boundaries were relatively stable (Booth, 2011). However, because of the decentralization process, many subdistricts split off from their original districts, forming new districts. The number of districts increased from 302 in 1999 to 514 in 2014, through a process known as pemekaran or blossoming (Bazzi and Gudgeon, 2021).

10 Indonesia’s major cities (kota) are also given separate district identifiers, and these designations are also used in the analysis. A.D. Rothenberg et al. Journal of Development Economics 176 (2025) 103503 Fig. 1. Map of treated districts.

Notes: Authors’ calculations using BPS district shapefiles. Information on treated districts was taken from the text of various presidential decrees, listed in Table 1. Here, we assume that districts with poorly implemented KAPET programs were not treated. In our empirical work, because of concerns about data quality, we drop Papua and KAPET Biak entirely from the analysis; these areas are not shown on the map.

Output, Expenditure, Employment, and Industrial Activity. We use two different indicators to measure economic activity at the district level: (1) annual data on real non-oil gross domestic product from subnational product accounts data produced by BPS; and (2) annual data on nighttime light intensity from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Henderson et al., 2012). Although light intensity may not be a good proxy for economic activity in rural areas, it has been shown to predict economic activity in urban settings (Gibson et al., 2021).

We also use various waves of the national socioeconomic survey (Survei Sosial Ekonomi Nasional or Susenas) to measure the total consumption expenditures of households and the fraction of the population that is classified as poor, according to BPS definitions.11 We combine these measures of economic activity with employment estimates from the National Labor Force Survey (Survei Angkatan Kerja Nasional or Sakernas). The Sakernas provides annual, district-level estimates of the fraction of workers who are employed, and who work in the formal and informal sectors. Following Comola and De Mello (2011) and BPS, we measure the share of employed workers who work in the informal sector as the share of workers who are self-employed or family/unpaid workers.12 Finally, we use firm-level data from an annual plant-level survey of medium and large firms, the Survey of Manufacturing Establishments (Survei Tahunan Perusahaan Industri Pengolahan, or SI). The SI is intended to be a complete annual enumeration of manufacturing plants with 20 or more employees. The survey records information on plant employment sizes, their industry of operation, cost variables, and measures of output and value added. Capital is measured as the firm’s reported book value of capital. We construct district-level aggregates of the SI data, but we also use the annual firm-level panel structure of the data in our analysis below.

3.1. Pre-treatment summary statistics Table 2 presents summary statistics of several variables, each measured before the KAPET program was launched in 1998. The first set 11 Official poverty lines use thresholds for total expenditures per capita that differ by rural and urban areas. We use official poverty lines from BPS, reported by Priebe (2014).

12 Only workers who work for a salary are considered to work in the formal sector. 5 of columns reports the means, standard deviations, and sample sizes of variables for districts where the KAPET program was well implemented; we drop poorly implemented KAPET districts from this analysis.13 The second set of columns reports the difference in means between treated and ‘‘all non-treated’’ districts, where this sample includes all districts in Indonesia that were not selected by the KAPET program.

Finally, in the third set of columns, we report the difference in means between treated and non-treated districts in the Outer Islands. This final comparison excludes districts on Java and Bali which were not targeted by the policy.

Panel A reports summary statistics for geographic characteristics. Compared to all non-treated districts, KAPET districts are more rugged and farther from Jakarta. While some geographic differences are statistically significant, differences tend to shrink and significance levels fall when comparing treated districts to non-treated counterparts in the Outer Islands. In Panel B, we compare districts on the basis of economic activity. In 1993, average GDP was smaller in treated districts, as expected given that policymakers were targeting poorer areas for the program. Relative to all non-treated districts, treated districts also experienced significantly lower intensity of nighttime lights in 1992 as well as significantly smaller pre-treatment growth in nighttime lights from 1992–1997. While treated districts had lower employment rates, a greater share of informal employment, and fewer manufacturing firms, these differences are not always significant. Again, when we restrict our comparison to non-treated districts in the Outer Islands, these differences tend to attenuate and lose significance.

In Panel C, we show that relative to all non-treated districts, KAPET districts were less populated in 1990, but there were no significant educational differences between treated and non-treated districts. However, these differences grow smaller when comparing treated to nontreated districts within the Outer Islands. Panel D also shows that there were no significant differences in the quality of public goods and infrastructure between treated and non-treated districts. Overall, the results shown in Table 2 emphasize negative selection of KAPET districts.
