Keywords: Neo-liberalization; Spatially selective liberalization; Globalization; Developmental state; Graduated sovereignty; South Korea Traditionally, state territoriality and sovereignty have been seen to manifest themselves within ﬁxed boundary lines. Political geographers and political scientists, however, have increasingly called for openness in understanding the territoriality of state sovereignty, with the argument that there is no need to comprehend a state’s territory and its boundary as closed and strictly bound entities (Agnew, 1994; Ong, 2000; Passi, 2003). In particular, with increasing economic ﬂows across national boundaries in the globalizing economy, increasing numbers of political geographers have become interested in the ways in which state territoriality has been challenged by the actors and forces that cross the boundaries of formal state territories.

Based on this general theoretical orientation, I aim to examine the ways in which the sovereign territoriality of the state has been contested and (re)constructed in relation to globalization and economic liberalization, especially in the context of the East Asian developmental state. In particular, by building on Aiwa Ong’s concept of ‘‘graduated sovereignty’’, I will address how the forms of state regulation and sovereignty can be spatially diﬀerentiated or graduated within a national territory, with a focus on the spatial processes of economic liberalization in South Korea.

South Korean governments have actively promoted the globalization of the ‘‘national economy’’; this was accelerated in the 1990s, especially after the ﬁnancial crisis. In particular, the state has drastically shifted its policy positions toward international investment and tradedfrom a nationalist and protectionist orientation to liberalization. In this context, the South Korean government recently announced an ambitious plan to develop global hubs of international movement of capital and skilled labor in several localities, designating these ‘‘special economic zones’’, ‘‘economic free zones’’, and ‘‘international free cities’’. In this paper, I will question why and under what political and economic circumstances the Korean government has decided to use this spatial strategy.

The idea of ‘‘special economic zones’’ is nothing new. As Woo-Cumings (2003, 12) has pointed out, while developing countries were taking oﬀon the wings of an abundant supply of cheap labor that was used to produce low-end products for the rest of the world, the favored idea of spatial organization was called ‘‘special economic zones’’, ‘‘export processing zones’’, or ‘‘special export zones’’. In other words, this spatial strategy has been widely used by many developing countries that were promoting export-oriented industrialization. Consequently, the question that may be asked is why South Korean policy-makers have revived this old idea in this new millennium.

Old V.S. New 852 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 One answer to this question can be provided by using the concept of the ‘‘hub economy’’. With economic globalization, it has been widely suggested that moving from a manufacturing-oriented to a service-oriented economy requires the development of global hubs for the international movement of capital, goods, technology and skilled labor within the national territory. A way to develop these global hubs may be to build special zonesdwhich can be called ‘‘special economic zones’’, ‘‘economic free zones’’ or ‘‘international free cities’’din which the government provides preferential support, and greatly relaxes its regulations on business activities in order to attract international investment, and foreign technology and expertise. It may certainly be true that this kind of economic rationality provides an important background for the revival of the idea of ‘‘special economic zones’’ in South Korea.

In this paper, however, I argue that the revival of this spatial strategy in South Korea is not merely an outcome of policy choice based on an economic rationality, but results from very complex political processes and negotiations among conﬂicting interests. More speciﬁcally, I see the revived strategy of building ‘‘special economic zones’’ in South Korea partly as a spatial outcome of East Asian ‘‘neoliberalization’’, stemming from politically contested interactions between inherited institutional forms and policy frameworks of the developmental state, and the emergent forces of economic liberalization. In other words, the Korean government’s plan to build ‘‘special economic zones’’ or ‘‘economic free zones’’ can be considered a strategy of ‘‘spatially selective liberalization’’; it demonstrates strong properties of path dependency, in which established institutional arrangements constrain the scope and trajectory of neo-liberal reform in South Korea.

Theoretical background: ‘‘graduated sovereignty’’ and the politics of ‘‘neo-liberalization’’ For the last decade, there has been increasing criticism of a state-centered account of spatiality, which has tended to link state power and territorial sovereignty intimately together. In particular, Aiwa Ong’s concept of ‘‘graduated sovereignty’’ gives valuable insights into the reconstruction of territoriality of the state in the globalizing era. According to Ong (2000), ‘‘graduated sovereignty’’ refers to the state’s diﬀerential treatment of the population based on ethno-racial diﬀerences and the dictates of developmental programs. Ong (2000, 57) proposes two aspects of graduated sovereignty. The ﬁrst is related to the diﬀerential treatment by the state of segments of the population in relation to market calculations; thus, intensifying the fragmentation of citizenship that was already pre-formed by social distinctions of race, ethnicity, gender, class and region. The policy of bumiputra in Malaysia is an example of this aspect of ‘‘graduated sovereignty’’. The second aspect of the state’s diﬀerential treatment of the population is associated with the development of production and technological zones (for example, ‘‘export process zones’’), in which some aspects of state power and authority are taken up by foreign corporations.

Thus, the concept of ‘‘graduated sovereignty’’ explains how state sovereignty can be 853 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 diﬀerentiated and graduated within a national territory with reference to the situation at hand, in which the state ﬂexibly experiments with diﬀerent forms of sovereignty and governance by imposing diﬀerent disciplines or privileges on diﬀerent segments of the population, in relation to market calculations.

With respect to ‘‘graduated sovereignty’’, however, an important question has not been satisfactorily answered: What leads to the state’s ﬂexible experimentation with diﬀerent forms of sovereignty? Why does the state want to treat segments of the population diﬀerently? Actually, Ong (2000) provides an answer to this question.

Attributing the state’s diﬀerential treatment of the population to the former’s interaction with global forces, she argues that in order to be globally competitive in the globalizing economy, the state treats segments of the population diﬀerently in relation to their varying degrees of participation in globalized market activities. This explanation is, however, unsatisfactory in explaining what leads to the state’s diﬀerential treatment of the population. It is especially too simple as an explanation of the actions of the capitalist state, allowing little reﬂection of the complex relations between state and society.

In understanding the actions of the state in the capitalist economy, I rely on a ‘‘society-centered’’ view of the state in this paper. Even though this view admits that class relations and capital-accumulation processes have crucial constraining and enabling eﬀects on the forms and functions of capitalist states and that the capitalist state needs to carry out the economic functions required by capital (for example, maintaining capitalist property rights, providing infrastructure and educated workers, etc.), it emphasizes that class forces do not mechanistically produce the sort of capitalist state needed for capital accumulation and the reproduction of capitalist social relations (Glassman, 1999, 677). Instead, the state is seen as a site of struggle and contestation among diverse forces acting in and through the state, including diﬀerent branches of the state, class forces, gender forces, regional interests, etc. (Glassman, 1999; Jessop, 1990). In this sense, the state is ‘‘not a unitary or homogeneous entity but rather is an ensemble of diﬀerent institutions among which there is enough contention to insure that there is no simple, mechanical production of the kinds of policies favored by any one element of the capitalist class’’ (Glassman, 1999, 677). Thus, the actual activities of the state rely on how the forms and functions of the state are produced and reproduced through social struggle. In other words, according to this ‘‘society-centered’’ view of the state, the speciﬁc actions of the state need to be understood in terms of the political struggles and collaborations among social forces and class fractions, which want to pursue their interests or ideas by producing or reproducing certain forms or functions of the state.

The globalization of economic activities, however, implies that the ways in which the state’s actions are determined become more complicated. In particular, according to Glassman (1999, 678), the internationalization of capital creates problems related to territorial non-coincidence between the economic reach of international ﬁrms within the global economy and the political reach of nation-states that have economic responsibilities vis-a` -vis these internationalized fractions of capital. The need to resolve this non-coincidence increases the possibilities for alliances of the more globally oriented and internationalized fractions of capital (for example, 854 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 TNCs, ﬁnancial capital, etc.), which want to have more inﬂuence on state policies.

Under increasing pressure from the more internationalized fractions of capital, the state has become more ‘‘internationalized’’ in the sense that state action increasingly takes place in a much wider international context. More speciﬁcally, the state apparatus becomes increasingly oriented toward facilitating capital accumulation for the most of international investors, regardless of their nationality (Glassman, 1999, 673). Also, policy regimes are becoming more oriented toward a focus on ‘‘international competitiveness’’. As alliances between the state and more globally oriented fractions of capital become stronger, the state has become oriented toward neo-liberal policies in order to promote international accumulation.

This tendency toward the ‘‘internationalization’’ of the state, however, is not simply the outcome of political alliances between the state and internationalized fractions of capital, which are driven by global economic forces and logic. Recent literature on globalization has emphasized that neo-liberal changes and the globalization of the state have been materially and discursively constituted of complex interactions among diverse social, political, and economic processes occurring at various geographical scales (Cox, 2005; Dicken, Peck & Tickell, 1997; MacKinnon & Phelps, 2001; Park, 2003; Yeung, 2002). In other words, the tendency toward an ‘‘internationalization’’ of the state may be signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced through the roles of various social and political actors; and political, ideological, institutional and economic conditions at various geographical scales.1 Furthermore, the tendency toward the internationalization of the state is not a complete process. There are various forms of resistance and counter-tendencies to this process. Given this, the internationalization of the state should involve very dynamic and politically contested processes.

A recent special issue of Antipode on ‘‘The Urbanization of Neo-liberalism’’ provides insights into these political processes. An important point made in the issue was the emphasis given to the path-dependent character of neo-liberal reform projects. In particular, focusing on the so-called ‘‘actually existing neo-liberalism’’, Brenner and Theodore (2002) emphasize the contextual embeddedness of neo-liberal restructuring projects insofar as they have been produced within the national, regional, and local contexts deﬁned by the legacies of inherited institutional frameworks, policy regimes, regulatory practices, and political struggles. More speciﬁcally, they argue that ‘‘an adequate understanding of actually existing neoliberalism must explore the path-dependent, contextually speciﬁc interactions between inherited regulatory landscapes and emergent neo-liberal, market-oriented restructuring projects on a broad range of geographical scales’’ (Brenner & Theodore, 1 Similarly, Cerny (in press) argues that the neo-liberalization of the state is ‘‘overdetermined’’, in the sense that multiple actors and dimensions play a role in the process. According to him, the following actors and dimensions are especially important in the change toward neo-liberalism: (1) state actors (politicians, bureaucrats, political parties, etc.); (2) ‘‘global governance’’ institutions (like The World Bank, IMF, WTO, the G7/8, etc.); (3) wealthy countries (for example, the United States); (4) international businesses; and (5) the ‘‘discourse’’ of neo-liberalism.

855 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 2002, 351). In this sense, it is suggested that recent restructuring processes need to be understood as ‘‘neo-liberalization’’ rather than neo-liberalism. In other words, the recent changes induced by neo-liberal reform projects need to be seen as ‘‘a historically speciﬁc, ongoing, and internally contradictory process of market-driven sociospatial transformation, rather than as a fully actualized policy regime, ideological form, or regulatory framework’’ (Brenner & Theodore, 2002, 353).

Such processes of neo-liberalization may deeply inﬂuence the spatiality of the state. In particular, nation-states have experienced a signiﬁcant restructuring of their spatial and scalar organizations.

Recent literature on urban and regional development has explained these spatial changes of the state in terms of ‘‘glocalization’’, ‘‘hollowing-out of the state’’ and ‘‘the rise of new regionalism’’ (Jessop, 1994; MacLeod, 2001; Swyngedouw, 1997). According to Brenner (2003), the ‘‘glocalization’’ of the state space is associated with the state’s spatial strategies to diﬀerentiate national politicaleeconomic space through a re-concentration of economic capacities within strategic sub-national sites such as cities, city-regions and industrial districts, which are in turn to be positioned strategically within global economic ﬂows. In this sense, the rise of the ‘‘glocalized’’ state space is associated with the state’s diﬀerential treatment of the population because diﬀerent regulatory rules or institutions can be established in the selected strategic urban and regional growth centers. The emergent ‘‘glocalized’’ spatiality of the state, however, should not be seen as a necessary outcome of neo-liberalism or broader regulatory changes.

Rather, as Brenner (2003) highlights, it needs to be viewed as forged through a dialectic of strategic interaction and socio-political contestation within and beyond state institutions, which happen with respect to the changes toward neoliberalization.

In building on this view, I suggest more speciﬁcally in this paper that the state’s geographically diﬀerentiated treatment of the population through the ‘‘glocalization’’ of state spatiality can be deeply inﬂuenced by politically contested interactions between inherited institutional forms or spatial organizations of regulation, and emergent forces of economic liberalization. This is especially so when a drastic and full-scale shift to neo-liberalism seems impossible due to ﬁrm resistance from social forces, which insist on defending existing institutional and spatial frameworks of regulation; the state may utilize the strategy of ‘‘spatially selective’’ liberalization by imposing more liberalized regulatory frameworks only to selected spaces. In other words, the reason the state treats the population diﬀerentially by imposing diﬀerent forms of regulation and governance in selected areas can be, at least partly, explained in terms of the political negotiations between the defenders of the old regulatory frameworks and the proponents of neo-liberal reform. Furthermore, due to the strong properties of path dependencydin which established institutional arrangements constrain the scope and trajectory of neo-liberal reformdeven the selected (and supposedly) ‘‘neo-liberal’’ spaces cannot be ﬁlled with truly neo-liberal rules or institutions; instead, they can be constructed as hybrid spaces composed of neoliberalization and the existing regulatory strategies. Nevertheless, regardless of whether the selected spaces are truly neo-liberal or hybrid, the processes of ‘‘spatially selective’’ liberalization may facilitate the state’s imposition of diﬀerent regulatory 856 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 rules, disciplines or privileges to diﬀerent segments of the population living in diﬀerent sub-national spaces; thereby, resulting in the graduation or diﬀerentiation of state sovereignty within a national territory.

Research context: developing special economic zones in South Korea In April 2002, the Korean government unveiled an ambitious project for a ‘‘Northeast Asian Business Hub’’. Aimed at creating a business hub in Northeast Asia, this project focused on developing Korea into a ﬁnancial, business and logistic center in Northeast Asia. The action plan for this project, which was announced in July 2002, included the improvement of logistics infrastructure (for example, the expansion of airports, seaports and railroads, the development of an eﬃcient logistics network, etc.); and the development of international business and ﬁnancial centers through the establishment of special economic zones, in which foreign direct investment and the location of regional headquarters of TNCs, foreign IT and media ﬁrms, and foreign ﬁnancial institutions would be strongly encouraged. Following the announcement of the action plan, the National Parliament in November 2002 enacted a bill on the special economic zones, called ‘‘Free Economic Zone (FEZ)’’.

This law allows the Korean government to provide various incentives and beneﬁts to those foreign ﬁrms operating in designated FEZsdin order to attract foreign investment and foreign ﬁrms into the special economic zones. By September 2003, the Korean government had designated three FEZs: (1) Incheon FEZ; (2) Busan and Jinhae FEZ; and (3) Gwangyangman FEZ (see Fig. 1).

Simply speaking, this project focuses on creating special areas in which the government imposes diﬀerent regulatory rules on private economic activities. In these FEZs, for example, companies will be exempted from paying income and corporate taxes for the ﬁrst 3 years, and will only need to pay 50% of the amount for the following 2 years. Also, the imposition of land-use regulations on factory construction and enlargement will be minimal, and restrictions on entering businesses reserved for small- and medium-sized ﬁrms will be lifted. More importantly, labor regulation will be greatly liberalized in these areas. For instance, currently, employers pay for weekly holidays, while ‘‘unpaid’’ weekly holidays will be allowed. Several other incentives and beneﬁts will be given to foreigners and foreign ﬁrms in the FEZs (see Table 1). In this sense, the FEZ project pursued by the Korean government may be seen as an example of the state’s diﬀerential treatment of the population. In other words, by allowing the imposition of diﬀerent regulatory rules and by providing diﬀerent beneﬁts and privileges, the establishment of the FEZs will create a situation where the forms of governance and sovereignty in South Korea can be spatially diﬀerentiated and graduated.

The main research question in this paper is: Why does the Korean government want to develop these special economic zones? An answer to this question can be provided on the basis of the concept of the ‘‘hub economy’’. As Woo-Cumings (2003) has pointed out, it has been widely suggested that as manufacturing-oriented economies have shifted to become service-oriented ones through economic Fig. 1. Thus, many Asian countries have tried to develop big hub economies in their territories, thereby, serving as a kind of ‘‘gateway’’ to various parts of the Asia-Paciﬁc. One way to develop the hub economy may be by building special zones, 858 B.-G. Actually, this kind of economic rationality has been an important mode of reasoning for Korean policy-makers to justify the ambitious FEZ project.

My ‘‘society-centered’’ view of the state, however, suggests that the Korean government’s FEZ project and ‘‘graduated sovereignty’’, which is expected to occur in South Korea as a result of the establishment of the special economic zones, are not merely outcomes of policy choices based on a certain economic rationality; instead, they may have resulted from very complex political processes and negotiations among conﬂicting interests and ideas. In particular, based on insights from the literature on ‘‘actually existing neo-liberalism’’, I would like to propose that the special economic zone project in South Korea may be better seen as an outcome of ‘‘spatially selective’’ liberalization, which occurs through the political processes of ‘‘neo-liberalization’’. Therefore, the analytical focus of this paper will be on how the FEZ project in South Korea has been shaped through politically contested 859 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 interactions between the inherited institutional and spatial forms and policy frameworks of the ‘‘developmental state’’, and emergent forces of economic liberalization.

‘‘Neo-liberalization’’ under the inherited regulatory landscape of state-led industrialization in South Korea Inherited regulatory framework of the ‘‘developmental state’’ The old regulatory framework in South Korea before the 1990s was based on the active regulatory role played by the so-called ‘‘developmental state’’. The rapid economic growth and successful capitalist industrialization in South Korea from the 1960s to the 1980s would have been impossible without the active intervention of the state in economic activities. The accumulation strategy adopted by the South Korean developmental state focused on the intensive mobilization of capital and labor. First of all, in order to facilitate the intensive mobilization of capital, the Korean state formed a growth coalition with domestic large capitalists (Park, 1998). On the basis of a state-controlled ﬁnancial regulatory system and nationalistic industrial policies, the state provided preferential ﬁnancial and institutional support to selected domestic ﬁrms that were operating in state-designated strategic industries; in return, the selected businesses followed the government’s direction and played a leading role in manufacturing and exporting (Amsden, 1990). In addition, the state set up a system of repressive labor regulation for the intensive mobilization of labor (Park, 2001). It imposed harsh restrictions on labor union activities, which reduced the organizational protection of workers, thereby, forcing them to tolerate harsh working conditions and low incomes.

This regulatory system was essential for the rapid economic growth and industrialization of South Korea. The regulatory role, played by the developmental state, however, had certain spatial selectivity.2 Thus, the beneﬁts of industrialization, however, were not evenly distributed across the diﬀerent regions. More speciﬁcally, the strategy of export-led industrialization favored the more urbanized and alreadyindustrialized regions. In order to promote export-led industrialization, the Korean government provided much ﬁnancial and institutional support to labor-intensive export industries such as textiles, clothes, shoes, plywood and wigs. Therefore, those regions with heavier concentrations of these industries were more likely to enjoy the beneﬁts of the industrialization process (Cho, 1991). Since the Japanese colonial 2 According to Jones (1997), ‘spatial selectivity’ refers to a tendency of the state to privilege certain places through accumulation strategies and hegemonic projects. Such ‘spatial selectivity’ is derived from the tendency of what Jessop (1990) terms ‘strategic selectivity’. Strategic selectivity refers to the ways in which the state diﬀerentially privileges the access of some forces of representation to formulate speciﬁc policies and secure their support within the state apparatus, and then to eﬀectively implement these policies in relation to the social and material bases of the state (Jones, 1997, 847). Spatial selectivity refers to the spatial eﬀects of the strategic selectivity.

860 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 period (1910e1945), Seoul has been the most industrialized region in Korea. Thus, Seoul and its surrounding cities beneﬁted more from the state’s accumulation strategy of export-led industrialization than did other regions. Furthermore, in the 1960s, the Korean government constructed the industrial complexes and physical infrastructure necessary for industrialization, mostly in Seoul, in order to maximize the eﬃciency of regional policies by taking advantage of existing industrial facilities (KRIHS, 1996).3 As a result of such spatial selectivity, throughout the 1960s, economic activities were increasingly concentrated in Seoul and its sprawling metropolitan area. In other words, the state’s export-led industrialization strategy in the 1960s resulted in the increasing primacy of the Seoul Metropolitan Area.

In response to this increasing economic gap between Seoul and the rest of the country, the Korean government began to introduce various legal and institutional measures from the 1970s to curb Seoul’s growth. In particular, it has implemented a wide range of decentralization policies to disperse the population and economic activities away from the Seoul Metropolitan Area, and to promote the growth of peripheral regions. For the last three decades, the Korean regional policies have been primarily characterized by the persistent eﬀorts for decentralization through the construction of industrial complexes in the peripheral regions and strict prohibition on the location of industrial activities in the Seoul Metropolitan Area.

Challenges to the old regulatory framework: democratization and liberalization From the 1980s, the existing regulatory system began to face increasing challenges. In particular, various national and international forces imposed pressure on the South Korean government to move away from its authoritarian and interventionist policy orientation toward democratization and liberalization (Park, 2003). These internal and external pressures began to be signiﬁcant from the 1980s.

Internally, by the 1980s, there were increasing popular quests for democratization. Since the 1960s, students and intellectualsdsuch as professors, ministers, and journalistsdwho were aroused by the great injustice done to the workers and other subordinated groups, have organized social movements against military authoritarianism, requesting more democracy and a more equal distribution of wealth and social inclusion (Park, 2001). In particular, they viewed the state’s preferential support of selected capitalists as having something to do with political corruption, and criticized the growth coalition between the state and chaebols for its exclusivity and biasness in terms of the allocation of resources. In addition, the repressive practices of labor regulation had been another main target of the social movements.

3 In addition to Seoul, the southeast (including cities and provinces in North Gyeongsang and South Gyeongsang) beneﬁted relatively more than other regions from the export-led industrialization policies in the 1960s (Park, 2003). Due to its practice of spatial selectivity, however, the Korean government’s accumulation strategy in the 1960s gave much more favor to Seoul than to the southeast.

861 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 From the 1970s, students, intellectuals, and workers organized diverse forms of social movements to protest against the state’s repressive labor policies (Park, 2001).

Furthermore, democratic transition since 1987 has facilitated the expansion of civil society, in which workers have been able to occupy a strategic position (Kim & Moon, 2000). In this open political space, unions have been able to enhance their organizational and functional strength, and increase their political and industrial bargaining power. As a result, repressive means have become ineﬀective in the mobilization of labor, because they would only provoke severe resistance from the empowered working class (Park, 2001).

Even though the demands for democratization have been an important challenge to the old regulatory system, a bigger and much more serious challenge has been identiﬁed as part of the increasing pressure to liberalize the Korean economy.

Pressure for liberalization has come from both internal and external forces. Internally, by the 1980s, some chaebolsdon the basis of their increasing economic powerdwere beginning to see their strategic interests as being better served by a selective relaxation of state regulation on their market activities (Henderson, 1998, 19). Even though the chaebols did not want to ruin their good relationship with the statedso that they could continue to receive various incentives and support from the governmentdthey tried to enjoy relatively more autonomy from the state by campaigning for a deregulated economic environment. Furthermore, owing to processes of political democratization that started in the late 1980s, the chaebols became more politically autonomous from the state; hence, they intensiﬁed their pressure for deregulation.

In addition, there was increasing external pressure for deregulation. Until the mid-1980s, South Korean policy-makers had been able to insulate themselves from external pressure for change largely because of the willingness of the United States of America to accept a trade deﬁcit and South Korea’s signiﬁcance to the Western alliance as a frontline state. From about the mid-1980s, however, the United States of America under the Reagan administration began to pressure countries that had large trade surpluses with them to reduce barriers, so as to allow greater access for United States companies by way of both trade and investment (Bishop, 1997, 109).

Also, the new General Agreement on Tariﬀs and Trade (GATT) required member countries to grant greater access to their markets. Furthermore, South Korea’s membership of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) required it to embrace the principle of free capital ﬂows (Yeung, 2002).

These circumstances propelled policy-makers in South Korea to adopt a more market-oriented position in relation to trade and investment (Bishop, 1997, 119). Due to these increasing internal and external pressures, the South Korean government from the 1980s began to relax some of its regulations on business activities. In particular, from the early 1990s, the industrial and ﬁnancial policies of the South Korean government shifted signiﬁcantly toward liberalization in ﬁnancial regulation, exchange-rate management, and investment coordination. This liberalization was so drastic that Chang (1998) even saw it as the demise of ‘‘planning’’ and the ‘‘developmental state’’. Of course, it is questionable if the South Korean ‘‘developmental state’’ saw its demise in the early 1990s, but it is true that the old 862 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 regulatory system based on the interventionist role of the ‘‘developmental state’’ has gradually been dismantled. Even more important and drastic changes for liberalization occurred in the late 1990s. The 1997 ﬁnancial crisis lent crucial momentum to the neo-liberal reforms in South Korea. The IMF’s plan for recovery emphasized policy reforms in three major areas: the ﬁnancial system, corporate governance, and FDI (Bishop, 2001). In other words, the IMF asked the South Korean government to implement more drastic and extensive neo-liberal reforms in exchange for rescue loans to bail out the troubled economy. As a result, liberalization was greatly accelerated in South Korea.

These liberalization reforms have profoundly altered the foreign investment environment in South Korea. Responding to these changes enthusiastically, foreign companies have rapidly increased their investments in the nation. For example, the amount of inward FDI increased almost ﬁvefold from US$3203 million in 1996 to US$15,690 million in 2000. Actually, since 1997, South Korea has been one of the most successful countries in Asia in attracting FDI. This change is clearly shown in the trends of FDI inﬂows and outﬂows in the nation (see Fig. 2). Until 1997, South Korea always had higher volumes of outward FDI than inward FDI. As a result of the ﬁnancial liberalization of the South Korean government, from 1998, the volume of inward FDI rapidly increased and began to outweigh the volume of outward FDI.

Resistance to liberalization and ‘‘spatially selective liberalization’’ Despite these drastic liberalization reforms, the South Korean government has not fully liberalized its economy. This is because there are still signiﬁcant social and political barriers to liberalization. These barriers are related to the legacies of the old regulatory system. In particular, some social actors, who had beneﬁted fromdor at least grown up within the socio-political context ofdthe old regulatory framework have been very critical of the ideas of liberalization and deregulation.

First, the chaebols have put great pressure on the government to maintain protectionist policies for domestic companies. In other words, the chaebols were keen to preserve the protection of cheap credit while demanding that the government not use ﬁnances to restrict their operations (Amsden & Euh, 1993, 380). Thus, the general deregulatory pressure by the chaebols fell short of their rhetoric for supporting economic liberalization as desired by advocates of neo-liberal reform (Bishop, 1997, 112).

Rather, the chaebols have been very resistant to those policies that seek to terminate ‘‘governmentebusiness collusion’’ as a way of restructuring the chaebols (Gills & Gills, 2000).

Second, another important barrier to liberalization is related to the pathdependent attitude of bureaucrats to the idea of opening doors to foreign investors. In the 1960s and the 1970s, the South Korean government was successful in promoting national economic growth on the basis of a state-led and interventionist industrialization paradigm, which had emphasized the prominence of the state, rather than the market, in inﬂuencing economic activity. Also, with the growth alliance between the state and the chaebols, the state-led industrialization program contained a strong nationalist orientation, thereby, promoting the development of domestic ﬁrms. The ordinary bureaucrats had been strongly inﬂuenced by this tradition. In particular, bureaucrats in the Ministry of Commerce and Industrydthe main oﬃce to set up and implement industrial policiesdhad developed a strong nationalist attitude toward the development of national industries (Bishop, 1997). In addition, there had been concern that the state’s withdrawal from a strongly interventionist role in economic activity would result in less power for the bureaucracy. In this context, with regard to neo-liberal reform, some of ordinary bureaucrats had been somewhat unwilling to abandon the interventionist and nationalistic policies of the past, despite that top policy-makers’ had advocated for more drastic neo-liberal reform (Bishop, 1997).

Third, labor unions have strongly opposed to the idea of liberalization, especially with respect to the neo-liberal reforms of labor regulation. Labor unions in South Korea have grown up through social struggle against the repressive practices of labor regulation. Also, they have greatly increased their political and industrial bargaining power on the basis of the democratic transitions since 1987. Given the empowerment of the working class since the late 1980s, there have been increasing needs for the development of an alternative system of labor regulation, based on more balanced power relations between capital and labor. The establishment of a new system of labor regulation has been unsuccessful, however, due to unsettled conﬂicts among the state, capital and labor (Park, 2001). Thus, the hostility between capital and labor continued. While workers called for higher wages, greater bargaining power and workplace democracy, management was actively seeking wage stability through the creation of more ﬂexible labor-market conditions (Kim & Moon, 2000, 57). In this context, when the Korean government tried to enact a new labor law in 1997 that focused on the enhancement of labor-market ﬂexibility, labor unions strongly protested against the labor reform by organizing massive strikes. More than 500,000 workers, approximately 82% of total organized workers, joined the strikes held in 864 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 January 1997 in support of the re-amendment of labor law (Park, 2001). Nevertheless, labor-market ﬂexibility has been greatly increased by a series of labor reforms made before and after the 1997 ﬁnancial crisis. Also, post-crisis economic restructuring has led to mass unemployment, increased employment insecurity, and a sharp reduction in workers’ incomes, wealth, and welfare. Given this situation, labor unions are in no position to accept further liberalization and labor reforms.

As a result of these barriers and the resistance to liberalization, some of the regulations on business activities and labor market still remain, leading foreign investors in South Korea to complain about the lack of liberalization. For example, a survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in South Korea indicates that foreign businesses in Korea cite heavy regulations and labor inﬂexibility as the worst obstacles restricting them from investing in South Korea (‘‘Is Korea Attractive for Business?’’, 2001). Foreign investors especially complained about the inﬂexible labor market in South Korea, in the sense that it is very hard to ﬁre workers when the need arises. Given this situation, and in order to more aggressively attract FDI, Korean policy-makers have wanted to build a more business-friendly environment by substantially lifting regulations. It has been very diﬃcult to push for further deregulation and liberalization on a large scale, however, due to enormous social resistance from various forces.

Given this situation, the Korean government decided to develop special economic zones in which more drastic deregulation and liberalization measures could be implemented. In other words, the Korean policy-makers took the strategy of ‘‘spatially selective liberalization’’ because it was seen as being more acceptable than broader liberalization reforms on a larger scale. With regard to this, a statement by former Prime Minister Nam Duck-Woo is quite interesting. In an interview with Korea Herald, he said: We cannot make the entire nation as special economic zone because of political and social barriers. Hence we need to limit a special economic zone to a speciﬁed area. Let’s hope that the boundary of the SEZ gradually expands to cover the entire nation through a learning process (‘‘Korea’s new vision: hub plan need to focus on logistic infrastructure construction’’, 2002).

In other words, the promotion of the FEZ project is an outcome of politically contested interactions between the resisting forces against liberalization and neoliberal reformers in South Korea.

Continuing interplay between inherited and emergent regulatory projects The strategy of ‘‘spatially selective liberalization’’dmore speciﬁcally, the FEZ projectdcannot completely resolve the political tensions taking place with respect to the processes of ‘‘neo-liberalization’’ in South Korea. Instead, the FEZ project has provided a new arena, in which another round of battle between the proponents and opponents of neo-liberal reforms can be waged. Since the policies for developing FEZs are not ﬁxed but are continuously (re)constructed through socio-political processes, the actual contents of the FEZ project would have been, and will be, 865 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced by the ways in which diﬀerent interests and ideas are mediated and (re)negotiated through political struggle. This section discusses how the dialectical interplay between inherited and emergent regulatory projects has ensued with respect to the FEZ project.

Interplay between inherited and emergent spatial strategies With respect to the FEZ project, an interesting negotiation was made between inherited spatial selectivity of the ‘‘development state’’ and the emergent ‘‘neoliberal’’ spatial strategy. This interplay was clearly reﬂected in the decision-making processes for the location of FEZs. In 2003, three citiesdIncheon, Busan and Gwangyangdwere designated FEZs. Yet, in the original plan for the ‘‘Northeast Asian Business Hub’’, proposed in April 2002, only Incheon was considered a possible location for a special economic zone because it was seen to have the greatest potential in becoming a ﬁnancial and logistic hub of Northeast Asia, due to its geographical proximity to Seoul and being equipped with a world-class international airport and the third largest port in the nation (‘‘Three areas in IncheondYeongjongdo, Songdo, and Kimpodwill be designated as a special economic zone next year’’, 2002). The other two cities, Busan and Gwangyang, were not included in the original plan.

This original plan, however, was harshly criticized for aggravating the eﬀects of regional disparity between the Seoul Metropolitan Area and the rest of the country.

As discussed earlier, reducing the regional economic gap by promoting a decentralization of population and industrial activities from the Seoul Metropolitan Area has been one of the most important spatial strategies of the South Korean ‘‘developmental state’’ for the last 30 years. Despite the widely accepted criticism of the decentralization policies for their ineﬀectiveness, the spatial strategy was successful, at least, in slowing down the growth of the Seoul Metropolitan Area. As shown in Table 2, the Seoul Metropolitan Area’s share in national manufacturing employment increased by 8.5% from 1963 to 1972, while it increased by only 0.3% from 1972 to 1982. On the contrary, the southeast became more important in manufacturing employment in the 1970s, mainly because several industrial complexes were built in the southeastern coastal areas at that time. In other words, the South Korean developmental state was able to reduce the primacy of the Seoul Metropolitan Area to some degree by the late 1970s on the basis of its decentralization policies.

Since the 1990s, however, the economic gap between Seoul and the rest of the country has widened again due to changes in the spatial selectivity of the government’s industrial and regional policies. Given the increasing signiﬁcance of the information-related industries, from the late 1980s, the government’s industrial policies began to focus on the promotion of knowledge-based and technologyintensive industries. This industrial restructuring has resulted in the concentration of high-tech industries in the Seoul Metropolitan Area. Furthermore, the Korean government has attempted to change its spatial strategies since the 1990s. Given increasing international competition, the central oﬃcials from the mid-1990s began to emphasize the important role of Seoul and the surrounding urban regions in leading the growth of new, high-tech industries.

The government has subsequently adopted new regional policies through which the agglomeration economies of the Seoul Metropolitan Area are to be maintained so as to be feasible for industrial competitiveness in the world market (Yim, 2003). More speciﬁcally, some regulations on the location of industrial activities in the Seoul Metropolitan Area have been greatly relaxed. As a result, the primacy of Seoul has been greatly strengthened since the 1980s. Table 2 shows that the Seoul Metropolitan Area’s share of national manufacturing employment has been continuously 867 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 increasing since 1982, while other region’s (including the southeast) shares have been declining in this same period.

Given this situation, from the mid-1990s, there was increasing criticism from cities and regions outside the Seoul Metropolitan Area towards the new spatial strategy adopted by the state, which has been considered the main reason for the increasing gap between the Seoul Metropolitan Area and the rest of the country. In this context, an important concern about the government’s original plan to develop a special economic zone in Incheon was that because of Incheon’s location within the Seoul Metropolitan Area, the project might aggravate the concentration of economic means and population in the Seoul Metropolitan Area. In other words, the original plan for a special economic zone was seen to be tantamount to the virtual scrapping away of the long-held decentralization policy (‘‘Blueprint for NE Asian Hub, survival for Korea’’, 2002). Thus, when the original plan was ﬁrst announced, cities and provinces outside the Seoul Metropolitan Area protested strongly. It was necessary for the special economic zone project to address the issue of uneven regional development; hence, the government came up with a new plan to include Incheon, Busan and Gwangyang as special economic zone locations (‘‘Heaven and hell in Korea’’, 2002).

Creation of hybrid spaces Another important issue around which political battles have taken place has to do with the nature of the special economic zones. When the plan to develop special economic zones was ﬁrst proposed in 2002 under the Kim Dae-Jung administration, these zones were mainly planned as ﬁnancial and logistic centers in Northeast Asia.

With emphasis on the urgency for a full range of ﬁnancial liberalization measures, neo-liberal reformers within the government, especially those in the Ministry of Finance and Economy, aimed to develop ﬁnancial centers within the national territory through the special economic zone project.4 There are, however, those who have been less enthusiastic about ﬁnancial liberalization within the government, as they have been more skeptical of the idea of developing ﬁnancial centers. This is especially the case with the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Energydthe main oﬃce in charge of industrial policies and manufacturing development since the 1960sdwhich has suggested that more emphasis be placed on the development of high-tech manufacturing and R&D activities in the special economic zones. With the election of President Roh Moo- Hyun in December 2002, this view became even more inﬂuential in the formulation of plans for FEZs because the newly elected president and his camp had been relatively more critical than former president Kim Dae-Jung of drastic neo-liberal 4 This is based on an interview with an oﬃcial in Presidential Committee on Northeast Asian Business Hub, held in June 2003.

868 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 reforms.4 Thus, after the presidential election in December 2002, the presidential transition team began to emphasize that the Northeast Asian business hub vision would initially target the building of a regional information technology manufacturing base in South Korea (‘‘Business hub plan to focus on IT’’, 2003). Also, seeing that it would be unlikely for TNCs operating in Hong Kong and Singapore to relocate their regional headquarters to South Korea just for the sake of more incentives and tax breaks, the transition team suggested that the special economic zones be developed as global R&D hubs in Northeast Asia (‘‘Sondgo to be developed into IT research hub’’, 2003).

What makes this renewed idea on special economic zones very diﬀerent from the previous one is its emphasis on the creation of ‘‘sticky places’’, to which TNCs are more attached and become less mobile, in the special economic zones. In the previous plan, the emphasis was mainly put on the relaxation of regulations on business activities and the provision of ﬁnancial and institutional incentives and beneﬁts to foreign ﬁrms operating in the special economic zones in order to attract FDI; while policy-makers in the new administration began to look for opportunities to attract foreign investment and receive beneﬁts from TNCs without providing too many incentives and beneﬁts.4 For this purpose, the transition team proposed the development of an attractive industrial cluster ﬁrst in the special economic zones, and then to use the attractiveness of the cluster as leverage to attract foreign ﬁrms to the areas and develop ﬁnancial and logistics hubs (‘‘Sondgo to be developed into IT research hub’’, 2003).

This new idea, however, has not fully materialized in the FEZ project due to strong resistance from neo-liberal reformers both within and outside the government. Within the government, the Ministry of Finance and Economy has strongly opposed the idea proposed by the presidential transition team, instead emphasizing the urgency of developing ﬁnancial centers in special economic zones.4 Neo-liberal reformers outside the government also attacked the new idea. The Seoul Financial Forum, organized by a group of leading economists in South Korea, for example, strongly advised the government to focus on ﬁnancial centers (‘‘President- Elect Roh Advised to Focus on Financial Hub’’, 2003). Support for the ﬁnancial centers idea came also from foreign investors. At a seminar hosted by the Federation of Korean Industries, for example, William Oberlindthe president of the American Chamber of Commerce in South Koreadsaid: ‘‘all economic centers start with ﬁnances. It is urgent Korea designs a plan for transforming Seoul into a ﬁnancial hub’’ (‘‘AmCham head says ﬁnances key to hub project’’, 2003). Through the processes of political negotiation, these two diﬀerent views on special economic zones have been mixed, and the Korean government has decided to focus on both ﬁnancial centers and the R&D hub in developing special economic zones. In other words, the special economic zones will not become truly neo-liberal spaces ﬁlled with neo-liberal rules and institutions. Rather, the dynamic interplay between the inherited regulatory forces of the developmental state and the emergent neo-liberal forces have resulted in the creation of ‘‘hybrid spaces’’, composed of neoliberalization and active state intervention in industrial development, in the special economic zones.

Continuing political battle 869 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 In addition to these issues, there are a lot of other issues around which political battles are taking place. In particular, anti-neoliberalism forces in South Korea (including labor unions, NGOs, etc.) have strongly opposed the FEZ project since the government’s ﬁrst proposal of the plan in April 2002. They have seen it as ‘‘a ﬁrst step toward a full-scale change for liberalization’’, even though liberalization at this moment is meant only for selected areas.

In particular, labor unions have fervently protested against some proposed changes in labor regulation for foreign ﬁrms operating in the special economic zones.

Under the current labor law, for example, ﬁrms can relocate workers only for 26 government-designated workplaces for a period of up to 2 years, but the plan for special economic zones proposes to allow foreign companies in these zones to freely relocate their employees to other workplaces. Also, under the current labor law, ﬁrms have to give all employees a paid day oﬀevery month, but the government has proposed unpaid monthly leave for workers in special economic zones. Fearing that these ‘‘beneﬁts’’ in special economic zones will be eventually extended to ﬁrms in the entire nation, labor unions have severely criticized the FEZ plan (‘‘Labor Threatens Strike Against Law on Special Economic Zones’’, 2002).

The anti-neoliberalism groups have also criticized the plan to deregulate the establishment of foreign education institutes in special economic zones. Allowing foreign education institutes that are meant only for foreigners is not a big issue, but the Korean government plans to allow domestic residents to attend foreign schools in the FEZs in order to increase the size of the education market for foreign schools, thereby, facilitating the location of more foreign education institutes in the FEZs.

The education circle, including NGOs and even the Ministry of Education, have resisted to the FEZ plan, with the argument that the liberalization of the education market and the inﬂux of foreign schools will destroy an already troubled public education system in South Korea (‘‘An SEZ dilemma’’, 2002). The proposed deregulation of foreign investment in the medical sector in special economic zones has been another issue criticized by anti-neoliberalism groups. Under current regulation in South Korea, medical service centers are not allowed to be established for proﬁt but only for public beneﬁts; allowing foreign-ﬁnanced hospitals and pharmacies in special economic zones may be seen as the start of the liberalization of the medical market in South Korea (Choi & Yoon, 2002). The anti-neoliberalism camp has argued that the eﬀects of medical market liberalization will be devastating for the Korean people because high-quality medical services will only be made available to those who can aﬀord it, while the majority will be left lacking in basic healthcare.

As a result of such resistance, the government’s original plan for the establishment of special economic zones was modiﬁed by the time the bill on special economic zones, called ‘‘Free Economic Area Law’’, was ﬁnally approved by the National Parliament in December 2002. For example, due to resistance from labor unions to the original plan, the modiﬁed bill does not allow the relocation of blue-collar workers in the manufacturing sectors (Lee & Park, 2003, 70). The modiﬁcation in the 870 B.-G. Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 bill, however, was minor and the basic concept was not changed. Despite some other minor changes, the FEZ project still basically calls for relaxed regulations for foreign companies and their employees residing in FEZs in order to provide them with a better business and living environment. Thus, protests against the FEZ project have continued even after the ‘‘Free Economic Area Law’’ was passed by the National Parliament in December 2002.5 Conclusion By focusing on the special economic zone project recently pursued by the South Korean government, I aim in this paper to examine the complex political processes through which state sovereignty can be re-territorialized in this globalizing economy.

The special economic zone project facilitates the ‘‘state’s diﬀerential treatment of the population’’ within the national territory of South Korea by imposing diﬀerent forms of governance and regulatory rules within and outside the special economic zones. In order to understand the complexities of the political processes that have contributed to the state’s diﬀerential treatment of the population and the resultant ‘‘graduated sovereignty’’ in South Korea, I have attempted to explore the driving forces behind the special economic zone project. In particular, I have examined how the special economic zone project has been created and (re)shaped through complex political struggle, and processes associated with ‘‘neo-liberalization’’ in South Korea.

More speciﬁcally, by viewing the special economic zone project as a spatial outcome of ‘‘East Asian neo-liberalization’’, my analysis has focused on how and why the state has taken up the strategy of ‘‘spatially selective liberalization’’ within the context of politically contested interactionsdbetween the opponents of neoliberal reform, who have grown up under the socio-political context of the old regulatory framework of the developmental state; and the proponents of neo-liberal reform. More speciﬁcally, this paper has suggested that even though diverse internal and external forces have promoted diverse forms of neo-liberal reform in South Korea, the path-dependent and politically contested interactions between the inherited regulatory landscape and the emergent neo-liberal restructuring projects have made it very diﬃcult to realize abrupt and full-scale liberalization at the national scale in South Korea; hence, the state has pursued ‘‘spatially selective liberalization’’dmore speciﬁcally, the special economic zone projectdas a way of circumventing oppositions to neo-liberal reform.

William Oberlin, the president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Korea, for example, urged: ‘‘the chamber as a whole prefers the idea of making all of Korea a ‘special economic zone’ as opposed to designating just a few speciﬁc areas’’ in an interview with Korea Herald (‘‘AmCham head says ﬁnances key to hub project’’, 2003).

Park / Political Geography 24 (2005) 850e873 In addition, I have shown in this paper that dynamic interplay between the inherited and emergent regulatory projects has persisted, and it has signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced the actual content of the special economic zone project in South Korea. In particular, it has been demonstrated that the current locations of special economic zones in Incheon, Gwangyang and Busan were the outcomes of dialectical interactions between the inherited spatial selectivity of the ‘‘developmental state’’ and the new neo-liberal spatial strategies. Also, due to the strong tendencies of path dependency, the special economic zones have been constructed as ‘‘hybrid spaces’’ composed of neo-liberalization and state-led industrial development, rather than truly neo-liberal spaces. The direction of this special economic zone project, however, is still uncertain due to continuing political battles with respect to the nature of the project.

In conclusion, I have suggested in this paper that the processes of neoliberalization are deeply inﬂuenced by political struggles and negotiations among various social and political forces. In particular, I have highlighted the signiﬁcance of the properties of path dependency in the politically contested processes of neoliberalization. More speciﬁcally, I argue that the processes of neo-liberalization would have strong features of uneven ‘‘spatial’’ development due to the dialectical interplay between the past and new changes. In such situations of ‘‘spatially selective’’ liberalization, the state may impose diﬀerent regulatory rules or institutions on (spatially) diﬀerentiated segments of people, thereby, facilitating the rise of ‘‘graduated sovereignty’’.

University of Bern, Department of Economics, Schanzeneckstrasse 1, 3001 Bern, Switzerland A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T JEL classiﬁcation: C21 O40 H54 R11 Keywords: Regional transfers Local average treatment effects European Union 1. Introduction The European Union (EU) runs a system of public transfers to subnational regions. The general idea of EU transfers – which are labeled European Agricultural Guarantee Fund (EAGF) and European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD) in the context of agriculture and Structural Funds and Cohesion Fund in the context of infrastructure, education, and labor markets – is to foster structural and economic homogeneity across countries and regions in order to make the EU’s system of market integration viable. As early as 1973, the British Commissioner for Regional Policy, George Thomson, argued that regional policy is “necessary” to help the poorer regions of Europe.

We focus on Structural and Cohesion Funds, the second-largest budget line after the EU’s agricultural expenses. Economic research in recent years focused on its effectiveness.1 The insights from this work were three: expenses through the EU’s Structural and Cohesion Funds (i) induced positive average effects on per-capita income growth in subnational regions that lagged behind the EU average; (ii) more expenses did This paper analyzes the regional effects of EU Regional Policy during four programming periods: 1989-1993, 1994-1999, 2000-2006, 2007-2013. In particular, the focus is on the impact of transfers during the Financial and Economic Crisis and on the effects of gaining versus losing treatment status under the main Regional Policy subprogram – referred to as Objective 1 or Convergence Objective. We ﬁnd that effects of Objective 1 status on growth are positive though not very long-lived: the effects of losing Objective 1 status on economic growth are negative, and the earlier positive effects on growth in the period(s) of Objective 1 treatment more or less undone.

We show that the effects are weaker during the Crisis than before, in particular, on per-capita income in countries where the Crisis hit harder. not generally induce proportionately larger effects; (iii) regions responded heterogeneously, with smaller effects found in regions where the institutions are bad (corruption is high) and where human capital is scarce.

Most of the work on the EU’s regional transfer scheme identiﬁed positive effects on recipient-region economic growth.2 The present paper considers all programming periods 1989-93, 1994- 99, 2000-06, and 2007-13. Including the latest completed programming period, 2007-13, goes beyond previous work and might speak to the effectiveness of EU Regional Policy at times of the Economic and Financial Crisis relative to “normal” times. In particular we explore heterogeneity across transfer recipients in terms of their exposure to the Financial and Economic Crisis. We concentrate on the effects of Objective 1 treatment (now called Convergence Objective) on a variety of outcomes such as growth of per-capita income and employment, and total as well as public investment intensity.

Going beyond cross-sectional identiﬁcation, we seek to estimate the effects on economic growth and other outcomes when a region switches into, and eventually loses, Objective 1 status – an issue which requires * Corresponding author.

2 See Ederveen et al. (2002); Cappelen et al. (2003); Dall’erba and Le Gallo (2008); Becker et al. (2010), (2012), (2013); Pellegrini et al. (2013); Cerqua and Pellegrini (2015); Rodríguez-Pose and Di Cataldo (2015) see Mohl and Hagen (2010), for an overview.

S.O. Becker et al. Regional Science and Urban Economics 69 (2018) 143–152 data from the last two programming periods 2000-06 and 2007-13 and which, with the exception of Barone et al. (2016), has not been studied.3 A region may lose Objective 1 status for two reasons: being just below the 75% threshold in the previous period, it might overtake other regions and end up above the 75% threshold. Alternatively, the expansion of the EU into Eastern Europe pulled down the 75% threshold in absolute terms: the same absolute level of GDP per capita which made a region eligible beforehand, no longer satisﬁes eligibility.

The associated results may speak to the longevity – or, conversely, the short-livedness – of the growth effects from receiving funding. A priori, one could imagine three possible scenarios for regions which lose Structural and Cohesion Funds recipient status: (i) the earlier funding might have put them on a permanently higher growth trajectory; (ii) the loss of funding status might make them return more or less rapidly to a growth trajectory corresponding to their economic fundamentals without funding; or (iii) they might suffer from the “sudden stop” of losing large amounts of EU funding and face a growth of even less than the one corresponding to their economic fundamentals without funding. Transfers associated with Objective 1 did, on average, over the quarter of a century, 1989-2013, generate additional growth in per-capita income among the funded regions in the EU, but less strongly so in 2000-13 than on average. Regions that lose Objective 1 status fall behind the average non-recipient region in terms of economic growth, and earlier positive growth effects from such funding are more than undone, at least in the short run. Focusing on regions that receive Objective 1 transfers for the ﬁrst time we ﬁnd immediate positive effects which are not signiﬁcantly different from the effects observed for the average recipient region.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 outlines the econometric setup. Section 3 describes the data, and Section 4 presents the empirical results. Finally, Section 5 provides a policy discussion and concludes.

2. Empirical approach We consider an approach, where the treatment is a binary Objective 1/Convergence Objective indicator for NUTS2 region i and program period r. We will generally use Yir for economic outcomes and Xir for the forcing variable. In particular, we need to distinguish between funding eligibility (according to the 75% cutoff rule regarding EU average percapita income), Eir, and actual treatment, Dir, as there were some exceptions from the treatment rule, giving rise to a fuzzy regressiondiscontinuity design (RDD). Fig. 1 shows the corresponding discontinuity in the treatment probability for the pooled sample across all prebudgetary-period years in the data. We estimate the fuzzy RDD in a two-stage least-squares approach where the ﬁrst- and second-stage regression equations, respectively, are given by: Dir ¼ h0ðXirÞ þ Eir½γ1 þ h1ðXirÞ  h0ðXirÞ þ ζir þ νir; (1) Yir ¼ f0ðXirÞ þ Dir½α1 þ f1ðXirÞ  f0ðXirÞ þ ηir þ εir; (2) with α1 measuring the local average treatment effect (LATE) of binary Objective 1 transfer treatment. Akin to h1ðXirÞ and h0ðXirÞ in the ﬁrst stage, f1ðXirÞ and f0ðXirÞ are ﬂexible, smooth (differentiable) functions of pre-budgetary-period normalized log-per-capita income in purchasing power parity. The functions h1 (f1) and h0 (f0) are separately estimated 3 Barone et al. (2016) study the case of one Italian region (Abruzzi) that lost its funding status de jure at the end of 1999 and de facto at the end of 2000.

They use a synthetic control method (i.e., they generate an artiﬁcial Abruzzi region by weighting other Italian regions). In contrast, our approach focuses on the loss of Objective 1 status at large, considering all EU regions, and it is based on a regression discontinuity design, which identiﬁes the treatment effect from a subsample of EU regions in the vicinity of the 75% of EU average per-capita income threshold.

3. Data and descriptive statistics We downloaded data on most variables from Eurostat Regional Statistics. We complement this by data from Cambridge Econometrics. The information about Objective 1 status and eligibility as well as information on expenditures stem from the European Commission. See Table A1 for details about the data sources.

Treatment variable The binary Objective 1 treatment indicator variable, Dir, is determined on the basis of NUTS2 real per-capita levels in speciﬁc years prior to each programming period.5 Given non-compliance, we need to distinguish between eligible and recipient NUTS2 regions. Two important reasons for non-compliance are: (i) regions that did not qualify for Objective 1 status based on the data available at the time when regional funds were assigned, turned out to be eligible ex post (or vice versa), when GDP ﬁgures were revised; (ii) speciﬁc exceptions were granted to regions with a low population density and in peripheral locations.6 Outcome variables We consider the following outcomes: average annual PPP-adjusted GDP-per-capita growth; average annual employment growth; average annual total investment intensity (gross ﬁxed capital formation relative to GDP); and average annual public investment intensity (gross ﬁxed capital formation of the public sector relative to GDP).

Control variables In some of the regressions we control for ﬁxed 4 We do not consider non-parametric speciﬁcations of these functions for two reasons: ﬁrst, we focus on switchers with respect to Objective 1 status and the mass of switchers is not large enough to support non-parametric estimation; second, there is no existing procedure to determine the optimal bandwidth for non-parametric RDD with panel data and ﬁxed effects.

The latter were collected from the European Central Bank (ECB) and the OECD.7 Sample composition We do not include Bulgaria, Romania, and Croatia in the analysis for reasons of data availability. We brieﬂy discuss the numbers in Panel A. Altogether, of 902 NUTS2- region-by-period observations covered, 343 were eligible for Objective 1 treatment, while 279 actually got funding. Objective 1 treatment eligibility generally guaranteed actual treatment unless national governments did not provide data on percapita incomes at the appropriate regional level. Objective 1 treatment for ineligible regions roots in a number of exceptions that were formulated in the respective budgets (see Section 3 for examples).

Table A2 shows summary statistics for key variables of interest, pooled over the four programming periods 1989-93, 1994-99, 2000-06, and 2007-13: GDP per capita growth is measured as the average annual difference of the logarithms of end-of-period and prior-to-period GDP per capita. The prior-to-period years are 1988 for 1989-93, 1993 for 1994-99, 1999 for 2000-06, and 2006 for 2007-13.9 Employment growth is also deﬁned in terms of logarithms and for the same years, while (total) Investment per GDP and Public investment per GDP are average ratios observed across all years during a programming period. Hence, with GDP per capita growth, an average of 0.03 indicates an average annual growth rate of about 3 percent during a programming period.

With, e.g., Investment per GDP, an average of 0.23 indicates an average annual investment rate of 23 percent of GDP during a programming period. The means of 0.31 for actual treatment (Dir) and of 0.28 for treatment eligibility (Eir) are consistent with the numbers in Table 1.

The ﬁnal row displays per-capita GDP in purchasing-power parity terms as a deviation from the respective EU average: negative numbers indicate normalized values of by-rule eligible NUTS2 regions, while positive numbers indicate normalized values of by-rule ineligible NUTS2 regions.

Validity of the RDD setup Fig. 2 shows the density distribution of GDP per capita relative to the 75% threshold when pooling observations across all four programming periods. This ﬁgure following McCrary (2008) does not indicate any manipulation of GDP per capita in order to gain eligibility for Objective 1 funds, as would be suggested by a spike in the number of regions just below the 75% threshold. In particular, we obtain an estimate of 0:02 for the discontinuity of the density function at the threshold and a relatively large standard error of 0:11.

A further test for the validity of the RDD setup is to check whether not only the treatment (as illustrated in Fig. 1) but also covariates displayed a discontinuity at the threshold. All of these variables could be thought of as determinants of economic growth.10 These tests together suggest that (a) there is no manipulation of GDP per capita to obtain eligibility and (b) there is no jump in any of the covariates at the 75% threshold, so the only jump of interest is the one in treatment status and subsequently in the outcomes of interest.

4. Local average effects of binary Objective 1 treatment Period 1989-2013 Table 2 summarizes results based on the approach in Section 2 and the pooled data for 1989-2013 in Section 3.

Column (1) pertains to a linear speciﬁcation in terms of the forcing variable, Xir. Column (2) is the same as Column (1) except that NUTS2 ﬁxed effects across programming periods are included. (2010).

146 neighborhood of Xir ¼ 0 – including such ﬁxed effects (or any other control variable) would not be necessary as observations on both sides of the thresholds are quasi identical. However, given the limited number of NUTS2 regions at hand, it may be that unobserved factors still vary across eligible and non-eligible regions and thus controlling for ﬁxed NUTS2 effects might be desirable. Columns (3) and (4) correspond to Columns (1) and (2), respectively, except that they use linear as well as quadratic terms of Xir.

The parameters in Panel A of Table 2 are relatively stable across the four columns of interest, and they vary between 0.012 in Column (3) and 0.019 in Columns (2) and (4). These ﬁndings support an increase in period-speciﬁc per-capita-income growth by somewhat less than 2 percentage points due to Objective 1 treatment. These results are quantitatively close to the ﬁndings in Becker et al. (2010) for only three programming periods. The fact that including versus excluding the region-speciﬁc ﬁxed effects is of little bearing for the statistical (and economic) signiﬁcance of the results suggests that omitted variables are of minor importance, and the RDD is quite successful in isolating the causal effect of Objective 1 treatment on per-capita income growth.

This is much less the case for Employment growth and (total) Investment per GDP (i.e., investment intensity) in Panels B and C, respectively. There, we ﬁnd statistically signiﬁcant effects on employment growth (negative) and investment intensity (positive) only when not controlling for regionspeciﬁc ﬁxed effects, whereas the impact of Objective 1 treatment is statistically insigniﬁcant when accounting for those effects. This suggests that Objective 1 treatment and/or the forcing variable is correlated with time-invariant determinants of employment growth and investment intensity (this is different from the determinants of and results for percapita income growth). With regard to Public investment per GDP we ﬁnd a signiﬁcant and robust effect of about 2.2 percentage points. Hence, we should be more cautious in interpreting the effects on employment and private investment relative to the ones on per-capita-income growth or on public investment intensity. Moreover, the results suggest that the increased accumulation of public capital stock crowds out some private investments.

Period 2000-13 and the Financial and Economic Crisis Table 3 repeats the analysis of Table 2 for only the last two programming periods. This serves two purposes: ﬁrst, it allows us to understand whether effects of Objective 1 transfers are stable over time; second, it provides estimates for the role of Objective 1 transfers for regions in more versus less crisis-stricken countries. The table is organized in six columns. The results in Columns (1)-(3) are based on linear functions of the forcing variable, Xir, while Columns (4)–(6) are based on quadratic functions of it. Columns (2) and (5) include NUTS2-region and time ﬁxed effects, whereas the other columns only include country and time ﬁxed effects.

Columns (3) and (6) account for the average treatment effect as a parameter on the Objective 1 indicator, on the main effect of the Financial and Economic Crisis through the government-bond-yield spreads (GBYS) variable, and an interaction term of the former with the demeaned GBYS. Considering the immediate drop in income and the slow response of labor markets this seems plausible. For investments, we do not ﬁnd any signiﬁcant effects.

These ﬁndings suggest that the positive contemporaneous responses to transfers are not permanent and seem to vanish when transfers are stopped. While there is a signiﬁcant and sizable contemporaneous effect of Objective 1 transfers this may be largely due to consumption effects and it remains questionable, whether self-sustaining growth is triggered by the transfers, at least by their recipience over less than two decades.

The evidence suggests that the contemporaneous beneﬁts of transfers are undone after losing Objective 1 status. This ﬁnding is very much in line with Barone et al. (2016) who ﬁnd the same result in their study of the Italian Abruzzi region. Our result that Objective 1 treatment effects are not long-lasting is in line with the overall pattern of GDP per capita (PPP) disparities across EU15 NUTS2 regions measured in terms of the coefﬁ- cient of variation (CV) and the ratio of the distribution’s range and the mean (Range/mean) as summarized in Table 6. While it is impossible to isolate the causal role of transfers regarding this descriptive evidence, it nevertheless indicates that overall economic disparities among the EU15 NUTS2 regions did not decline such that transfers were at least not capable of compensating any other trends that contributed to increasing disparities among the respective regions over a relatively large time window.

5. Discussion and conclusions After agricultural assistance, the European Union’s Regional Policy is the second-biggest line in the Union’s budget. At times of tighter budgets due to stagnation if not economic downturn, voters and politicians in netcontributing (to the EU budget) countries and regions ask about the justiﬁcation of such budgets, even more so than at times of economic prosperity.

This paper sheds light on the effects of the Structural Funds in recipient regions. It illustrates that the programme induced positive effects not only over all periods for which data exist in the past but also in the two most recent completed budgetary periods (2000–06 and 2007- 13) which were affected adversely by cyclical phenomena. The effects of transfers in the Crisis period were weaker than before, in particular, on per-capita income in countries where the Crisis hit harder. Adjustments with regard to co-ﬁnancing were successful in strengthening the treatment effect of Objective 1 or Convergence Objective transfers on employment growth but not on income growth in particularly Crisis-prone regions. Another insight is that transfers tend to display immediate effects, but they do not show much longevity beyond a programming period when it comes to stimulating real per-capita-income growth in recipient regions. Hence, previous growth gains seem to be largely undone once Objective 1 status is lost. This ﬁnding is consistent with the idea that Objective 1 status – when awarded at all – should probably be kept for longer periods and should be geared towards investments that support long-term growth prospects. Otherwise, some regions might just see a one-off bonanza without any long-term beneﬁts.
