In developing countries, where the enforcement of land property rights tends to be weak, arson is allegedly used to destroy slums in premium neighborhoods, force residents out, and clear the land for sale or development (Ockey, 1997; Rahman, 2001; D’Andrea, 2012; Barcelos and Viana, 2017; Malhotra, 2018). For urban landowners, using this strategy could be more advantageous than engaging in overt armed confrontation, which is typically the case in rural land conflicts. Because fires in slums spread fast, it is hard to determine their true causes, let alone find potential arsonists (Braga and Landim, 2008; Walls et al., 2017). Therefore, landowners could use arson to enforce their claim over contested land while still evading the high-monitoring environment of dense urban areas.

To examine the use of arson, I study how the incentives for engaging in violent land conflict vary according to prices and legal ownership (private or public) of slum-occupied land. On the one hand, higher land value drives higher willingness to remove slums (Jimenez, 1985; Turnbull, 2008; Brueckner and Selod, 2009; Brueckner et al., 2019). I refine this idea with an optimal stopping model, suggesting a non-linear relationship between land value and removal. On the other hand, ownership matters: private landowners should have stronger incentives to remove slums than public entities. While private owners make an individual decision, public owners face a collective action problem that may reduce their incentives to intervene (Olson, 1971).

To test these implications, I construct a unique database spanning from 2001 to 2016, incorporating geocoded information on slums, fires, and land prices in São Paulo, one of the world’s largest cities (United Nations, 2018). With a cross-sectional analysis and a Difference-in- Differences design, I explore variation in both land value and ownership across slums and over time, examining how these factors affect the prevalence of arson against slums.

São Paulo provides an interesting setting to study arson and urban land conflicts for three main reasons. First, as in other cities in the developing world, São Paulo has had many cases of fires reportedly intended to remove slums (Mahmud, 2016; Rahman, 2001; Malhotra, 2018; Ockey, 1997). 4 These events gained such proportion that an inquiry commission was instituted by the city council. Although hard proof of wrongdoings is scarce, there is suggestive evidence that a large share of slum fires in the city are caused by arson (Bruno, 2010). 5 Second, the city has slums on both private and public lands spread across several neighborhoods with varying land prices. Finally, there is rich data available for a long period of time—a rarity when studying slums.

The main hypotheses to be tested are derived from a dynamic framework inspired by classical models of real estate development (Capozza and Sick, 1994). In my context, I show that landowners decide whether to set fire to slums based on whether land value exceeds a critical threshold. When it is sufficiently high, it becomes optimal for the landowner to burn the slum and proceed with development, rather than waiting for legal institutions to remove the occupants. Conversely, when land value is below this threshold, delaying action and relying on legal mechanisms is preferred. This model predicts that the relationship between arson and land value is not only positive but also non-linear, featuring a discontinuous jump in the likelihood of arson once land value crosses the critical threshold.

3 In Hoboken, for instance, rent control in a rapidly gentrifying area drove strong incentives for landlords to displace tenants, renovate units, and rent at a higher price afterwards.

4 For a more complete documentation of episodes covered in media articles, please refer to the Appendix. 5 Bruno (2010) shows that 30 % of slum fires in São Paulo in the beginning of the 2000’s were caused by arson, although there is no data on the motivation behind these cases.

2 Journal of Public Economics 248 (2025) 105436 Such behavior should be mostly driven by private landowners because they can retain all the value from removing the slum. If the land is public, there are some detracting factors. First, removing slums from government land could be interpreted as a publicly provided urban amenity for neighboring property owners, since it may positively affect house prices (Shah, 2014). In such case, there is a classical coordination problem resulting in under-provision of removals. Second, there can be reputational costs for incumbent authorities, since people tend to blame them for not preventing fires. Finally, governments are often required to provide aid to displaced victims of fires.

I design two empirical exercises to investigate these theoretical results. In both cases, the main challenge arises from not observing arson directly, but rather slum fires in general. This type of measurement error can lead to omitted variable bias if slums with higher land value are also closer to jobs and amenities, drawing more residents and being subject to more domestic accidents involving fire, for instance.

First, I explore cross-sectional variation in slum land value to test whether the probability of arson increases non-linearly. I run a linear probability model to compare the yearly incidence of fire for slums in different quantiles of land value and across private and public lands. I rely on multiple features to mitigate potential omitted variable bias: (i) several controls for observable characteristics related to land value and fire hazard, such as slum density and infrastructure; (ii) district-year fixed effects to compare slums in similar locations; (iii) the fact that slums were built decades prior to current land price dynamics, which should limit sorting; (iv) the interaction of land value with private/public land ownership is exogenous to fires.

I find that the probability of fire increases discontinuously for slums in the highest quantiles of land value. However, the effect only exists for slums on private land. There is no evidence of strategic arson on public land.

I then run a Difference-in-Differences to provide more robustness to these findings. The estimated effect is more localized than in the cross-sectional analysis, but there is a clearer causal interpretation. I leverage a plausibly exogenous shock to land values caused by a large urban renovation program in São Paulo. Starting in 2004, the municipal government designated a specific area to receive large investments in urban infrastructure. To raise funds, it auctioned permits for developers to build above zoning restrictions in that area. The perspective of better urban amenities coupled with the possibility of constructing taller buildings attracted development, causing demand for land to increase, as well as land value.

I use the locations of slums relative to the intervention area to categorize their exposure to the shock. I then compare the probability of fire across more and less exposed slums before and after the intervention. I also compare outcomes for slums on private and public lands, expecting the effect to be driven mainly by the former.

Again, I find effects consistent with strategic arson. The probability of fire increases substantially for slums within the intervention area— but only when they are located on private land. This result is robust to the inclusion of various control variables, slum and year fixed effects, and alternative restrictions on the sample period and size.

Besides pointing to the same conclusion, results from the Differencein-Differences and the cross-sectional approaches are consistent with each other. The shock caused by the intervention to exposed slums is sufficient to move them across the theoretical land value threshold that makes strategic arson profitable, as estimated in the cross-sectional model.

Finding evidence of strategic arson to force slum removal contributes to the growing literature about land conflict and weak enforcement of property rights (Alston et al., 2000, 2012; Fetzer and Marden, 2017).

I document that urban land conflicts can also become violent, but the outcome is different from what we observe in rural or remote areas of developing countries.

Additionally, I contribute to a fundamentally theoretical literature about slum removal. Using fine-grained information on slums, this R. Pucci paper provides a within-city empirical test of the relationship between land value and attempts of eviction (Jimenez, 1985; Turnbull, 2008; Brueckner and Selod, 2009; Shah, 2014; Brueckner et al., 2019).

Moreover, I show both theoretically and empirically that such relationship is likely non-linear due to the dynamic nature of real estate development. Finally, this paper suggests that slum residents face extra—and potentially invisible—costs when the formal city expands towards their neighborhoods. This adds to the conclusions in Henderson et al. (2021), who develop a model to study the transition of neighborhoods from slum to non-slum status. Although we both use an optimal stopping framework, Henderson et al. (2021) are more interested in explaining city growth and how this interacts with informal property rights in slums. I focus on land conflicts that arise before the transition can happen and on how they may become violent.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes institutional factors behind strategic arson in slums and lays out a brief conceptual framework to guide the empirical analysis. Section 3 presents the data. Sections 4 and 5 show the main results of the paper using cross-sectional and Difference-in-Differences analyses, respectively.

Section 6 concludes. 2. Institutional background and conceptual framework 2.1. Land property rights and slum removal Land conflict is common in Brazil and often stems from weak enforcement or contestability of property rights (Alston et al., 2000, 2012; Fetzer and Marden, 2017; Chiavari et al., 2021). This issue arises not only from the state’s limited capacity to resolve disputes but also from convoluted regulations allowing for adverse possession. 6 Although originally designed to support land reform, adverse possession may also lead to judicial uncertainty and promote rather than prevent disputes (Holston, 1991; Gonçalves, 2009).

Lack of land property rights is widespread in Brazilian cities, where slums are built on lands legally owned by other agents, either private or public. 7 In 2000, 31 % of the country’s urban population lived in these informal neighborhoods (UN-Habitat, 2020). In São Paulo, the largest city in the Southern Hemisphere, 10 % of the population lived in slums in 2000 (Schneider et al., 2022; Pasternak, 2006). Most of these slums formed in a context of rapid rural-to-urban migration and restrictive zoning laws around the 1980s. Unable to access formal housing, migrants settled in peripheral areas, building their own homes on land they did not legally own (Rolnik, 1995).

Since informal property rights can be contested by legal landowners, slum residents are constantly vulnerable to removal (eviction), among other economic consequences (Field, 2007; Galiani and Schargrodsky, 2010; Marx et al., 2013). Removals are typically court-mandated and managed by local authorities. These events involve demolishing houses and displacing residents, with no guarantee of government assistance.

Data from Observatório das Remoções (2022) show that between 2017 and 2022, more than half of all slums in São Paulo either had been cleared or faced some risk of removal. 8 Still, slum removal is uncertain, even when the legal landowner has clear property rights. On the one hand, residents might resist eviction, especially if adverse possession is possible or if the removal could hurt 6 In Brazil, adverse possession is regulated by both the Constitution and additional federal laws (Civil, 1988; Brasil, 1981, 2002).

7 Legal ownership over the land is also known as de jure ownership. This is contrasted with de facto ownership, in which the owner may informally possess the land. This would be the case of slum residents. A more detailed explanation about de jure and de facto ownership and its relationship with land conflicts is provided in Alston et al. (2012).

8 Observatório das Remoções (2022) collects both self-reported and official information to try and map slum removals in the city. 3 Journal of Public Economics 248 (2025) 105436 mayors’ electoral outcomes. On the other hand, court decisions can take many years to conclude. 9 According to Observatório das Remoções (2022), only 15 % of slums under risk of removal have actually been removed either completely or partially between 2017 and 2022.

2.2. Real estate value and slum land ownership Land value is an important factor governing the pressure for slum removal. As real estate prices increase, alternative uses for slum-occupied land become more profitable. For instance, the legal landowner could build an apartment complex and rent the units on the land instead of having slum residents living there for free. Such changes in real estate value around slums could be related to gentrification of central areas or even city expansion towards some peripheral neighborhoods (Brueckner and Selod, 2009; Gechter and Tsivanidis, 2018; Henderson et al., 2021).

The influence of real estate value on slum removal likely depends on land ownership, with stronger incentives on private land. Data from Observatório das Remoções (2022) show, for instance, that slums on private land are twice as likely to be removed as those on public land.

Private landowners face an individual decision problem: they must weigh the potential profit from developing the plot after slum eviction against the cost of pursuing the removal (Jimenez, 1985; Hoy and Jimenez, 1991; Brueckner and Selod, 2009; Selod and Tobin, 2018). In contrast, slum removal on public land poses a collective action problem.

While eviction may be viewed as an urban amenity that enhances surrounding property values, the benefits are diffuse among many agents (Shah, 2014). As a result, the classical outcome is under-provision of this public service (slum removal). If some individuals value the removal less than others, there is insufficient pressure for local authorities to act.

The government may also have a direct interest in removing slums, but the gains are unclear. Revenue from selling the land may not benefit mayors or their allies directly. Additionally, there are political risks for incumbents, since evicted slum residents often earn sympathy from the unaffected population. Finally, there can be financial costs, as local regulations sometimes require the government to provide assistance to displaced slum residents.

2.3. Urban land conflicts and strategic arson Conflict may arise when landowners seek slum removal—potentially motivated by rising land values—but face significant obstacles. Since slums are contested territories, disputes can escalate into violence if authorities fail to promote a legal solution (Lombard and Rakodi, 2016).

This has been well documented in rural areas, where landowners and squatters arm themselves and clash over land (Alston et al., 2000; Fetzer and Marden, 2017). In cities, however, strategic arson might be preferred to overt armed conflict due to the stronger presence of formal institutions and law en forcement. Slum houses are often built with highly flammable materials, allowing fires to spread rapidly and making it difficult to determine their exact origin and cause (Braga and Landim, 2008; Walls et al., 2017).

Hence, setting fires to slums may serve as a covert tool to efficiently clear them and make land available for alternative use while leaving little evidence of wrongdoing (D’Andrea, 2012; Ockey, 1997; Rahman, 2001).

A similar reasoning was arguably behind the arson-for-profit events in the US in the 1980s, where landlords would set fires to displace tenants in gentrifying areas (Gottlieb, 2019).

- Discussion about strategic arson in slums is neither new nor specific to Brazil. In New Delhi, a fire devastated a slum while courts were still deliberating on the residents’ eviction (Malhotra, 2018). In Bangkok, Ockey (1997) documents a case where residents caught an 9 Among repossession lawsuits for formal houses in the city of São Paulo, which are supposed to be simpler than those involving slums, 25 % take more than 2 years to be ruled and some even last up to 9 years.

R. Pucci arsonist attempting to ignite a fire in a slum under threat of eviction. Similarly, Rahman (2001) reports at least five instances of arson used to displace squatters in Dhaka in the 1990s.

In Brazil, a large slum in Rio de Janeiro was destroyed by a suspicious fire in 1969. After resisting eviction tied to an urban renewal project, residents were ultimately displaced following the blaze (Brum, 2011). More recently, news reports suggest a similar pattern in São Paulo, where fires in high-value neighborhoods appear to be driven by economic incentives. 10 There is also a strong correlation between fires and slum removals.

Among a sample of 86 slums removed between 2001 and 2016 in São Paulo, 60 % experienced a fire during the same period. 11 Moreover, the probability of slum removal in a given year is seven times higher if the slum experienced a fire that year or in the previous one. Hard evidence on strategic arson, however, is still scarce. For São Paulo, Bruno (2010) estimates that 30 % of slum fires in the early 2000s were deliberately set, but the motivation behind them is unclear.

2.4. Conceptual framework This section provides a brief theoretical framework to motivate the empirical analysis. The main implication is that the probability of arson is positively correlated with land value, but in a non-linear fashion.

It should be higher than zero only for slums located in neighborhoods where land value is above a given threshold. The model builds on Henderson et al. (2021), Capozza and Li (1994), and Capozza and Sick (1994) and its full derivation is presented in Appendix B.

In this context, landowners face a dynamic decision: whether to wait for a court-mandated slum removal or to force it through arson. Courts may rule in favor of eviction, but there is uncertainty regarding the outcome and the duration of trials. Alternatively, burning the slum irreversibly clears the land for alternative use. By committing arson, however, landowners risk being arrested.

Real estate value governs the dynamics of this decision. As prices increase, so does the expected profit of clearing the slum. This means that waiting for a court decision entails an opportunity cost that is potentially growing over time. At sufficiently high prices, the cost of waiting another period can outweigh the risk of committing arson to clear the slum immediately.

Consequently, the probability of arson evolves non-linearly with land value. There is a threshold above which arson becomes profitable, also influenced by institutional factors such as the cost of arson, the likelihood of conviction, the probability of a favorable court ruling, and other legal costs. 12 3. Data and descriptive analysis To test the relationship between land value and the probability of arson, I rely on information about the location of slums, the number of fires in each of them, and some measures of value for the land they occupy. The following subsections provide details about these different pieces of information.

10 Appendix A provides news reports on suspicious slum fires that may have been economically motivated. 11 Observatório das Remoções (2022) contains self-reported observations. I used Google Earth images to verify, for a subsample, whether slum buildings were visibly destroyed.

12 As detailed in Appendix B, arson only becomes an option if the efficiency of courts and the probability of getting caught are sufficiently low. This aligns with the reality in São Paulo, where eviction lawsuits can be lengthy, and arson convictions are rare. Between 2011 and 2016, comparing the number of arson cases under investigation or in court with total fires in the city yields a ratio of less than 10 %. Conversely, Bruno (2010) suggests that 30 % of all fires in the city were caused by arson in the early 2000s.

3.1. Slums The municipal government of São Paulo provides geocoded, cross-sectional data for more than 2000 slums in the city collected between 2001 and 2003. Slums are defined as precarious, spontaneous, and self-constructed settlements with no street planning, no land property rights, poor infrastructure, and low-income families (Prefeitura de São Paulo, 2022). Apart from location, the data also document whether legal land ownership is private, public (government), or unknown.

Approximately 23 % of slums are located on land partially or fully owned by private agents. The remainder belongs to various levels of government or has unknown ownership. The latter category accounts for 10 % of all slums and does not necessarily indicate missing data, as unknown land ownership is relatively common in Brazil. 13 Throughout the paper, I treat these lands as public and include them in the analysis to improve precision. This assumption appears reasonable, as private owners should have stronger incentives to assert their property rights, making it less likely that their land is classified as “unknown”. Nevertheless, I discuss how this category affects results with robustness checks.

Using a spatial merge, I incorporate data from the 2000 Brazilian Census into the slum polygons, including the number of residents and households, income levels, and access to public services. Table 1 provides descriptive statistics at slum level and is split by land ownership status. Census variables should be interpreted as a blend of slum and neighborhood characteristics, because Census Tracts and slum polygons rarely align perfectly. 14 This helps explain the relatively high reported access to public services, for instance.

Table 1 indicates that slums on private and public lands are quite similar on average. Furthermore, Fig. 1 shows that these two types of slums are not clustered, but rather well distributed across the city. It also reveals that few slums are located close to the city center (represented by black triangle).

Despite this geographical distribution, slums are not confined to lowincome regions. Since the 1980s, São Paulo has undergone significant and uneven expansion, with rich households settling in peripheral areas.

As a result, slums often coexist alongside high-income neighborhoods, frequently sharing boundaries. Appendix Fig. C.1 illustrates this pattern, showing that nearly one-fifth of slums in São Paulo are surrounded by a higher-than-average share of high-income households. Moreover, Appendix Fig. C.2 suggests that the city is growing towards some slums in peripheral areas.

13 According to Freitas et al. (2018), ownership cannot be determined for nearly 20 % of the Brazilian territory. 14 To merge Census data with slums, I assign weights proportional to the area of intersection between slums and Census Tracts.

R. Pucci Fig. 1. Spatial distribution of slums in São Paulo in 2001–2003 period and land ownership. Notes: Figure depicts the municipality of São Paulo and its slums categorized by the legal ownership of slum-occupied land. City center is represented by a black triangle. Private includes lands that are entirely or partially owned by private agents. Public includes both lands owned by any level of government and those whose ownership is unknown.

3.2. Fires Data on fires range from 2001 to 2016, comprise the entire state of São Paulo, and were provided by the São Paulo State Fire Department (COBOM-SP). I observe whether the fire happened in a slum or not, as well as a street address. There are no details about size, duration or cause of fires.

Due to changes in recording methodology, the fire department divided the database into three periods: (i) 2001–2006, (ii) 2008–2010, and (iii) 2011–2016. Data for 2007 is entirely missing from the archive.

Additionally, address information is less precise for period (ii), as municipality names are absent. Instead, only district names are available, which are not always unique across municipalities in the state. For (iii), exact street address is often missing, but the fire department posted this information on their social media for almost all slum fires during this interval.

As a consequence, geocoding success rates vary across periods. Appendix Fig. C.3 illustrates this, showing that rates are comparable from 2001 to 2010 (around 10 %), but much higher from 2011 to 2016 (average of 42 %). Although inconvenient, this sort of problem is expected when working with data on informal activities, even when authorities are committed to producing high-quality information.

As long as accuracy issues are not correlated with slum land value, however, this poses little concern. To mitigate potential issues, I include year fixed effects in all specifications. I also run robustness tests restricting the sample period in multiple ways.

Table 2 provides the yearly average number and probability of fires in slums. Overall, slums on private land observe more fires than those on public land. However, the difference is not substantial given the standard deviations.

Moreover, frequency and probability are similar across public and private lands because there are few cases of multiple fires in the same slum within a year. The likelihood of observing two or more fires in any given year in the same slum is ten times lower than the average probability.

3.3. Slum land value Measuring land value in slum-occupied areas is challenging due to data limitations. To overcome this, I rely on proxies derived from formal housing market data, sourced from annual property tax records provided by the municipal government. I infer slum land value by aggregating indirect measures of formal land value within a 500-meter radius around each slum.

I rely on two alternative measures, each with its own advantages and limitations: (i) government-defined property prices per square meter for tax purposes, known as Assessed Values; and (ii) Floor-to-Area Ratio (FAR), which is total floor space divided by total plot area. They are available for all formal residential and non-residential buildings in São Paulo during the entire sample period. A priori, house prices and FAR should correlate well with land value (Brueckner and Singh, 2020; Wen and Goodman, 2013).

Assessed values are estimated by the government based on past market transactions, construction quality, and location parameters. 15 However, these values are subject to political discretion, as they directly influence tax revenues. Mayors, therefore, have incentives to adjust them strategically based on election cycles. Between 2001 and 2016, assessed values remained stagnant for extended periods, followed by abrupt increases driven by fiscal needs rather than market dynamics.

In contrast, FAR is updated incrementally as new floor space is built and it is less susceptible to political influence. It correlates with land value, as scarcer land (higher prices) is used more intensively (higher FAR). However, FAR grows slowly over time and may fail to reflect real estate booms, as seen in São Paulo during the 2010s. Moreover, it rarely decreases during market downturns, since buildings are long-lived and replaced gradually.

In the first part of the paper, I focus on cross-sectional variation within each year and use FAR as a proxy for land value, as it offers a more accurate snapshot of annual differences across locations. Although direct data on market prices are limited, Appendix Table C.1 provides suggestive evidence that FAR is reasonably correlated with housing prices, at least for cross-sectional comparisons.

In the second part, long-term temporal variation is key, and I instead rely on assessed values for two main reasons. First, while political discretion can freeze assessed values in the short run, periodic adjustments help preserve some of their longer-term trends. Second, I take advantage of significant revisions around 2015, which aimed to partially close the gap between assessed and market values.

15 For example, baseline values differ between commercial and residential properties and vary based on construction materials and building typology (e.g., multi-family vs. single-family). Additionally, property values are adjusted for depreciation and other factors.

Combining the data Fig. 2 presents the distribution of slum fires across fifty quantiles of Floor-to-Area Ratio, used as proxy for land value. The number of fires increases with slum land value in a non-linear fashion. While the average number of fires is roughly between 10 and 20 over most of the distribution, it increases sharply in the top quantiles. In particular, the fiftieth quantile is responsible for almost 10 % of all fires in the city.

Although not all fires result from arson, their distribution suggests a discontinuity consistent with strategic arson. Based on Section 2.4, if strategic arson is happening, we should observe a positive probability of arson only after a given land value threshold is exceeded.

The main competing explanation for this pattern is that slums in the top quantiles are disproportionately larger, denser, or have worse infrastructure—all of which could drive a larger number of accidental fires. However, the distributions of variables related to these potential confounders do not follow the same pattern as the fire data. These distributions are smoother, with no clear discontinuities in the top quantiles.

Appendix Fig. C.5 illustrates this, suggesting that the unusual behavior of slum fires in São Paulo is not simply a result of poorer infrastructure or higher density.

This pattern of fires also does not appear to be linked to sorting. Using Census data, I compare the evolution of slum density and infrastructure with land value trends between 2000 and 2010. 4. Cross-sectional approach 4.1. Empirical strategy The first empirical exercise compares the probability of fire across slums with different land values, but otherwise similar observable characteristics. Following predictions from the theoretical model, I test not only whether fires are positively affected by land value, but also whether this effect is non-linear. I explore variation coming from slums in different quantiles of the land value distribution, approximated by FAR. To add another source of identification, I also compare outcomes across slums on private and public lands.

The main challenge is that no direct measure of arson is available. Instead, the data contain all sorts of fires, including those that are accidental and unrelated to strategic arson. If the incidence of these accidents is also correlated with slum land value, this could lead to omitted-variable bias. 17 For example, slums on more expensive land might be denser because residents want to be closer to job opportunities.

This would mechanically increase the probability of fire simply due to more people causing accidents. I address this concern by including variables that account for heterogeneous fire hazards across slums in different quantiles of land value.

Whenever possible, these control variables are split into quantiles to allow for non-linear effects. Hence, identification stems from unconfoundedness conditional on observables. I rely on the assumption that the covariates included in the empirical model account for all factors that cause accidental fires and are correlated with land value.

I also assume there is no sorting of slums with higher probability of fire into higher-value land. The previous section mentioned descriptive evidence corroborating this assumption (in Appendix Fig. C.6).

Additionally, slums in São Paulo were largely built prior to 1990, much earlier than the sample period (2001–2016). Hence, slum settlers likely had limited information on the distribution of future land prices across the city at that time.

Even if covariates are insufficient to fully address these concerns, I leverage the fact that legal ownership of slum land creates plausibly exogenous variation in incentives to forcibly remove slums from highvalue plots. Specifically, I expect slums on private land to be a priori more vulnerable to strategic arson than those on public land. Moreover, land ownership does not seem to be correlated with density or infrastructure, as suggested by Table 1.

Finally, to deal with varying accuracy in the geocoding procedure, as discussed in Section 3.2, not only do I add year fixed effects, but I also calculate the quantiles of land value within each year. This means that almost all of the variation in land value and probability of fire is coming from the cross-section, thus avoiding comparisons of different periods.

On the one hand, such confounding factors would need to be quite specific. Not only would they be uncorrelated with observable characteristics included in the model, but also simultaneously associated with high land value and land ownership. On the other hand, the cross-sectional analysis does not control for slums’ unobservable initial conditions.

To improve identification, I run a Difference-in-Differences strategy leveraging a large shock on land value caused by the Operação Urbana Água Espraiada project in São Paulo. This was an urban renovation initiative focused on improving infrastructure and easing zoning restrictions for a set of neighborhoods still a bit far from the city center. The intervention boosted the demand for land, conceivably causing slums in the area to become more valuable for real estate development purposes.

Fig. 4 shows the location of urban intervention Água Espraiada in São Paulo, occupying approximately 13 square kilometers, or little less than 1 % of the city’s area. The figure also details all slums within a 4-kilometer radius of the intervention. Out of 546 slums in this region, 62 were inside the perimeter of Água Espraiada.

The intervention consisted of a series of public auctions starting in 2004. The municipal government sold permits to developers to build above zoning restrictions inside the intervention zone. 18 Revenue would then be invested in urban improvements in the same zone, such as new bridges and parks, more public transit services, and wider avenues. Fig. 5 shows the evolution of permitted extra floor space following the auctions. The amount of floor space quotas exceeding zoning restrictions by the end of 2016 represented 20 % of the intervention zone’s land area.

This region was not completely under-served prior to the intervention. Previous projects had already expanded its main avenue during the 1990s, removing some slums, and attracting new people to the area. The new urban intervention came after a relatively stagnant period, bringing visible improvements, especially in road quality and public transit (Nobre, 2009). Hence, land value is expected to have increased not only due to higher demand, but also due to better urban infrastructure and amenities.

Local land market demand reacted positively to the intervention. Both building permit requests and FAR increased following 2004. In 2003, the stock of permit requests within the perimeter of Água Espraiada was 50 % lower compared to neighboring areas (within 4 km). Empirical strategy With a Difference-in-Differences model, I explore both the timing of Água Espraiada intervention and the fact that slums inside its perimeter (treated group) were relatively more exposed to the shock in land value than those farther away from it (control group). Because São Paulo is a large city, sampling slums from too far away may compromise comparability. Robustness regarding this threshold is discussed in the next section.

5.3.2. Land value In this section, I provide some evidence that the abnormal increase in the probability of fires is linked to higher land values within the intervention zone. In this analysis, I use assessed values instead of FAR.

Given the importance of temporal variation, FAR may be less suitable because it is persistent, evolves slowly, and may exhibit less variation in more established areas.

To study the impact on land value, I rely on the fact that it reflects expectations about future housing prices—developers base their decisions on anticipated profits from selling new units built on vacant plots.

I therefore use long-term changes in assessed values to infer shifts in land value over time. Focusing on long-term price trajectories also offers two key advantages. First, it mitigates a primary concern with assessed values: their infrequent updates due to political discretion. Second, it allows me to incorporate a major reassessment during the 2013–2016 electoral cycle, when the municipal government adjusted assessed values to bring them closer to market prices. 22 To capture long-term trajectories, I run a two-period Differencein-Differences with IPW, restricting the sample to 2004 (the last pretreatment year) and 2016 (the most recent available year). Results indicate that slums within Água Espraiada experienced a 13 % rise in surrounding property values from 2004 to 2016, signaling that land in the area became more expensive. I find positive estimates for slums on private land, but coefficients are more sensitive to the inclusion of covariates.

Combined with previous findings, these results suggest that land value increased across the board, but only slums on private land faced a higher probability of fire. This pattern aligns with the idea that incentives for strategic arson are stronger among private landowners.

Finally, these estimates help reconcile the cross-sectional and Difference-in-Differences approaches. The increase in land value driven by the intervention seems large enough to push slums across the threshold implied by the cross-sectional analysis. In particular, shifting the average slum from the 9th to the 10th quantile would require a 6 %–7 % increase in land value, which is close to the estimated effects in Table 6.

6. Conclusion This paper investigates whether land conflicts also arise in urban settings, albeit in a different form. Instead of open confrontations 11 between armed groups, these conflicts may manifest through arson targeting slums as a violent means of displacement.

To overcome challenges such as measurement error and omitted variable bias, I run two empirical exercises: a cross-sectional analysis and a Difference-in-Differences. In both, I show evidence that fires are abnormally more likely to happen in slums with high land value. This effect is exclusive to slums on private land and it does not seem to be driven by accidents. Moreover, both approaches are consistent with each other and with theoretical predictions. The urban intervention studied in the Difference-in-Differences seems to move slum land value across the threshold implied by cross-sectional estimates.

Such findings corroborate the hypothesis that arson might be a violent tool in urban land conflict. These results also highlight the importance of addressing the lack of land property rights in slums. As is the case in rural areas, disputes between residents and landowners can escalate to violence if enforcement of land property rights is imperfect.

To compensate for this, governments could take a more active role in increasing the cost of violence, for instance, by pushing to improve slums’ infrastructure and land ownership status. Moreover, part of this issue might also be mitigated by policies that reduce the creation of new slums.

Theoretical model B.1. Basic structure The model focuses on the decision of a landowner who claims ownership of a squatted land plot. I assume that a repossession claim is already running in court and she is now waiting for a decision, which could take years. Uncertainty about the timing of a court ruling and its 12 Journal of Public Economics 248 (2025) 105436 outcome, combined with increasing land value, poses a dynamic tradeoff to the landowner: she can either wait another period for a court decision; or she can cause the slum to burn, anticipating the conclusion of the dispute. By doing this, she either gains control over the land or goes to prison with some probability.

This theoretical approach was originally used to explain landowners’ decisions to develop empty land plots based on housing prices (Capozza and Li, 1994; Capozza and Sick, 1994). The landowner would compare the potential gains from development with those of an outside option, such as a constant agricultural income. As housing becomes more expensive, developing an empty land plot becomes increasingly more attractive. Eventually, prices hit a threshold beyond which it is unequivocally more profitable to develop the plot. When this happens, the landowner irreversibly decides to convert the land plot into a building.

The decision to burn a slum entails some additional features. First, not only does it depend on the value of a reclaimed land plot, but also on how likely the court is to provide a decision on the matter. Second, it also hinges on how likely the decision is to favor the landowner. Third, it depends on the moral and financial costs of committing arson, as well as on the probability of destroying the slum in the process. Finally, waiting for courts imposes legal costs, such as lawyers’ hourly rates for example.

Analogously to the canonical case, in every period of time 𝑡 the agent faces a trade-off between waiting for another period or taking irreversible action to interrupt the slum occupation. Behind this decision is the value of the slum-occupied land 𝑖, 𝑝 𝑖𝑡 , which determines the landowner’s utility, 𝑢(𝑝 𝑖𝑡 ), in case of slum removal.

Price 𝑝 𝑖𝑡 can be more or less relevant depending on whether slumoccupied land is private or public. If it is private, 𝑝 𝑖𝑡 impacts directly what the landowner gains from the eviction. In the case of public lands, 𝑝 𝑖𝑡 might determine the size of the externality generated by slum removal to neighbors. Appendix C. Data details C.1. Formal city growth around slums Fig. C.1 presents the distribution of slums according to the proportion of high-income households living around them. Although most slums are in relatively poor neighborhoods, roughly 20 % of them are in rich areas.

Fig. C.2 shows FAR growth from 2001 to 2016 around slums according to their distance to São Paulo city center (a proxy for the theoretical Central Business Center). Overall, FAR expands across the city, but there is faster growth in some areas far from downtown. This reflects the expansion of the city into more peripheral areas, which could lead to higher land values and pressure to remove slums.

C.2. Geocoding success rates Fig. C.3 presents the number of slum fires in each year, as well as the three breaks in the data. Above each bar, it shows the geocoding success rate for each year. This is given by the number of slum fires successfully geocoded divided by the total number of slum fires in the state of São Paulo, 25 i.e., the total number of slum fires before geocoding the observations.

One concern is that missing municipal names could make geocoding success rates in group (ii) lower than in the others. This, however, does not seem to be the case when comparing groups (i) and (ii). Indeed, the success rate in geocoding is fairly comparable, at around 10 %, from 2001 to 2010.

Conversely, accuracy increases from 2011 through 2016. During this period, exact residential addresses are omitted in the data. However, the fire department systematically posted the locations of slum fires on their social media accounts.

Due to the sparse distribution of new developments, the data are aggregated at district level. D.2. Difference-in-differences D.2.1. Descriptive figures for Água espraiada intervention Fig. D.5 presents how the local housing market reacted to the urban intervention.
